title: From First Line to First Paper
section: Who this book is written for
text:
Who this book is written for
This book makes no assumptions about prior programming experience. Whether you are a public health student opening a coding environment for the first time, a biostatistician moving from SPSS or Stata to Python, or a quantitative researcher who wants to understand every equation and line of code from first principles, each chapter builds step by step without skipping a link in the chain.
By the end of Part VII, you will move beyond Python syntax to work like a disciplined research software engineer and applied machine learning scientist — taking raw epidemiological or clinical datasets through survey cleaning, leakage-free pipelines, PyTorch architectures, systematic ablation studies, subgroup fairness audits, and reproducible research releases.

section: The researcher’s 4-step problem-structuring blueprint
text:
The researcher’s 4-step problem-structuring blueprint
Beginners often freeze at a blank code cell because they try to write Python syntax before designing the logic. Across all 36 chapters, before writing code for any non-trivial problem, we complete four steps:

Inputs and units: What exact values enter the problem, what data types are they, and what units (kg, cm, mmHg, per 100,000) do they carry?
Edge cases and traps: What could silently go wrong — zero denominators, missing survey sentinel codes such as 999, operator precedence mistakes, floating-point truncation, or data leakage?
Step-by-step algorithm: Plain-English ordered steps written before Python.
Verification plan: Hand-calculated or domain-bounded sanity checks proving the output makes scientific sense.

section: 1.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: How Computers Actually Think
text:
1.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: How Computers Actually Think
Before touching a keyboard, let us clear up the biggest myth in programming:

Computers are not intelligent. A computer is an astonishingly fast, 100% literal clerk who follows a checklist one line at a time—and never guesses what you “meant.”







NoteMental Model — The Upazila Clinic Intake Clerk



Imagine a newly hired clerk at a rural Upazila Health Complex who has zero medical background, cannot improvise, and obeys written instructions literally:

If you write: “Measure temperature and write down if it is high,” the clerk freezes—what does “high” mean? Celsius or Fahrenheit? Where should it be written?
If instead you write an unambiguous numbered checklist:

Take the thermometer reading in Celsius (38.5).
Multiply that number by 9, divide by 5, and add 32.
Print the resulting Fahrenheit number on the intake slip.


The clerk executes those three steps accurately ten million times per second without ever getting tired or making an arithmetic slip.
A Python program is simply that exact numbered checklist—written in a tiny, unambiguous language called Python.



1.1.1 Why Python for Statistics, Public Health, and Machine Learning?
You may wonder why researchers worldwide—from WHO epidemiologists to deep learning labs—converged on Python:

Readable Like English: mean_sbp = (124 + 130 + 127) / 3 reads almost identically to a biostatistics notebook.
One Language from First Line to First Paper: Unlike tools that trap you inside point-and-click menus, Python handles raw messy household surveys (Pandas), classical hypothesis tests (SciPy/Statsmodels), gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost), and neural networks on GPUs (PyTorch) in one unified workflow.
Reproducibility: When a peer reviewer asks, “How did you compute your maternal anemia prevalence after excluding missing hemoglobin values?”, a Python script answers with exact mathematical transparency.

text:
1.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: Inside Google Colab & the Python Interpreter
When you open one of this book’s .ipynb notebooks in Google Colab, you are not running code on your laptop’s processor—you are sending Python instructions over the internet to a clean Linux computer hosted by Google (the Colab Runtime).






flowchart TD
    A["1. Your Browser<br/>(Google Colab Code Cell)"] -->|"Press Shift + Enter"| B["2. Python Interpreter<br/>(Checks Grammar / Syntax)"]
    B -->|"Evaluates Line by Line"| C["3. CPU & Working Memory<br/>(Stores Values & Computes Math)"]
    C -->|"Sends Printed Output Back"| D["4. Output Area Below Cell<br/>(Text, Numbers, Tables, or Error)"]


 Chapter 1 visual mental model: Inside Google Colab & the Python Interpreter 



Notice the two distinct checkpoints in that pipeline:

Grammar Check (Syntax Parsing): Before running any line in a cell, Python scans your grammar. If you forgot a closing quotation mark or parenthesis, Python stops immediately with a SyntaxError.
Step-by-Step Execution (Runtime): Once grammar passes, Python executes Line 1, then Line 2, then Line 3 in strict top-to-bottom order. If Line 3 asks Python to divide by zero, Lines 1 and 2 succeed and Line 3 stops with a ZeroDivisionError.







TipResearcher’s Note — Always Save Your Own Copy in Google Drive



When you click any Open in Colab link from this book, Google opens our master read-only copy. Always click File \(\rightarrow\) Save a copy in Drive immediately so every note, edit, and solved exercise stays safely inside your personal Google Drive folder.

section: 1.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
text:
1.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_01_python_foundations/ch01_first_program/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Colab and run each cell alongside the line-by-line dissections below.

1.3.1 Your Very First print() Statements & Comments
# Lines starting with '#' are comments — ignored by Python.
print("Upazila Health Complex — Morning Triage Started")
print("Patients waiting in queue:", 14)
Expected Output:
Upazila Health Complex — Morning Triage Started
Patients waiting in queue: 14
Line-by-Line Dissection:








Line
Code Element
What Python Does Internally




1
# Lines starting with '#' ...
Sees # and skips everything to the end of the line. Comments explain why to future humans (especially your future self six months later!).


2
print(...)
Calls Python’s built-in function print, which displays whatever sits inside its parentheses (...) onto the screen.


2
"Upazila Health Complex ..."
Quotation marks tell Python: “Treat these characters literally as text (a string, or str), not as Python commands.”


3
"Patients waiting in queue:", 14
A comma inside print() lets you pass multiple items (here, a text string and the whole number 14). Python automatically inserts one clean space between them.






1.3.2 Python as a Scientific & Epidemiological Calculator
Every quantitative researcher needs exact command over Python’s seven arithmetic operators:
# Basic arithmetic operators in Python
print("Addition (+):", 120 + 45)
print("Subtraction (-):", 120 - 45)
print("Multiplication (*):", 14 * 3)
print("True Division (/):", 10 / 4)       # Always returns float: 2.5
print("Floor Division (//):", 10 // 4)    # Whole groups only: 2
print("Remainder / Modulo (%):", 10 % 4)  # Leftover after packing: 2
print("Exponentiation (**):", 1.65 ** 2)  # Height squared for BMI: 2.7225
Expected Output:
Addition (+): 165
Subtraction (-): 75
Multiplication (*): 42
True Division (/): 2.5
Floor Division (//): 2
Remainder / Modulo (%): 2
Exponentiation (**): 2.7225
Let us zoom in on the three operators that surprise beginners most:

True Division (/) vs. Floor Division (//):

10 / 4 gives 2.5 (a decimal number, called a float). Even 8 / 2 gives 4.0!
10 // 4 asks: “How many complete groups of 4 fit inside 10?” Answer: 2 (an exact whole number, called an int). Think of packing vaccine vials into 24-vial cold boxes.

Modulo / Remainder (%):

10 % 4 asks: “After removing those complete groups of 4, how many items are left over?” Since \(2 \times 4 = 8\), the leftover is \(10 - 8 = 2\).
Golden Packing Invariant: For any positive integers \(a\) and \(b\), (a // b) * b + (a % b) == a.

Exponentiation (**), NOT ^:

To square height (\(1.65^2\)) for Body Mass Index, write 1.65 ** 2.
Never write 1.65 ^ 2—in Python, ^ is a completely different operator (bitwise XOR) that will crash on decimals and give wrong answers on integers!





1.3.3 Operator Precedence: Why Parentheses Save Lives in Biostatistics
Python follows standard mathematical PEMDAS order: Parentheses \(\rightarrow\) Exponents (**) \(\rightarrow\) Multiplication / Division (*, /, //, %) \(\rightarrow\) Addition / Subtraction (+, -).
Run this experiment in Cell 3 of 01_walkthrough.ipynb:
# Operator precedence: Why parentheses save lives in biostatistics!
wrong_mean = 120 + 130 + 140 / 3
right_mean = (120 + 130 + 140) / 3

print("Without parentheses (BUG!):", wrong_mean)
print("With parentheses (CORRECT):", right_mean)
Expected Output:
Without parentheses (BUG!): 296.6666666666667
With parentheses (CORRECT): 130.0






WarningCommon Trap — Silent Logic Bugs



Notice that wrong_mean = 120 + 130 + 140 / 3 did not produce a red error! Python happily calculated 140 / 3 = 46.67 first, then added 120 + 130 + 46.67 = 296.67—claiming the average systolic blood pressure of three normotensive adults is a fatal 296.7 mmHg!
Researcher’s Rule: Whenever you divide a sum, multiply a rate, or convert units, use explicit parentheses even when you think you know the precedence rule. Clarity beats cleverness every single time.





1.3.4 Break It On Purpose! (Error Anatomy Lab)
Beginners often treat red Python error boxes as a personal failure. Senior researchers treat them as free diagnostic reports. Let us trigger three classic errors deliberately so you can dissect how to read them from the bottom line upward.






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — NameError



print(Dhaka)
Python’s Traceback:
NameError: name 'Dhaka' is not defined
Diagnosis: Because Dhaka has no quotation marks around it, Python assumes Dhaka is the name of a stored variable—looks in memory, finds nothing, and tells you so.
Fix: Wrap text in quotes: print("Dhaka").








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — TypeError



print("Fever temperature: " + 38.5)
Python’s Traceback:
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "float") to str
Diagnosis: The + symbol glues two strings together ("A" + "B") OR adds two numbers (1 + 2), but refuses to glue a string and a float directly.
Fix: Pass separate arguments with a comma (print("Fever temperature:", 38.5)) or use an f-string (print(f"Fever temperature: {38.5}")).








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ZeroDivisionError



cases = 12
population = 0
rate = (cases / population) * 100000
Python’s Traceback:
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
Diagnosis: In epidemiology, missing or unpopulated catchment records sometimes enter datasets as 0. Dividing by zero is mathematically undefined, so Python halts cleanly rather than silently inventing a bogus incidence rate. (In Chapter 4 and Chapter 10, we will guard against this defensively!)

section: 1.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
text:
1.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Let us apply our signature 4-Step Problem-Structuring Blueprint to a realistic clinical intake task before writing code.
Scenario: A nurse at an Upazila clinic enters a patient’s ID ("UHC-0001"), weight (58.4 kg), height (160.0 cm), and body temperature (38.6 °C). Print a structured intake card showing Body Mass Index (\(\text{kg/m}^2\), rounded to 2 decimals) and temperature in both Celsius and Fahrenheit (rounded to 1 decimal).

1.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Inputs & Units:

patient_id = "UHC-0001" (str)
weight_kg = 58.4 (float, kilograms)
height_cm = 160.0 (float, centimeters — notice the unit!)
temp_c = 38.6 (float, degrees Celsius)

Edge Cases & Traps:

Unit Trap: BMI requires height in meters, not centimeters! Forgetting to divide height_cm / 100 produces an absurd BMI of 0.0023.
Exponent Trap: Square meters using height_m ** 2, not height_m * 2.
Precedence Trap: Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit as (temp_c * 9 / 5) + 32.

Step-by-Step Algorithm:

Convert height_cm to height_m by dividing by 100.
Compute bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_m ** 2), 2).
Compute temp_f = round((temp_c * 9 / 5) + 32, 1).
Print a clean, aligned intake card using f-strings.

Verification Plan (Hand Check):

\(160\text{ cm} = 1.60\text{ m}\); \(1.60^2 = 2.56\); \(58.4 / 2.56 = 22.8125 \approx 22.81\) (healthy adult range: 18.5–24.9).
\(38.6 \times 1.8 + 32 = 69.48 + 32 = 101.48 \approx 101.5^\circ\text{F}\) (consistent with mild-to-moderate fever).




1.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
# Step 1: Inputs (documented with explicit units!)
patient_id = "UHC-0001"
weight_kg = 58.4
height_cm = 160.0
temp_c = 38.6

# Step 2: Algorithm (convert cm -> m, compute BMI, convert C -> F)
height_m = height_cm / 100
bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_m ** 2), 2)
temp_f = round((temp_c * 9 / 5) + 32, 1)

# Step 3: Clean Structured Output
print("=== COMMUNITY CLINIC INTAKE CARD ===")
print(f"Patient ID : {patient_id}")
print(f"BMI        : {bmi} kg/m^2")
print(f"Temperature: {temp_c} C ({temp_f} F)")
Output:
=== COMMUNITY CLINIC INTAKE CARD ===
Patient ID : UHC-0001
BMI        : 22.81 kg/m^2
Temperature: 38.6 C (101.5 F)
Notice how writing the unit directly inside the variable name (weight_kg, height_cm, height_m, temp_c, temp_f) makes unit-mismatch bugs immediately visible to the human eye. This is a lifelong research software engineering habit.

1.7.1 Exam Task 1.1 (30 Points): Pediatric ORS Supply & Carton Logistics
A community clinic projects 140 pediatric diarrhea patients this week, each requiring 3 Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) packets, plus a 15% emergency safety buffer (* 1.15). Each shipping carton holds 50 packets. Compute:

base_packets (int)
total_packets (int, computed with round(base_packets * buffer_multiplier) to avoid binary float truncation)
full_cartons (int) and extra_packets (int)



1.7.2 Exam Task 1.2 (35 Points): Maternal Health Clinic Summary Card
Out of 320 registered mothers in Q1, 218 completed 4+ antenatal visits and 96 tested positive for maternal anemia. Compute:

anc_coverage_pct (rounded to 1 decimal)
anemia_prevalence_pct (rounded to 1 decimal)
summary_line: exact formatted report "ANC 4+ Coverage: 68.1% | Anemia Prevalence: 30.0%" generated dynamically using an f-string.



1.7.3 Exam Task 1.3 (35 Points): Rural vs. Urban Case Fatality Rate Disparity
Surveillance reports record 450 rural cases with 9 deaths, and 600 urban cases with 6 deaths. Compute:

cfr_rural_pct: \(\left(\frac{9}{450}\right) \times 100\)
cfr_urban_pct: \(\left(\frac{6}{600}\right) \times 100\)
cfr_ratio: cfr_rural_pct / cfr_urban_pct

text:
1.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

1.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

15 // 4 is 3; 15 % 4 is 3 (check: \(3 \times 4 + 3 = 15\)).
float (4.0) — true division / always returns a float.
NameError: name 'Chattogram' is not defined.
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str.
10 + 20 * 3 = 70; (10 + 20) * 3 = 90.
3 ** 2 = 9. In Python, ^ is bitwise XOR (3 ^ 2 == 1!), not exponentiation.
After Line 1: cases = 40. After Line 2: cases = 55. After Line 3: cases = 55, double_cases = 110.
Python evaluates (70 / 1.75) * 1.75 = 70.0 (division and multiplication execute left-to-right)! It must be 70 / (1.75 ** 2) or 70 / (1.75 * 1.75).
Encoding the unit (_cm) prevents silent cm-vs-meter errors during data cleaning and modeling.
Shared links are read-only; saving a copy to your Google Drive preserves your work permanently.



1.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)

1.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 1 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
# Exam Task 1.1 (30 pts)
patients = 140
packets_per_patient = 3
buffer_multiplier = 1.15
carton_size = 50
base_packets = patients * packets_per_patient           # 420
total_packets = round(base_packets * buffer_multiplier) # 483
full_cartons = total_packets // carton_size             # 9
extra_packets = total_packets % carton_size             # 33

# Exam Task 1.2 (35 pts)
total_mothers = 320
anc_4plus = 218
anemic_count = 96
anc_coverage_pct = round((anc_4plus / total_mothers) * 100, 1)       # 68.1
anemia_prevalence_pct = round((anemic_count / total_mothers) * 100, 1) # 30%
summary_line = (
    f"ANC 4+ Coverage: {anc_coverage_pct}% | "
    f"Anemia Prevalence: {anemia_prevalence_pct}%"
)

# Exam Task 1.3 (35 pts)
rural_cases, rural_deaths = 450, 9
urban_cases, urban_deaths = 600, 6
cfr_rural_pct = (rural_deaths / rural_cases) * 100      # 2.0
cfr_urban_pct = (urban_deaths / urban_cases) * 100      # 1.0
cfr_ratio = cfr_rural_pct / cfr_urban_pct               # 2.0


1.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 1 Failure Modes

The Famous IEEE-754 Binary Float Trap (int(420 * 1.15) == 482!): Because computers store decimals in base-2 binary, 420 * 1.15 evaluates internally to 482.99999999999994. Calling int(...) chops off everything after the decimal point and drops a packet (482), whereas round(...) properly rounds to 483. We will unpack binary floating-point representation deeply in Chapter 2.
Hardcoding Numbers Inside Summary Strings: Typing "ANC 4+ Coverage: 68.1%" manually instead of using {anc_coverage_pct} defeats the entire purpose of reproducible research—the next time Q2 clinic counts arrive, your printed report will silently contradict your data.
Inverting Epidemiological Ratios: Writing cfr_urban_pct / cfr_rural_pct yields 0.5 instead of 2.0. Always label which group is your reference (denominator) group—an essential habit we carry directly into logistic regression odds ratios in Chapter 20 and Chapter 23.

title: 2  Variables, Memory Models, Data Types, and Arithmetic Logic
section: 2.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Sticky-Note Name Tags, Not Storage Boxes
text:
2.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Sticky-Note Name Tags, Not Storage Boxes
Many introductory books tell beginners: “A variable is a box that holds a value.” That analogy feels cozy on Day 1—and then breaks painfully in Chapter 7 (when two list names point to the same patient list!) and Chapter 28 (when PyTorch tensors share GPU memory).
Let us learn the true Python mental model from Day 1.






NoteMental Model — Hospital Sample Tubes & Sticky-Note Labels



Picture a busy clinical laboratory shelf holding sealed sample tubes (Objects in Memory). Every tube has three permanent traits stamped on it the moment it is created:

A Type (e.g., int, float, str, bool) — what kind of specimen it is.
A Value (e.g., 1000, 10.6, "UHC-0042", True) — the data inside.
A Memory Address (id) — its exact physical slot on the shelf.

When you write cases = 1000, Python does not stuff 1000 into a box named cases. Instead, Python creates an int object holding 1000 on the memory shelf and attaches a sticky-note name tag labeled cases pointing to that object.
When you later write cases = cases + 250, Python computes a brand-new int object (1250) in a new memory slot, peels the cases sticky note off 1000, and sticks it onto 1250!



2.1.1 Variable Naming Rules & Researcher Hygiene
Python enforces four strict grammar rules for variable names:

May contain only letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9), and underscores (_).
Cannot start with a digit (visit_2 is valid; 2nd_visit triggers a SyntaxError).
No spaces (patient_age is valid; patient age is invalid).
Cannot reuse Python reserved keywords (such as if, for, class, return, True, None).

Beyond what Python requires, disciplined researchers follow PEP 8 snake_case + explicit units:








Poor Name
Disciplined Researcher Name
Why It Matters




w = 62.0
weight_kg = 62.0
Prevents kilograms-vs-pounds confusion.


h = 165
height_cm = 165
Immediately alerts you to divide by 100 for BMI.


f = True
has_fever = True
has_ / is_ prefixes scream “this is a bool!”


x1 = 10.4
maternal_hb_g_dl = 10.4
Self-documenting six months later during peer review.

2.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: Object Creation & Rebinding in Memory
Watch what happens inside memory across two lines of Python code:
cases = 1000
cases = cases + 250






flowchart LR
    subgraph Names["Name Tags (Namespace)"]
        N1["cases"]
    end
    subgraph Memory["Python Object Memory"]
        O1["Object A (old)<br/>type: int | val: 1000"]

 Chapter 2 visual mental model: Object Creation & Rebinding in Memory 



Notice the crucial direction of =: in mathematics, \(x = x + 1\) is impossible. In Python, = is NOT mathematical equality—it is the assignment (binding) arrow:

Golden Rule of Assignment: Python always evaluates the entire right-hand side first to produce an object, and then attaches the left-hand side name tag to that resulting object.

section: 2.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
text:
2.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_01_python_foundations/ch02_variables_types/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Colab and run every cell alongside the dissections below.

2.3.1 Proving Rebinding with id()
# A variable is a name tag attached to an object in memory
cases = 1000
print("Initial value:", cases, "| Memory ID:", id(cases))

# Rebinding attaches the tag 'cases' to a BRAND NEW integer object (1250)
cases = cases + 250
print("Updated value:", cases, "| Memory ID:", id(cases))
When you run this in Colab, you will see two completely different Memory IDs—direct experimental proof that cases moved to a brand-new int object (1250) rather than mutating 1000 in place!



2.3.2 The Four Core Primitive Types + None
Every piece of clinical, demographic, or statistical data you will work with starts as one of five foundational Python types:
patient_id = "UHC-0042"    # str  (text)
age_years = 29             # int  (exact whole number)
hb_g_dl = 10.6             # float (decimal measurement)
is_anemic = hb_g_dl < 11.0 # bool (True or False)
follow_up_date = None      # NoneType (explicitly missing / not recorded)

print(patient_id,     "->", type(patient_id))
print(age_years,      "->", type(age_years))
print(hb_g_dl,        "->", type(hb_g_dl))
print(is_anemic,      "->", type(is_anemic))
print(follow_up_date, "->", type(follow_up_date))
Expected Output:
UHC-0042 -> <class 'str'>
29 -> <class 'int'>
10.6 -> <class 'float'>
True -> <class 'bool'>
None -> <class 'NoneType'>






TipResearcher’s Note — Why None Matters in Biostatistics



Never store a missing lab measurement as 0! A patient with hb_g_dl = 0 is clinically dead—and including 0 in an average hemoglobin calculation will severely bias your entire study downward. In pure Python, None explicitly represents “no value recorded.” (In Part IV, Pandas extends this idea with NaN.)





2.3.3 Augmented Assignment & Execution Trace Tables
Updating a running total—such as vaccine vials in stock or cumulative outbreak cases—happens constantly in code. Python provides shorthand augmented assignment operators:



Shorthand
Exact Meaning
Clinic Example




x += 5
x = x + 5
waiting_patients += 5


x -= 3
x = x - 3
vaccine_stock -= 85


x *= 2
x = x * 2
buffer_dose *= 1.15


x /= 4
x = x / 4
total_sbp /= 3



vaccine_stock = 500
vaccine_stock -= 85   # 85 doses administered in morning clinic -> 415
vaccine_stock += 200  # District cold-chain resupply arrives    -> 615
print("End-of-day vaccine doses:", vaccine_stock)
Execution Trace Table (Step-by-Step State):









Step
Executed Statement
vaccine_stock Before
vaccine_stock After

vaccine_stock = 500
(unbound)
500


2
vaccine_stock -= 85
500

3

2.3.4 Explicit Type Conversion (Casting Messy Survey Strings)
When you read raw text files, web forms, or CSV exports from DHS/MICS surveys, every field arrives as a string (str)—even ages and blood pressures ("34", "38.5", "24.0"). Before doing math, you must explicitly cast them:
# Raw CSV rows always arrive as strings!
raw_age = "34"
raw_temp = "38.5"
raw_months = "24.0"

age_int = int(raw_age)
temp_float = float(raw_temp)
months_int = int(float(raw_months))  # Two-step idiom for decimal-strings!

print(age_int, type(age_int))
print(temp_float, type(temp_float))
print(months_int, type(months_int))
Expected Output:
34 <class 'int'>
38.5 <class 'float'>
24 <class 'int'>






WarningCommon Trap — int(‘24.0’) Crashes, and int(3.9) Does NOT Round!



Two casting traps catch almost every beginner:

int("24.0") raises ValueError: Python’s int() expects pure whole-number digits when given a string. Whenever SPSS, Stata, or Pandas exports integer counts with a .0 suffix ("24.0"), always chain int(float(raw_months)).
int(3.9) evaluates to 3, NOT 4: int() truncates toward zero—it violently chops off everything after the decimal point. Always use round(3.9) when you want nearest-integer rounding!






2.3.5 Solving Chapter 1’s Mystery: Binary Floating-Point Precision
Remember the surprise in Chapter 1’s Coding Exam where 420 * 1.15 evaluated to 482.99999999999994? Here is the exact mathematical reason—and it takes just 60 seconds to understand permanently.
In base-10 (human decimal math), the fraction \(\frac{1}{3}\) cannot be written finitely: \(0.3333333\ldots\) repeats forever. Computers do not count in base-10; their transistors only have two states (0 and 1, base-2 binary). In base-2, simple base-10 decimals like \(0.1 = \frac{1}{10}\) and \(1.15 = \frac{23}{20}\) are repeating infinite binary fractions! Under the universal IEEE-754 64-bit floating-point standard, Python stores the closest 53-bit binary approximation.
Run Cell 5 of 01_walkthrough.ipynb to see this live:
import math

print("0.1 + 0.2      =", 0.1 + 0.2)
print("0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ->", (0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3)
print("math.isclose()   ->", math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

# Paying off Chapter 1's ORS supply mystery:
print("420 * 1.15       =", 420 * 1.15)
print("int(420 * 1.15)  =", int(420 * 1.15), "  <-- chops decimal!")
print("round(420 * 1.15)=", round(420 * 1.15), " <-- nearest integer!")
Expected Output:
0.1 + 0.2      = 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 -> False
math.isclose()   -> True
420 * 1.15       = 482.99999999999994
int(420 * 1.15)  = 482   <-- chops decimal!
round(420 * 1.15)= 483  <-- exact nearest integer!






TipResearcher’s Rule — Never Compare Floats with ==



Across statistics, econometrics, and deep learning tests, never write a == b on floats. Always use math.isclose(a, b) (or np.isclose(a, b) in Part IV), which checks whether two decimals agree within tiny numerical tolerance (default relative tolerance \(10^{-9}\)).





2.3.6 Break It On Purpose! (Type & Casting Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — ValueError on Decimal String



months = int("24.0")
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '24.0'
Diagnosis: int() received the right type (str), so it is not a TypeError—but the value inside the string contains a dot ., which is not a base-10 integer digit.
Fix: Convert through float() first: months = int(float("24.0")).








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — ValueError on Survey Missing Text



hb = float("N/A")
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'N/A'
Diagnosis: Real public health CSVs routinely encode missing lab readings as "N/A", ".", or "unknown". Calling float() directly crashes cleanly rather than inventing a fake number. (In Chapters 4 and 10, we will detect "N/A" and convert it safely to None!)








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — TypeError on Uncast Comparison



raw_temp = "38.5"
has_fever = raw_temp >= 38.0
Python’s Traceback:
TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'float'
Diagnosis: Python refuses to ask whether a text string "38.5" is greater than the number 38.0—saving you from subtle alphabetical sorting bugs (where "9.0" > "38.5" would be True as text because '9' comes after '3'!).
Fix: Cast first: has_fever = float(raw_temp) >= 38.0.

section: 2.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
text:
2.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: A community health worker’s mobile form submits a single patient intake row where every field arrives as raw text: raw_weight_kg = "64.5", raw_height_cm = "168", raw_hb = "10.4", raw_temp_c = "38.2". Parse all values into proper numeric types, compute BMI (rounded to 2 decimals), flag fever (\(\ge 38.0^\circ\text{C}\)) and maternal anemia (\(< 11.0\text{ g/dL}\)) as booleans, and set needs_priority_review to True if either condition is triggered.

2.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Inputs & Units: Four raw str fields representing kg, cm, g/dL, and °C.
Edge Cases & Traps:

Comparing uncast strings to thresholds raises TypeError.
Height arrives in centimeters ("168") and must be divided by 100 before squaring.
Use Python’s logical or operator so needs_priority_review is True whenever at least one clinical flag is True.

Step-by-Step Algorithm:

Cast all four raw strings using float(...).
Convert height_cm \(\rightarrow\) height_m = float(raw_height_cm) / 100.
Compute bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_m ** 2), 2).
Compute is_febrile = temp_c >= 38.0, is_anemic = hb_g_dl < 11.0, and needs_priority_review = is_febrile or is_anemic.

Verification Plan (Hand Check):

\(1.68^2 = 2.8224\); \(64.5 / 2.8224 = 22.8528\ldots \approx 22.85\).
\(38.2 \ge 38.0 \Rightarrow \text{True}\); \(10.4 < 11.0 \Rightarrow \text{True}\); \(\text{True or True} \Rightarrow \text{True}\).




2.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
# Step 1: Raw CSV-like string inputs
raw_weight_kg = "64.5"
raw_height_cm = "168"
raw_hb = "10.4"
raw_temp_c = "38.2"

# Step 2: Explicit type normalization & unit conversion
weight_kg = float(raw_weight_kg)
height_m = float(raw_height_cm) / 100
hb_g_dl = float(raw_hb)
temp_c = float(raw_temp_c)

# Step 3: Derived metrics & boolean clinical screening flags
bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_m ** 2), 2)
is_febrile = temp_c >= 38.0
is_anemic = hb_g_dl < 11.0
needs_priority_review = is_febrile or is_anemic

# Step 4: Clean clinical triage summary
print(f"BMI: {bmi} kg/m^2 | Febrile: {is_febrile} | Anemic: {is_anemic}")
print(f"Priority Review Needed: {needs_priority_review}")
Output:
BMI: 22.85 kg/m^2 | Febrile: True | Anemic: True
Priority Review Needed: True

section: 2.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem
text:
2.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

2.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

b still points to 500! Rebinding a = 600 peels a’s sticky note off 500 and moves it to a new object 600, leaving b untouched on 500.
2nd_dose (starts with a digit) and class (reserved Python keyword) trigger SyntaxError.
type(10 / 2) is <class 'float'> (5.0); type(10 // 2) is <class 'int'> (5).
int(9.99) is 9 (truncation); round(9.99) is 10.
Raises ValueError; fix with int(float("18.0")).
Evaluates to True! Strings compare character-by-character alphabetically ('9' > '3'), so sorting uncast age strings puts a 9-year-old as “older” than a 38-year-old.
100 \(\rightarrow\) 65 \(\rightarrow\) 130 \(\rightarrow\) 140.
0 is a numeric value that silently corrupts means, minimums, and regression models; None explicitly signals missingness.
0.1 and 0.2 are repeating binary fractions in IEEE-754 base-2 (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004); replace == with math.isclose(...).
True is a genuine bool; "True" is a 4-character text str (even "False" is truthy when evaluated as a string!).



2.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import math

# To-Do 2.1
age_int = int("34")          # 34 (int)
hb_float = float("11.8")     # 11.8 (float)
visits_int = int("4")        # 4 (int)

# To-Do 2.2
waiting_patients = 12
waiting_patients += 7        # 19
waiting_patients -= 4        # 15
waiting_patients += 5        # 20

# To-Do 2.3
temp_c, sbp_mmhg, hb_g_dl = 37.2, 146, 10.2
has_fever = temp_c >= 38.0           # False
is_hypertensive = sbp_mmhg >= 140    # True
is_anemic = hb_g_dl < 11.0           # True

# To-Do 2.4
months_int = int(float("24.0"))      # 24 (int)

# To-Do 2.5
dose_a, dose_b, target_dose = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3
exact_eq = (dose_a + dose_b) == target_dose            # False
safe_eq = math.isclose(dose_a + dose_b, target_dose)   # True

# To-Do 2.6
daily_mg = 18.5 * 15 * 3                     # 832.5
exact_tablets = round(daily_mg / 250, 2)     # 3.33
dose_is_float = isinstance(daily_mg, float)  # True


2.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 2 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
# Exam Task 2.1 (30 pts)
weight_kg = float("54.6")                           # 54.6
height_m = float("156.0") / 100                     # 1.56
anc_visits = int(float("4.0"))                      # 4
bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_m ** 2), 2)         # 22.44

# Exam Task 2.2 (35 pts)
population = 250000
total_cases = 0
total_cases += 18
total_cases += 27
total_cases += 34
total_cases += 21                                   # 100
mean_daily_cases = total_cases / 4                  # 25.0
incidence_per_100k = (total_cases / population) * 100000  # 40.0
outbreak_alert = incidence_per_100k >= 35.0         # True

# Exam Task 2.3 (35 pts)
a, b = 45, 105
c, d = 20, 130
odds_exposed = round(a / b, 4)                      # 0.4286
odds_unexposed = round(c / d, 4)                    # 0.1538
odds_ratio = round((a * d) / (b * c), 2)            # 2.79
elevated_risk = odds_ratio > 1.0                    # True


2.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 2 Failure Modes

Missing Denominator Parentheses in the Odds Ratio ((a * d) / b * c): Because / and * share equal precedence and evaluate left-to-right, omitting parentheses around (b * c) multiplies by c instead of dividing—producing an impossible Odds Ratio of 1,114.29 instead of 2.79!
Intermediate Rounding Drift: Computing odds_ratio = round(odds_exposed / odds_unexposed, 2) divides two already-rounded numbers (0.4286 / 0.1538 = 2.7867...). Always compute statistical ratios from full-precision inputs (a * d) / (b * c) and round only once at final presentation.
Confusing Odds with Probability (Risk): In Task 2.3, the risk (prevalence) of anemia in the exposed group is \(\frac{45}{45 + 105} = 0.30\) (30%), whereas the odds of anemia are \(\frac{45}{105} = 0.4286\). Mastering this exact distinction now makes logistic regression coefficients in Chapter 23 effortless!

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Extract structured fields from clinical IDs and barcodes using 0-based indexing, negative indexing, and half-open slicing (s[start:stop]).
Explain string immutability and avoid the two classic beginner traps: trying to mutate a string in place (TypeError) and calling .strip() without reassigning the result.
Clean, normalize, search, split, and reassemble messy health-survey text using chained string methods (.strip(), .replace(), .title(), .upper(), .split(), .join()).
Format numbers, percentages, thousands separators, zero-padded IDs, and aligned console tables cleanly using publication-grade f-strings.
Sanitize and type-cast raw text coming from interactive input() prompts (and explain why automated notebooks simulate input() for reproducibility).
Build end-to-end text-cleaning mini-pipelines that turn dirty field-survey payloads into clean biostatistics summaries.

text:
3.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Laminated Hospital Wristbands
In public health and clinical research, over 70% of your real-world cleaning time happens on text: misspelled district names ("  sylhet_sadar  "), pipe-delimited hospital lab feeds ("PAT_109 | 38.4 C | pos"), structured specimen barcodes ("BD-CTG-2026-0094-MAL"), and blood pressure readings stuck together with a slash ("148/92 mmHg").
Before writing a single string method, anchor two permanent mental rules:






NoteMental Model — The Laminated Clinical Wristband



Picture a sealed, laminated patient wristband printed with a 16-character barcode (BD-DHK-2026-0042). Two physical laws govern every Python str object:

Every Character Has Two Addresses: Counting from the left starts at 0 (not 1!), so the last character sits at len(s) - 1. Counting backwards from the right starts at -1 (-1 is the final character, -2 is second-to-last, and so on).
The Band Is Permanently Laminated (Immutable): Once a str object is created in memory, you can never scratch out or overwrite a single character inside it. If you want to fix a typo or strip spaces, Python prints a brand-new laminated wristband in a new memory slot—and unless you attach a variable name tag (clean = ...) to that new band, it falls straight into the trash!




3.1.1 Why Half-Open Slicing ([start:stop]) Is Brilliant
When slicing s[start:stop], Python includes the character at start and stops right before stop (excluding stop). Mathematicians write this as the half-open interval \([ \text{start}, \text{stop} )\). That single design choice gives you two superpowers:

Instant Length Formula: The length of s[start:stop] is always stop - start (e.g., patient_id[3:6] has exact length \(6 - 3 = 3\) characters: "DHK").
Seamless Adjacent Splits: s[:k] + s[k:] always reconstructs the exact original string s with zero overlap and zero missing characters!

 Chapter 3 visual mental model: Immutable String Transformation Pipeline 



Notice the crucial insight: raw_clinic itself never changes! Each method in the chain returns a brand-new str object, passes it straight to the next method on the right, and clean_clinic = ... binds our new name tag to the final cleaned object.

Open part_01_python_foundations/ch03_strings_input/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Colab and execute every cell alongside the dissections below.

patient_id = "BD-DHK-2026-0042"
print("Length:", len(patient_id))
print("First char [0]:", patient_id[0], "| Last char [-1]:", patient_id[-1])
print("Country [:2]:", patient_id[:2])
print("District [3:6]:", patient_id[3:6])

Expected Output:
Length: 16
First char [0]: B | Last char [-1]: 2
Country [:2]: BD
District [3:6]: DHK
Year [7:11]: 2026
Serial [-4:]: 0042
Notice the two convenient slice shortcuts: omitting start ([:2]) starts from index 0, and omitting stop ([-4:]) slices all the way through the final character!



3.3.2 String Immutability & Method Chaining
raw_clinic = "   dhaka_medical_college   "

# Calling a method WITHOUT reassignment discards the cleaned copy!
raw_clinic.strip()
print("Unchanged raw_clinic:", repr(raw_clinic))

# Capture the new string object with assignment + method chaining
clean_clinic = raw_clinic.strip().replace("_", " ").title()
print("Cleaned clinic:", repr(clean_clinic))
print("Starts with 'Dhaka'?:", clean_clinic.startswith("Dhaka"))
print("Count of 'a':", clean_clinic.lower().count("a"))
Expected Output:
Unchanged raw_clinic: '   dhaka_medical_college   '
Cleaned clinic: 'Dhaka Medical College'
Starts with 'Dhaka'?: True
Count of 'a': 3






TipResearcher’s Tool — Using repr() to Catch Invisible Whitespace



When debugging messy survey text, print("  Dhaka  ") hides trailing spaces visually. Wrapping any string in repr(s) displays explicit quotes and escape characters ('  Dhaka  ', 'line1\n'), exposing invisible whitespace bugs in one second!


Here is your everyday Public Health string-method reference card:








Method / Operator
Purpose
Example




.strip()
Remove leading & trailing whitespace
"  42 \n".strip() \(\rightarrow\) "42"


.upper() / .lower()
Standardize letter casing
"dhk".upper() \(\rightarrow\) "DHK"


.title()
Capitalize first letter of each word
"sylhet sadar".title() \(\rightarrow\) "Sylhet Sadar"


.replace(a, b)
Replace all occurrences of a with b
"38.4 C".replace("C", "") \(\rightarrow\) "38.4 "


.startswith(p) / .endswith(s)
Check prefix or suffix (bool)
"BD-MAL".endswith("MAL") \(\rightarrow\) True


sub in text
Membership test (bool)
"pos" in "ns1_pos" \(\rightarrow\) True


.split(sep)
Split text into a list of tokens
"148/92".split("/") \(\rightarrow\) ["148", "92"]


sep.join(items)
Join strings with delimiter sep
",".join(["A", "B"]) \(\rightarrow\) "A,B"






3.3.3 Splitting Delimited Records & Joining Fields
Hospital lab systems (such as HL7 feeds) frequently separate columns with pipe symbols (|) or semicolons (;) instead of commas. Calling .split("|") breaks one raw row into indexable pieces (parts[0], parts[1], …), and ",".join([...]) reassembles clean string tokens into a standard CSV line:
raw_row = "  PAT-019 | 31 | 10.4 g/dL | positive  "
parts = raw_row.split("|")

pat_id = parts[0].strip()
age = int(parts[1].strip())
hb = float(parts[2].replace("g/dL", "").strip())
status = parts[3].strip().upper()

# Reassemble a clean CSV row with .join()
clean_csv = ",".join([pat_id, str(age), str(hb), status])
print("Clean CSV row:", clean_csv)
Expected Output:
Clean CSV row: PAT-019,31,10.4,POSITIVE
Notice that ",".join(...) requires every item in the list to be a str—that is why we wrap str(age) and str(hb) before joining!



3.3.4 Publication-Grade f-String Formatting
When reporting epidemiological tables or manuscript statistics, raw floating-point prints like 0.02233062330623306 look amateurish. Python f-strings accept a mini-language after a colon : inside {...} to format numbers with journal-grade precision:








Format Specifier
Meaning
Input \(\rightarrow\) Output




:.1f / :.2f
Fixed decimal places
128.467 \(\rightarrow\) 128.5


:,
Thousands comma separator
18450 \(\rightarrow\) 18,450


:.2%
Multiply by \(100\) & append %
0.02233 \(\rightarrow\) 2.23%


:04d
Zero-padded integer (width 4)
42 \(\rightarrow\) 0042


:<14 / :>10
Left- or right-align in fixed width
"Site" \(\rightarrow\) "Site          "



site = "Chattogram"
seq_num = 42
screened = 18450
cases = 412
positivity = cases / screened
mean_sbp = 128.467

print(f"Facility ID : CTG-{seq_num:04d}")
print(f"Screened    : {screened:,} adults")
print(f"Positivity  : {positivity:.2%} ({cases} / {screened:,})")
print(f"Mean SBP    : {mean_sbp:.1f} mmHg")
print(f"{'Site':<14} | {'Screened':>10} | {'Positivity':>10}")
print(f"{site:<14} | {screened:>10,} | {positivity:>10.2%}")
Expected Output:
Facility ID : CTG-0042
Screened    : 18,450 adults
Positivity  : 2.23% (412 / 18,450)
Mean SBP    : 128.5 mmHg
Site           |   Screened | Positivity
Chattogram     |     18,450 |      2.23%






WarningCommon Trap — Never Multiply by 100 When Using :.2%



Python’s % format specifier already multiplies by 100! If positivity = 0.02233, writing {positivity:.2%} gives 2.23%. Writing {positivity * 100:.2%} accidentally multiplies by \(100\) twice and prints 223.31%!





3.3.5 Interactive User Input (input()) & Validation Hygiene
In an interactive Python script or Colab cell, input("Prompt: ") pauses execution, waits for the user to type text and press Enter, and always returns a str—even when the user types 38.4 or 28.
Because interactive input() pauses execution forever in automated research pipelines and cloud notebook runners, disciplined researchers isolate raw input at the top of a cell (or simulate it cleanly during automated testing):
# In an interactive Colab session, you can uncomment the line below:
# raw_temp = input("Enter patient temperature (e.g., 38.4 C): ")

# For reproducible, non-blocking execution, we simulate the user's text:
raw_temp = "  38.4 C  "
print("Raw input type:", type(raw_temp), "| Value:", repr(raw_temp))

temp_c = float(raw_temp.replace("C", "").strip())
has_fever = temp_c >= 38.0
print(f"Parsed Temp: {temp_c:.1f} C | Fever Flag: {has_fever}")
Expected Output:
Raw input type: <class 'str'> | Value: '  38.4 C  '
Parsed Temp: 38.4 C | Fever Flag: True
Golden Rule of User Input: Treat every string returned by input() as untrusted messy text—always .strip() whitespace, strip expected units, and explicitly cast to int or float before arithmetic!



3.3.6 Break It On Purpose! (String Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — IndexError (Off-by-One Indexing)



code = "DHK-042"
last_char = code[7]
Python’s Traceback:
IndexError: string index out of range
Diagnosis: len("DHK-042") is 7, which means valid positive indices run from 0 through 6 (len(code) - 1). Index 7 steps one slot past the end of the string!
Fix: Use negative indexing code[-1] (always the last character, regardless of length) or code[len(code) - 1].








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — TypeError (String Immutability)



patient_id = "uhc-0042"
patient_id[0] = "U"
Python’s Traceback:
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
Diagnosis: Python strings are immutable—you cannot modify individual characters in place.
Fix: Construct a brand-new string via slicing/concatenation (patient_id = "U" + patient_id[1:]) or .upper() (patient_id = patient_id.upper()).








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ValueError on Dirty Unit String



raw_temp = "38.6 C"
temp_c = float(raw_temp)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: could not convert string to float: '38.6 C'
Diagnosis: float() tolerates outer spaces (float(" 38.6 ") succeeds), but crashes on non-numeric unit suffixes like "C", "kg", or "mmHg".
Fix: Strip the unit first: temp_c = float(raw_temp.replace("C", "").strip()).

section: 3.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
text:
3.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: A rural community health worker texts a rapid dengue triage SMS to the district surveillance desk: raw_sms = "  barishal_sadar | 007 | 39.1 C | 112000 /uL  ". The four pipe-delimited fields represent upazila name, patient serial number, body temperature (\(^\circ\text{C}\)), and platelet count (normal \(\ge 150{,}000\text{ /}\mu\text{L}\)). Parse all fields cleanly, generate a zero-padded case ID ("BRS-0007"), evaluate urgent_referral (True if febrile \(\ge 38.0^\circ\text{C}\) and platelets \(< 150{,}000\)), and print a clean two-line clinical alert.

3.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Inputs & Units: One raw str containing 4 |-separated fields: messy text (upazila), zero-padded integer (serial), float with "C" unit (temp_c), and integer with "/uL" unit (platelets).
Edge Cases & Traps:

Leading/trailing spaces inside every token after .split("|").
Unit suffixes ("C", "/uL") will trigger ValueError if not removed before float()/int().
Calling int("007") turns "007" into 7; we must re-pad with :04d to format "BRS-0007".

Step-by-Step Algorithm:

Split raw_sms on "|" into parts.
Clean parts[0] with .strip().replace("_", " ").title().
Parse serial, temp_c, and platelets after removing units and whitespace.
Build case_id = f"BRS-{serial:04d}", compute boolean flags, and print formatted alert lines.

Verification Plan (Hand Check):

upazila \(\rightarrow\) "Barishal Sadar"; case_id \(\rightarrow\) "BRS-0007".
39.1 >= 38.0 (True) and 112000 < 150000 (True) \(\Rightarrow\) urgent_referral = True.
112000 with :, prints "112,000".




3.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
# Step 1: Raw incoming clinic SMS text
raw_sms = "  barishal_sadar | 007 | 39.1 C | 112000 /uL  "

# Step 2: Split on '|' and sanitize each text field
parts = raw_sms.split("|")
upazila = parts[0].strip().replace("_", " ").title()
serial = int(parts[1].strip())
temp_c = float(parts[2].replace("C", "").strip())
platelets = int(parts[3].replace("/uL", "").strip())

# Step 3: Derive clinical triage flags & standardized ID
case_id = f"BRS-{serial:04d}"
is_febrile = temp_c >= 38.0
low_platelets = platelets < 150000
urgent_referral = is_febrile and low_platelets

# Step 4: Format publication-clean clinical alert
print(f"[{case_id}] {upazila} | Temp: {temp_c:.1f} C")
print(f"Platelets: {platelets:,} /uL | Urgent Referral: {urgent_referral}")
Output:
[BRS-0007] Barishal Sadar | Temp: 39.1 C
Platelets: 112,000 /uL | Urgent Referral: True

section: 3.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem
text:
3.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

3.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

len(code) is 7; code[7] raises IndexError because valid positive indices are 0 through 6.
s[0:3] returns "EPI" (length \(3 - 0 = 3\)); s[-4:] returns "LOGY".
Prints '  dhaka  '! Because strings are immutable, city.strip().upper() created a new string and immediately discarded it since it was never reassigned (city = ...).
Fails because str objects are immutable; Python raises TypeError ('str' object does not support item assignment).
serial_str preserves leading zeros ("0042", str); int("0042") drops leading zeros and evaluates to integer 42 (int).
Produces ["148", "92"]—a list of strings (str), not integers! Always cast with int(...) before comparing blood pressures numerically.
f"{rate:.1%}" produces "4.5%". Writing f"{rate * 100:.1%}" multiplies by \(100\) twice and wrongly prints "450.0%"!
Evaluates to "PAT-00019" (:05d pads 19 with three leading zeros to reach an exact total width of 5 digits).
Always returns <class 'str'>—input() never automatically converts text to float or int.
raw = "  malaria_pos  " \(\rightarrow\) clean = "MALARIA_POS" \(\rightarrow\) result = "MALARIA-POS".



3.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)

3.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 3 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
# Exam Task 3.1 (30 pts)
raw_barcode = "  bd-ctg-2026-0094-mal  "
clean_barcode = raw_barcode.strip().upper()  # "BD-CTG-2026-0094-MAL"
tokens = clean_barcode.split("-")

sample_number = int(tokens[3])                         # 94
is_malaria_panel = clean_barcode.endswith("MAL")       # True

# Exam Task 3.2 (35 pts)
raw_payload = (
    "  rahim_uddin ; 45 yrs ; 72.4 kg ; 168.0 cm ; 148/92 mmHg  "
)
fields = raw_payload.split(";")
patient_name = fields[0].strip().replace("_", " ").title()
age_years = int(fields[1].replace("yrs", "").strip())  # 45
weight_kg = float(fields[2].replace("kg", "").strip()) # 72.4
height_m = float(fields[3].replace("cm", "").strip()) / 100
bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_m ** 2), 2)            # 25.65
bp_parts = fields[4].replace("mmHg", "").strip().split("/")
sbp_mmhg, dbp_mmhg = int(bp_parts[0]), int(bp_parts[1])

# Exam Task 3.3 (35 pts)
facility_code, report_seq = "uhc-syl-03", 14
population, confirmed_cases, deaths = 340500, 512, 9
report_id = f"{facility_code.upper()}-R{report_seq:04d}"
incidence_per_100k = round((confirmed_cases / population) * 100000, 2)
cfr_pct_str = f"{deaths / confirmed_cases:.2%}"        # "1.76%"
bulletin_line = (
    f"[{report_id}] Pop={population:,} | "
    f"Cases={confirmed_cases:,} ({incidence_per_100k:.1f}/100k) | "
    f"CFR={cfr_pct_str}"
)


3.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 3 Failure Modes

The Silent Immutability Trap (raw.strip() Without Assignment): Calling raw_district.strip() looks like it should clean raw_district, and Python produces zero error message—yet raw_district stays completely unchanged! Always bind the returned copy (clean_district = raw_district.strip()).
Double-Multiplying Percentages ({rate * 100:.2%}): Because the % format specifier automatically multiplies proportions by \(100\), multiplying by 100 beforehand turns a 1.76% Case Fatality Rate into an impossible 175.78%! Always pass the raw decimal proportion (deaths / confirmed_cases) directly into :.2%.
Hidden Spaces Breaking .endswith() and Exact Matching: Checking raw_barcode.upper().endswith("MAL") before calling .strip() silently returns False because the last two characters are spaces ("  "), not "MAL"! Make .strip() the very first link in every text-cleaning chain.

title: 4  Boolean Logic, Conditionals, and Decision Trees in Code
section: 4.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Clinical Triage Protocols as Boolean Gates
text:
4.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Clinical Triage Protocols as Boolean Gates
Up to Chapter 3, every Python script you wrote ran strictly top-to-bottom—like a single-lane corridor where every single line executes unconditionally. Real medicine and public health never work that way.
When a mother walks into an Upazila Health Complex in Sylhet or Rangpur, a triage nurse does not give every patient the exact same treatment. Instead, the nurse walks down a rapid yes/no decision checklist:

Is hemoglobin missing (None or 999)? \(\rightarrow\) Flag for lab draw immediately.
Is hemoglobin below \(7.0\text{ g/dL}\)? \(\rightarrow\) Severe anemia (urgent referral!).
Otherwise, is it below \(10.0\text{ g/dL}\)? \(\rightarrow\) Moderate anemia.
Otherwise, is it below \(11.0\text{ g/dL}\)? \(\rightarrow\) Mild anemia.
Otherwise? \(\rightarrow\) Normal.







NoteMental Model — Every Branch Asks a Yes/No (Boolean) Question



In Python, a conditional statement (if, elif, else) is a railroad switch controlled by a Boolean expression (True or False).

Boolean expressions are the questions (hb_g_dl < 7.0, sbp_mmhg >= 140 and has_headache).
Indented code blocks (4 spaces after a colon :) are the actions taken only when that specific track is switched open.
In an if / elif / else chain, Python walks top-to-bottom and executes at most one branch—the very first condition that evaluates to True—then jumps straight to the end of the entire chain.




4.1.1 Boolean Truth Tables (and, or, not)
Every compound clinical rule boils down to three logical operators named after 19th-century mathematician George Boole:

A or B (At least one true)
not A (Flip)

4.1.2 Operator Precedence & Python’s Indentation Law
When mixing logical operators in one expression, Python always evaluates in strict priority order:
\[\text{Comparisons } (<, \le, ==, \neq, \ge, >) \;\longrightarrow\; \texttt{not} \;\longrightarrow\; \texttt{and} \;\longrightarrow\; \texttt{or}\]
Just like arithmetic PEMDAS, never force a reader to memorize precedence during clinical triage—wrap compound clauses in explicit parentheses so your scientific intent is unmistakable!

4.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: Clinical Decision Tree Flowchart
Watch how Python evaluates a guarded WHO Maternal Anemia & Triage Decision Tree from top to bottom. Notice how the missing-value guard sits at the very top gate, before any < comparison can touch None or misread 999:






flowchart TD
    S["Start: Receive raw_hb"] --> G{"raw_hb is None<br/>or raw_hb == 999?"}
    G -->|Yes| M["anemia = 'Missing'<br/>(Guard exits early)"]
    G -->|No| A{"raw_hb < 7.0?"}
    A -->|Yes| SEV["anemia = 'Severe'<br/>Triage: Urgent"]
    A -->|No| B{"raw_hb < 10.0?"}
    B -->|Yes| MOD["anemia = 'Moderate'<br/>Triage: Moderate"]
    B -->|No| C{"raw_hb < 11.0?"}
    C -->|Yes| MLD["anemia = 'Mild'<br/>Iron + Follow-up"]
    C -->|No| NRM["anemia = 'Normal'<br/>Routine ANC"]


 Chapter 4 visual mental model: Clinical Decision Tree Flowchart 



Notice the elegance of mutually exclusive elif arrows: the moment Python takes the No arrow out of raw_hb < 7.0, we already know mathematically that raw_hb >= 7.0. Therefore, the next gate only needs to ask raw_hb < 10.0—it automatically captures the exact half-open interval \(7.0 \le \text{Hb} < 10.0\) with zero gaps and zero overlaps!

title: 4  Boolean Logic, Conditionals, and Decision Trees in Code
section: 4.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
text:
4.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_01_python_foundations/ch04_conditionals_logic/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Colab and run every cell alongside the dissections below.

4.3.1 Comparison Operators & Chained Clinical Ranges
Python supports all six relational operators (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=)—and unlike C or Java, Python lets you chain comparisons directly just as you write them in biostatistics papers:
sbp_mmhg = 114
hb_g_dl = 12.2
temp_c = 38.4

# Chained comparisons mirror clinical reference intervals directly
is_normal_bp = 90 <= sbp_mmhg < 120
is_normal_hb = 11.0 <= hb_g_dl <= 16.0
has_fever = temp_c >= 38.0

print("Normal BP:", is_normal_bp)
print("Normal Hb:", is_normal_hb)
print("Has Fever:", has_fever)
Expected Output:
Normal BP: True
Normal Hb: True
Has Fever: True
Under the hood, Python translates 90 <= sbp_mmhg < 120 into (90 <= sbp_mmhg) and (sbp_mmhg < 120)—evaluating sbp_mmhg only once and keeping the clinical interval crystal clear.



4.3.2 Boolean Algebra (and, or, not) & Operator Precedence
In outbreak surveillance, case definitions almost always combine multiple symptoms and vaccination status:
has_fever = True
has_rash = True
is_vaccinated = False

# Precedence: not > and > or (parentheses make clinical intent explicit!)
suspect_measles = has_fever and has_rash and (not is_vaccinated)
needs_isolation = suspect_measles or (has_fever and not is_vaccinated)

print("Suspect measles:", suspect_measles)
print("Needs isolation:", needs_isolation)
Expected Output:
Suspect measles: True
Needs isolation: True






TipResearcher’s Note — Always Write == for Equality, Never =



Remember Chapter 2: a single = assigns a value (age = 30), whereas a double == tests equality (age == 30 \(\rightarrow\) True or False). For checking None, Python best practice uses the identity operator is None or is not None rather than == None.





4.3.3 if / elif / else Clinical Decision Trees & the if vs. elif Bug
Compare these two side-by-side WHO maternal anemia classifiers on a critically ill mother whose hemoglobin is hb_g_dl = 6.4 g/dL:
# Correct WHO maternal anemia severity ladder (mutually exclusive elif)
hb_g_dl = 6.4

if hb_g_dl < 7.0:
    severity = "Severe"
elif hb_g_dl < 10.0:
    severity = "Moderate"
elif hb_g_dl < 11.0:
    severity = "Mild"
else:
    severity = "Normal"

print(f"Hb {hb_g_dl} g/dL -> Correct severity: {severity}")
Expected Output:
Hb 6.4 g/dL -> Correct severity: Severe
Now watch what happens if a hasty programmer writes three separate if statements instead of elif:
# Silent Logic Bug: independent 'if' statements overwrite earlier matches!
hb_g_dl = 6.4
buggy_severity = "Normal"

if hb_g_dl < 7.0:
    buggy_severity = "Severe"
if hb_g_dl < 10.0:
    buggy_severity = "Moderate"
if hb_g_dl < 11.0:
    buggy_severity = "Mild"   # DANGEROUS: overwrites 'Severe' with 'Mild'!

print(f"Hb {hb_g_dl} g/dL -> Buggy severity:   {buggy_severity}")
Expected Output:
Hb 6.4 g/dL -> Buggy severity:   Mild






WarningSilent Clinical Danger — No Error Message, Wrong Diagnosis!



Notice that Python raised zero exceptions in the buggy cell! Because \(6.4 < 7.0\) is True, and \(6.4 < 10.0\) is True, and \(6.4 < 11.0\) is True, every independent if block executed in sequence—silently downgrading a life-threatening Severe anemia case to Mild. Whenever categories are mutually exclusive, always link them with elif.





4.3.4 Short-Circuit Evaluation & Defensive Guard Clauses
Python evaluates and and or lazily from left to right:

In A and B, if A is False, the entire expression can never be True—so Python stops immediately and never evaluates B.
In A or B, if A is True, the entire expression is already True—so Python stops immediately and never evaluates B.

This behavior—called short-circuit evaluation—lets you place a guard condition on the left to protect dangerous operations (like dividing by a possibly zero population or comparing a possibly None lab value) on the right:
# Guard 1: Short-circuit prevents ZeroDivisionError when population == 0
cases = 18
population = 0

high_outbreak = population > 0 and (cases / population) * 100000 >= 50.0
print("High outbreak (safely guarded):", high_outbreak)

# Guard 2: Missing-value guard intercepts BOTH None and DHS sentinel 999
raw_hb = 999
if raw_hb is None or raw_hb == 999:
    hb_label = "Missing"
elif raw_hb < 11.0:
    hb_label = "Anemic"
else:
    hb_label = "Normal"

print("Guarded Hb status:", hb_label)
Expected Output:
High outbreak (safely guarded): False
Guarded Hb status: Missing
Look closely at Guard 2: in real DHS, MICS, and hospital EHR exports, missing laboratory values are frequently coded as numeric sentinels like 999 or -9. If you forget to check raw_hb == 999 first, Python happily evaluates 999 < 11.0 as False and misclassifies a patient who never got a blood test as "Normal"!



4.3.5 Break It On Purpose! (Conditional & Guard Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — TypeError Comparing None to a Number



hb_g_dl = None
is_anemic = hb_g_dl < 11.0
Python’s Traceback:
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'float'
Diagnosis: Unlike ==, Python refuses to order None relative to a float—protecting you from silently treating missing measurements as zero.
Fix: Guard None first: is_anemic = (hb_g_dl is not None) and (hb_g_dl < 11.0).








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — ZeroDivisionError from Reversed Guard Order



cases = 12
population = 0
high_rate = (cases / population) > 0.05 and population > 0
Python’s Traceback:
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
Diagnosis: The author wrote the right guard (population > 0), but placed it on the right side of and! Because Python evaluates left-to-right, cases / population crashed before Python ever reached the guard.
Fix: Always put the guard first: high_rate = population > 0 and (cases / population) > 0.05.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — NameError on Lowercase Boolean



is_eligible = true
Python’s Traceback:
NameError: name 'true' is not defined
Diagnosis: Unlike JavaScript, R (TRUE), or JSON (true), Python’s Boolean literals are strictly capitalized True and False. Writing lowercase true makes Python search for a variable named true.
Fix: Capitalize the first letter: is_eligible = True.

section: 4.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
text:
4.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: Build an automated Upazila Health Complex Maternal Triage Router. Given a pregnant patient’s hemoglobin (hb_g_dl = 6.8), systolic blood pressure (sbp_mmhg = 152), and severe headache symptom (has_headache = True), classify her WHO maternal anemia severity (with a missing-value guard for None or 999), flag potential preeclampsia (sbp_mmhg >= 140 AND has_headache), and route her clinic triage_priority:

"Urgent" if anemia_grade == "Severe" OR sbp_mmhg >= 160 OR preeclampsia_flag
"Moderate" if anemia_grade == "Moderate" OR sbp_mmhg >= 140
"Routine" otherwise


4.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Inputs & Units: hb_g_dl (g/dL, possibly None or 999), sbp_mmhg (mmHg), has_headache (bool).
Edge Cases & Traps:

Guard hb_g_dl is None or hb_g_dl == 999 at the very top of the anemia ladder before < 7.0.
Use mutually exclusive elif branches so "Severe" cannot be overwritten by "Mild".
Test "Urgent" before "Moderate" in the triage router so high-risk red flags always win.

Step-by-Step Algorithm:

Classify anemia_grade via guarded if / elif / else.
Compute preeclampsia_flag = (sbp_mmhg >= 140) and has_headache.
Route triage_priority from most urgent ("Urgent") to least urgent ("Routine").
Print a clean structured triage summary.

Verification Plan (Hand Check):

hb_g_dl = 6.8 < 7.0 \(\Rightarrow\) anemia_grade = "Severe".
sbp_mmhg = 152 >= 140 and has_headache = True \(\Rightarrow\) preeclampsia_flag = True.
Both red flags trigger the first branch \(\Rightarrow\) triage_priority = "Urgent".




4.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
# Step 1: Patient intake readings from Upazila Health Complex
hb_g_dl = 6.8
sbp_mmhg = 152
has_headache = True

# Step 2: Missing-value guard + WHO maternal anemia classification
if hb_g_dl is None or hb_g_dl == 999:
    anemia_grade = "Missing"
elif hb_g_dl < 7.0:
    anemia_grade = "Severe"
elif hb_g_dl < 10.0:
    anemia_grade = "Moderate"
elif hb_g_dl < 11.0:
    anemia_grade = "Mild"
else:
    anemia_grade = "Normal"

# Step 3: Preeclampsia warning & clinic triage routing
preeclampsia_flag = (sbp_mmhg >= 140) and has_headache

if anemia_grade == "Severe" or sbp_mmhg >= 160 or preeclampsia_flag:
    triage_priority = "Urgent"
elif anemia_grade == "Moderate" or sbp_mmhg >= 140:
    triage_priority = "Moderate"
else:
    triage_priority = "Routine"

# Step 4: Structured clinical triage readout
print(f"Anemia: {anemia_grade} | Preeclampsia Flag: {preeclampsia_flag}")
print(f"Upazila Triage Priority: {triage_priority}")
Output:
Anemia: Severe | Preeclampsia Flag: True
Upazila Triage Priority: Urgent

4.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

False—because the right half 120 < 120 is strictly false (120 is equal to 120, not less than it).
True—because and has higher precedence than or, so Python evaluates True or (False and False) \(\rightarrow\) True or False \(\rightarrow\) True.
"Normal"—because the second if is independent (not elif), so 17.2 < 25.0 executes and overwrites "Underweight".

elif raw_hb < 11.0:
    anemia_status = "Anemic"
else:
    anemia_status = "Normal"

if sbp_mmhg >= 160 or (not hb_missing and raw_hb < 7.0):
    triage_priority = "Urgent"
elif sbp_mmhg >= 140 or hb_missing:
    triage_priority = "Moderate"
else:
    triage_priority = "Routine"

# Exam Task 4.2 (35 pts)

else:

    rate_b = round((cases_b / pop_b) * 100000, 2)
    if rate_b >= 50.0:
        alert_b = "Red"

else:

    alert_b = "Data Error"


4.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 4 Failure Modes

Missing Parentheses Around Mixed and / or Clauses (Task 4.1): Writing bmi_category == "Underweight" and anemia_severity == "Severe" or anemia_severity == "Moderate" evaluates as (Underweight and Severe) or Moderate because and binds tighter than or—misclassifying a normal-weight mother with moderate anemia as high-risk malnutrition! Always wrap or clauses in explicit parentheses.
Unreachable Shadowed Branches (Question 8 & Task 4.2): Checking a broad rule (sbp >= 140 or temp_c >= 38.5) above a stricter critical rule (sbp >= 160 or platelets_k < 50) permanently shadows the emergency branch. Always order triage ladders from highest urgency / strictest threshold down to routine.
Late Missing-Value & Zero-Denominator Guards (Task 4.3): Checking cases / pop before pop > 0 triggers ZeroDivisionError, and checking hb < 11.0 before hb is None or hb == 999 either crashes with TypeError or silently turns a missing survey code (999) into a "Normal" lab result. Notice also how repetitive writing Ward A and Ward B twice felt in Task 4.3—in Chapter 5 (Loops) and Chapter 6 (Functions), we will eliminate that repetition forever!

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Iterate cleanly over sequences and integer ranges using for loops and the half-open interval range(start, stop, step).
Implement the 4 Universal Loop Patterns—Accumulator, Counter, Filter, and Running Max/Min—in a single clean pass over clinical data.
Skip DHS missing-value sentinels (999, None) with continue and exit outbreak scans early with break.
Track human-readable 1-based weeks or days alongside values using enumerate(..., start=1).
Model unknown-duration processes—such as epidemic doubling and hospital bed surge capacity—using condition-driven while loops without creating infinite loops.
Build Loop Execution Trace Tables to verify nested loops, catch off-by-one bugs, and prevent TypeError, NameError, and ZeroDivisionError.

section: 5.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: The Triage Conveyor Belt
text:
5.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: The Triage Conveyor Belt
In Chapter 2, you totaled 4 days of dengue cases by writing four copy-pasted lines: total_cases += day_1, += day_2, += day_3, += day_4. That works for 4 days—and collapses completely when your thesis analyzes 365 days of national surveillance across 64 districts or 20,000 mothers in the Bangladesh DHS.
Loops let you write the clinical rule once and instruct Python to apply it faithfully to every patient record automatically.






NoteMental Model — The Hospital Triage Conveyor Belt



Picture two different stations in a district hospital:

The for Loop (Fixed Stack of Patient Charts): A triage nurse receives a finite stack of charts (hb_readings). She picks up Chart 1, checks hemoglobin, updates her clipboard tallies (total_hb, anemic_count), sets it down, and repeats for Chart 2, Chart 3, …, stopping automatically when the stack is empty.
The while Loop (Emergency Ward Bed Monitor): A hospital director watches active dengue admissions climb day by day. She does not know in advance whether beds will run out on Day 6 or Day 14—she simply keeps simulating “as long as occupied_beds <= bed_capacity,” stopping the moment capacity is breached.




5.1.1 Choosing for vs. while








Loop Type
When to Choose It
Public Health Example




for loop
You have a known collection (list of readings) or exact count (range(1, 8)).
Computing clean mean hemoglobin across 500 survey rows.


while loop
You do not know how many steps it will take until a condition becomes False.
Simulating days until epidemic doubling overflows 200 hospital beds.

section: 5.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: The Loop Execution Cycle
text:
5.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: The Loop Execution Cycle
Every loop in Python—whether processing 5 clinic rows or 50 million genomic reads—follows the exact same cyclic execution engine:






flowchart TD
    Init["1. Initialize State<br/>total = 0 | count = 0"]
    Next{"2. Next item left<br/>or condition True?"}
    Body["3. Run Loop Body<br/>Inspect current item"]
    Skip{"Hit continue?"}
    Stop{"Hit break?"}
    Update["4. Update State<br/>total += val | count += 1"]
    Done["5. Loop Finished<br/>Use final state"]

    Init --> Next
    Next -- "Yes" --> Body
    Body --> Skip
    Skip -- "Yes (skip rest)" --> Next
    Skip -- "No" --> Stop
    Stop -- "Yes (exit early)" --> Done
    Stop -- "No" --> Update
    Update --> Next
    Next -- "No (exhausted)" --> Done


 Chapter 5 visual mental model: The Loop Execution Cycle 




Golden Rule of Loop Initialization: Always initialize accumulators (total = 0), counters (count = 0), and filter lists (results = []) ONCE before the loop begins. Putting total = 0 inside the loop body wipes out your progress on every iteration; forgetting it entirely triggers a NameError!

text:
5.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_01_python_foundations/ch05_loops_tracing/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Colab and execute each cell while reading the step-by-step Loop Execution Trace Tables below.

5.3.1 for Loops & range() (Half-Open Intervals)
Python’s range(start, stop, step) follows the half-open mathematical interval \([start, stop)\)—it includes start and stops one step before stop.
# range(start, stop, step) stops BEFORE 'stop' (half-open interval)
for day in range(1, 6):
    print(f"Day {day}: Surveillance report submitted")

print("Days counted:", list(range(1, 6)))
print("Even clinic hours:", list(range(8, 17, 2)))
Expected Output:
Day 1: Surveillance report submitted
Day 2: Surveillance report submitted
Day 3: Surveillance report submitted
Day 4: Surveillance report submitted
Day 5: Surveillance report submitted
Days counted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Even clinic hours: [8, 10, 12, 14, 16]



5.3.2 The 4 Universal Loop Patterns
Over 90% of real-world data processing loops are combinations of just four universal patterns:

Accumulator: Running sum (total_hb += hb), initialized to 0 or 0.0.
Counter: Running tally of matching records (anemic_count += 1), initialized to 0.
Filter: Growing list of qualifying items (anemic_cases.append(hb)), initialized to [].
Running Max / Min: Tracking the extreme value seen so far (max_hb = hb_readings[0]).

hb_readings = [10.4, 12.1, 9.6, 11.8, 10.9]

total_hb = 0.0           # Pattern 1: Accumulator
anemic_count = 0         # Pattern 2: Counter
anemic_cases = []        # Pattern 3: Filter
max_hb = hb_readings[0]  # Pattern 4: Running Max

for hb in hb_readings:
    total_hb += hb
    if hb < 11.0:
        anemic_count += 1
        anemic_cases.append(hb)
    if hb > max_hb:
        max_hb = hb

mean_hb = round(total_hb / len(hb_readings), 2)
print("Mean Hb:", mean_hb, "| Anemic count:", anemic_count)
print("Anemic list:", anemic_cases, "| Highest Hb:", max_hb)
Expected Output:
Mean Hb: 10.96 | Anemic count: 3
Anemic list: [10.4, 9.6, 10.9] | Highest Hb: 12.1

5.3.3 continue & break (DHS Missing Codes & Early Outbreak Alert)
Real epidemiology datasets are never pristine. Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) routinely encode “refused / not measured” as 999 or None. Use continue to skip bad rows immediately, and break to stop an alert scan the instant a threshold is crossed:
# Part A: continue skips DHS missing sentinels (999 or None)
raw_sbp = [122, 999, 148, None, 134, 999]
valid_total = 0
valid_count = 0

for sbp in raw_sbp:
    if sbp is None or sbp == 999:
        continue
    valid_total += sbp
    valid_count += 1

print("Clean SBP mean:", round(valid_total / valid_count, 1))

# Part B: break halts scan on FIRST outbreak threshold breach (>= 50)
daily_cases = [14, 28, 53, 61, 40]
first_alert_day = None

for day_num, cases in enumerate(daily_cases, start=1):
    if cases >= 50:
        first_alert_day = day_num
        break

print("First outbreak alert on Day:", first_alert_day)
Expected Output:
Clean SBP mean: 134.7
First outbreak alert on Day: 3

TipResearcher’s Note — Check is None Before Arithmetic



Notice we wrote if sbp is None or sbp == 999:. Checking is None first is good defensive habit: because of Python’s short-circuit or, if sbp is None, Python skips immediately without ever attempting numeric comparisons like None < 11.0 (which would crash with TypeError)!





5.3.4 enumerate() for Peak Dengue Week Identification
Whenever you need both the position (e.g., Week 1, Week 2, …) and the value, reach for enumerate(sequence, start=1). Passing start=1 aligns Python’s 0-based indexing with human epidemiological week numbers:
# Weekly dengue cases across 6 monsoon weeks
weekly_cases = [32, 48, 79, 115, 94, 61]
peak_week = 1
peak_cases = weekly_cases[0]

for week, cases in enumerate(weekly_cases, start=1):
    if cases > peak_cases:
        peak_cases = cases
        peak_week = week

print(f"Peak dengue week: Week {peak_week} ({peak_cases} cases)")
Expected Output:
Peak dengue week: Week 4 (115 cases)



5.3.5 while Loops: Epidemic Doubling & Hospital Bed Capacity
When you want to simulate forward in time until a clinical threshold is breached—without knowing how many steps it will take—use a while loop:
# Simulate cases doubling every 3 days until exceeding 200 beds
active_cases = 25
bed_capacity = 200
days = 0

while active_cases <= bed_capacity:
    active_cases *= 2
    days += 3

print(f"Capacity exceeded on Day {days} with {active_cases} cases")
Expected Output:
Capacity exceeded on Day 12 with 400 cases

WarningCommon Trap — Infinite Loops!



If you forget to update the state variable inside a while loop (for instance, forgetting active_cases *= 2), the condition 25 <= 200 stays True forever! In Google Colab, click the Stop (■) button on the cell—and always verify on paper that every while body moves strictly closer to terminating.





5.3.6 Nested Loops: Multi-Ward Surveillance Summary
Real health data is hierarchical: clinics inside districts, days inside wards, visits inside patients. A nested loop places one loop inside another. Watch carefully where ward_total = 0 is reset:
# Each inner list holds 3 daily dengue admissions for one ward
ward_admissions = [
    [6, 9, 11],    # Ward 1 -> sum 26
    [14, 18, 12],  # Ward 2 -> sum 44
]
grand_total = 0

for ward_num, daily_counts in enumerate(ward_admissions, start=1):
    ward_total = 0
    for count in daily_counts:
        ward_total += count
    grand_total += ward_total
    print(f"Ward {ward_num} 3-day total: {ward_total}")

print("Hospital grand total:", grand_total)
Expected Output:
Ward 1 3-day total: 26
Ward 2 3-day total: 44
Hospital grand total: 70
Notice the two accumulator scopes: grand_total = 0 is initialized outside both loops (accumulates the entire hospital), while ward_total = 0 is reset inside the outer loop so Ward 2 does not inherit Ward 1’s 26 admissions!



5.3.7 Break It On Purpose! (Loop Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — TypeError: ‘int’ object is not iterable



for day in 5:
    print("Day:", day)
Python’s Traceback:
TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable
Diagnosis: A single integer (5) is a scalar object, not a sequence of items. Python cannot loop over a single number directly.
Fix: Wrap the count in range(5) (or range(1, 6) for 1-based days): for day in range(1, 6):.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — NameError on Uninitialized Accumulator



for cases in [12, 18, 25]:
    uninitialized_total += cases
Python’s Traceback:
NameError: name 'uninitialized_total' is not defined
Diagnosis: uninitialized_total += cases means uninitialized_total = uninitialized_total + cases. On the very first iteration, Python looks up uninitialized_total on the right-hand side and discovers it does not exist yet!
Fix: Initialize uninitialized_total = 0 on the line above the for header.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ZeroDivisionError When All Readings Are Missing



all_missing_hb = [999, 999, 999]
hb_sum = 0.0
valid_n = 0
for val in all_missing_hb:
    if val == 999:
        continue
    hb_sum += val
    valid_n += 1
mean_missing = hb_sum / valid_n
Python’s Traceback:
ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
Diagnosis: Every reading hit continue, leaving valid_n == 0. Dividing 0.0 / 0 crashes your entire pipeline on the first empty clinic subgroup!
Fix: Always guard the division: mean_missing = round(hb_sum / valid_n, 2) if valid_n > 0 else None.
