Trailing dims 2 vs. 4 neither equal nor 1



Watch both column-wise and row-wise broadcasting in action:
# Feature matrix: 3 patients x 2 biomarkers [hb_g_dl, sbp_mmhg]
X = np.array([
    [10.0, 120.0],
    [12.0, 130.0],
    [14.0, 140.0],
])

# 1. Column centering: (3, 2) - (2,) broadcasts across all 3 rows
col_means = np.mean(X, axis=0)
centered = X - col_means
print("Column means (2,):", col_means)
print("Centered (3, 2):\n", centered)

# 2. Row-wise scaling via [:, None]: (3, 4) / (3, 1)
pop = np.array([250_000, 120_000, 90_000], dtype=float)
weekly_inc = np.round((cases / pop[:, None]) * 100_000, 2)
print("pop[:, None] shape:", pop[:, None].shape)
print("Weekly incidence per 100k:\n", weekly_inc)
Expected Output:
Column means (2,): [ 12. 130.]
Centered (3, 2):
 [[ -2. -10.]
 [  0.   0.]
 [  2.  10.]]
pop[:, None] shape: (3, 1)
Weekly incidence per 100k:
 [[ 4.8  10.   16.    9.2 ]
 [25.   12.5   8.33  4.17]
 [ 5.56  8.89 13.33 22.22]]
Look closely at pop[:, None]: inserting None (equivalent to np.newaxis) turns a 1D (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column vector so it broadcasts horizontally across all 4 weeks!



16.3.6 Linear Algebra in Action (@, Sigmoid & Norms)
Every linear model, logistic classifier, and neural network layer computes \(z = Xw + b\) using Python’s dedicated matrix-multiplication operator @, while k-NN and clustering algorithms measure row-wise Euclidean (\(L_2\)) distances \(\|x_i - r\|_2\):
Z = np.array([
    [-1.2,  0.8],
    [ 0.0,  0.0],
    [ 1.5, -0.5],
])
w = np.array([-0.9, 1.1])
b = 0.2

# Linear logits (3, 2) @ (2,) -> (3,), then logistic sigmoid
logits = Z @ w + b
probs = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-logits))
print("Logits:", np.round(logits, 4))
print("Probs: ", np.round(probs, 4))

# Euclidean (L2) distances from healthy centroid [0.0, 0.0]
ref = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
dists = np.round(np.linalg.norm(Z - ref, axis=1), 4)
print("L2 distances to ref:", dists)
Expected Output:
Logits: [ 2.16  0.2  -1.7 ]
Probs:  [0.8966 0.5498 0.1545]
L2 distances to ref: [1.4422 0.     1.5811]
Never confuse * with @: Z * w multiplies elementwise and returns a (3, 2) matrix, whereas Z @ w computes the inner product of each patient row with w, collapsing the feature axis cleanly into a (3,) score vector!



16.3.7 Break It On Purpose! (NumPy Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — ValueError (Incompatible Broadcasting Shapes)



mat = np.ones((3, 2))
vec = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
bad_sum = mat + vec
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,2) (4,)
Diagnosis: Aligning from the right compares trailing dimension 2 against 4. Neither is equal nor 1, so NumPy refuses to guess.
Fix: Ensure the 1D vector matches the trailing column count (shape (2,)) for column-wise ops, or reshape a length-3 vector to (3, 1) (vec[:, None]) for row-wise ops.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — ValueError (Misaligned Matrix Multiply @)



A = np.ones((3, 2))
B = np.ones((3, 1))
bad_prod = A @ B
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0,
with gufunc signature (n?,k),(k,m?)->(n?,m?) (size 3 is different from 2)
Diagnosis: Matrix multiplication \((n \times k) \mathbin{@} (k \times m)\) requires the inner dimensions \(k\) to match. Here A has \(k = 2\) columns, while B has \(3\) rows!
Fix: Check .shape on both operands and transpose (A.T @ B) or fix the weight vector length so inner dimensions match.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — IndexError (Out-of-Bounds 2D Axis Index)



grid = np.zeros((3, 4))
bad_cell = grid[3, 0]
Python’s Traceback:
IndexError: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3
Diagnosis: A (3, 4) matrix has valid row indices 0, 1, 2 along axis=0 and column indices 0, 1, 2, 3 along axis=1. Index 3 steps one past the last row.
Fix: Use 0-based indices (0..shape[axis] - 1) or -1 to select the final row cleanly.

section: 16.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
text:
16.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: A Dhaka hospital triage system receives a raw 2D vital-sign matrix raw_X of shape (n_patients, n_features) containing both 999.0 scanner sentinels and np.nan gaps, plus a constant clinic-code column. Build a single zero-loop function run_vectorized_triage(raw_X, weights, bias, cutoff=0.5) that cleans, imputes, standardizes, scores via logistic regression, and returns (probs, flags) without mutating raw_X.

16.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Non-Mutating Sentinel Cleaning:

Allocate X = np.array(raw_X, dtype=float, copy=True) so integers promote to float and the caller’s matrix stays intact.
Replace 999.0 with np.nan using boolean masking: X[X == 999.0] = np.nan.

Broadcasted Imputation & Safe Standardization:

Compute column means col_means = np.nanmean(X, axis=0) (shape (p,)).
Fill missing cells in one broadcasted line: X = np.where(np.isnan(X), col_means, X).
Compute means = np.mean(X, axis=0) and stds = np.std(X, axis=0). Substitute 1.0 where stds == 0 via np.where, standardize (X - means) / safe_stds, and set constant columns to 0.0.

Linear Algebra Inference & Verification Plan:

Compute logits = Z @ np.asarray(weights, dtype=float) + bias.
Apply logistic sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{-z})\) and cast (probs >= cutoff).astype(int).
Hand-check that patient 0 (low Hb 9.5, high fever 39.1) gets high probability (> 0.9, flag 1), patient 2 (healthy Hb 12.5, normal temp 36.8) gets low probability (< 0.1, flag 0), and raw_vitals[1, 0] remains 999.0.




16.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
def run_vectorized_triage(raw_X, weights, bias, cutoff=0.5):
    """Clean, impute, standardize, and score a vital matrix."""
    # Step 1: Copy as float & replace sentinel 999.0 with np.nan
    X = np.array(raw_X, dtype=float, copy=True)
    X[X == 999.0] = np.nan

    # Step 2: Broadcasted column-mean imputation
    col_means = np.nanmean(X, axis=0)
    X = np.where(np.isnan(X), col_means, X)

    # Step 3: Column Z-score standardization with zero-std guard
    means = np.mean(X, axis=0)
    stds = np.std(X, axis=0)
    safe_stds = np.where(stds == 0, 1.0, stds)
    Z = (X - means) / safe_stds
    Z[:, stds == 0] = 0.0

    # Step 4: Linear logits (@), sigmoid probs, and 0/1 flags
    logits = Z @ np.asarray(weights, dtype=float) + bias
    probs = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-logits))
    flags = (probs >= cutoff).astype(int)
    return np.round(probs, 4), flags

# 4 patients x 3 features: [hb_g_dl, temp_c, clinic_code]
raw_vitals = np.array([
    [ 9.5, 39.1, 1.0],
    [999.0, 38.4, 1.0],
    [12.5, 36.8, 1.0],
    [11.0, np.nan, 1.0],
])
w_triage = np.array([-1.2, 1.5, 0.5])
probs, flags = run_vectorized_triage(raw_vitals, w_triage, bias=0.1)

print("Risk probabilities:", probs)
print("Triage flags (0/1):", flags)
print("Raw sentinel intact:", raw_vitals[1, 0])
Output:
Risk probabilities: [0.9733 0.6547 0.0191 0.525 ]
Triage flags (0/1): [1 1 0 1]
Raw sentinel intact: 999.0

To-Do 16.2 (Masking & np.nanmean — clean_and_mean_hb(hb_array)): Replace sentinel 999 with np.nan on a float copy without mutating input, and return a native Python float rounded to 2 decimals via np.nanmean (or None if all values are NaN).
To-Do 16.3 (Broadcasting & axis=0 — standardize_columns(X)): Given a 2D (n, p) array, compute column-wise Z-scores \((X - \mu) / \sigma\) along axis=0 via broadcasting, setting zero-std columns to 0.0 without mutating X.
To-Do 16.4 (Boolean Masking — flag_fever_mask(temps_c, cutoff=38.0)): Return a 2-tuple (bool_ndarray, int_count) flagging all temperatures >= cutoff (inclusive).
To-Do 16.5 (Matrix Multiply @ — weighted_risk_scores(X, weights, bias)): Compute X @ weights + bias and return a 1D np.ndarray rounded to 4 decimal places.
To-Do 16.6 (Broadcasting & Norms — pairwise_l2_distances(points, reference)): Compute broadcasting Euclidean distances np.linalg.norm(points - reference, axis=1) and return a 1D np.ndarray rounded to 4 decimal places.

text:
16.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

16.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

a * 2 repeats the Python list \(\rightarrow\) [10, 20, 10, 20]; b * 2 scales each element \(\rightarrow\) array([20, 40]).
Prints [5. 6. 0. 8.] — arr[1:3] is a memory view, so window[1] = 0.0 overwrites arr[2].
np.sum(cases, axis=1) collapses columns \(\rightarrow\) (5,); np.mean(cases, axis=0) collapses rows \(\rightarrow\) (12,).
NumPy int64 arrays cannot represent IEEE-754 floating-point NaN. Cast on a float copy first: np.array(x, dtype=float, copy=True).
np.mean(...) returns nan; np.nanmean(...) skips NaN and returns 12.0.
np.ones((3, 4)) / np.ones((3, 1)) succeeds with shape (3, 4); (3, 2) + (4,) raises ValueError because trailing dimensions 2 and 4 are incompatible.
(37.0 - 37.0) / 0.0 computes 0.0 / 0.0, producing nan across the entire column (and a RuntimeWarning).
X * w broadcasts elementwise to shape (4, 3); X @ w takes row dot products and returns shape (4,).
Omitting axis=1 computes a single scalar Frobenius norm across all \(10 \times 2 = 20\) entries instead of a (10,) array of row distances.
\(\sigma(0.0) = 1 / (1 + e^0) = 1 / 2 =\) 0.5, and (0.5 >= 0.5).astype(int) assigns integer label 1.



16.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import numpy as np

# To-Do 16.1
def vectorized_bmi(weights_kg, heights_cm):
    """Compute 1D NumPy array of BMIs rounded to 2 decimals."""
    w = np.asarray(weights_kg, dtype=float)
    h_m = np.asarray(heights_cm, dtype=float) / 100.0
    return np.round(w / (h_m ** 2), 2)

# To-Do 16.2
def clean_and_mean_hb(hb_array):
    """Replace 999 with NaN on a float copy and return nanmean."""
    arr = np.array(hb_array, dtype=float, copy=True)
    arr[arr == 999] = np.nan
    if arr.size == 0 or np.all(np.isnan(arr)):
        return None
    return round(float(np.nanmean(arr)), 2)

# To-Do 16.3
def standardize_columns(X):
    """Column-wise Z-score standardization with zero-std guard."""
    arr = np.array(X, dtype=float, copy=True)
    means = np.mean(arr, axis=0)
    stds = np.std(arr, axis=0)
    safe_stds = np.where(stds == 0, 1.0, stds)
    z = (arr - means) / safe_stds
    z[:, stds == 0] = 0.0
    return z

# To-Do 16.4
def flag_fever_mask(temps_c, cutoff=38.0):
    """Return (bool_mask, int_count) for temperatures >= cutoff."""
    arr = np.asarray(temps_c, dtype=float)
    mask = arr >= cutoff
    return mask, int(np.sum(mask))

# To-Do 16.5
def weighted_risk_scores(X, weights, bias):
    """Compute vectorized linear risk scores X @ weights + bias."""
    X_arr = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    w_arr = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    return np.round(X_arr @ w_arr + bias, 4)

# To-Do 16.6
def pairwise_l2_distances(points, reference):
    """Return 1D Euclidean distances from each row to reference."""
    pts = np.asarray(points, dtype=float)
    ref = np.asarray(reference, dtype=float)
    return np.round(np.linalg.norm(pts - ref, axis=1), 4)


16.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 16 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
# Exam Task 16.1 (30 pts)
def normalize_vital_matrix(X):
    """Clean 999.0, impute column nanmeans, and min-max scale [0, 1]."""
    arr = np.array(X, dtype=float, copy=True)
    arr[arr == 999.0] = np.nan
    col_means = np.nanmean(arr, axis=0)
    arr = np.where(np.isnan(arr), col_means, arr)
    col_min = np.min(arr, axis=0)
    span = np.max(arr, axis=0) - col_min
    safe_span = np.where(span == 0, 1.0, span)
    scaled = (arr - col_min) / safe_span
    scaled[:, span == 0] = 0.0
    return np.round(scaled, 4)

# Exam Task 16.2 (35 pts)
def district_weekly_summary(cases_2d, pop_1d):
    """Aggregate district surveillance grid across axes & population."""
    cases = np.asarray(cases_2d, dtype=float)
    pop = np.asarray(pop_1d, dtype=float)
    total = np.sum(cases, axis=1)
    weekly_mean = np.round(np.mean(cases, axis=0), 2)
    peak_week = np.argmax(cases, axis=1)
    incidence = np.round((total / pop) * 100_000, 2)
    return {
        "total_per_district": total,
        "weekly_mean": weekly_mean,
        "peak_week_index": peak_week,
        "incidence_per_100k": incidence,
    }

# Exam Task 16.3 (35 pts)
def linear_clinical_scorer(X, weights, bias, threshold=0.5):
    """Compute logistic risk probabilities and 0/1 class predictions."""
    X_arr = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    w_arr = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    z = X_arr @ w_arr + bias
    probs = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))
    preds = (probs >= threshold).astype(int)
    return np.round(probs, 4), preds


16.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 16 Failure Modes

Mutating Input Arrays via Views or In-Place Masking: Running X[X == 999.0] = np.nan directly on the caller’s argument permanently corrupts raw survey data upstream (and crashes on int64 arrays). Always open data-cleaning functions with arr = np.array(X, dtype=float, copy=True).
Swapping axis=0 and axis=1 on 2D Feature Tables: On a square (3, 3) test matrix, swapped axes silently return the same shape with completely wrong science! Always test axis reductions on rectangular (3, 4) grids where axis=0 yields (4,) and axis=1 yields (3,).
Confusing * (Elementwise) with @ (Matrix Multiply) or Omitting axis=1 in Norms: Remember that * preserves 2D shape by multiplying cell-by-cell, whereas @ computes dot products across the inner feature dimension, and np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1) reduces each row independently.








NoteUp Next — Pandas & Tabular Data Wrangling



NumPy gave you blazing-fast, contiguous numeric matrices—but real research datasets mix string district names, timestamps, missing values, and heterogeneous clinical columns. In Chapter 17, you will master Pandas (Series and DataFrame), which wraps NumPy arrays in labeled axes for expressive filtering, groupby epidemiology tables, joins, and tidy data pipelines.

title: 17  Pandas Foundations — Series, DataFrames, Indexing, Filtering, and Reshaping
section: 17.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Tabular Research Needs Pandas
text:
17.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Tabular Research Needs Pandas
In Chapter 16, you saw how NumPy accelerates homogeneous numerical arrays—a matrix where every entry shares the exact same float64 type. Real clinical cohorts, economic surveys, and genomics metadata are almost never homogeneous: a single patient row mixes a string ID ("UHC-0001"), a categorical district ("Sylhet"), an integer age (55), and floating-point vitals (37.5 °C, 12.2 g/dL).
Pandas sits directly on top of NumPy to give each column its own typed NumPy/Arrow vector while binding every row and column to explicit, alignment-aware labels:

Series (1D Labeled Vector): One typed column paired with a row Index (for example, df["temp_c"] holds 120 float64 body temperatures).
DataFrame (2D Labeled Table): An ordered dictionary of Series sharing one common row Index—each column can hold a different dtype (str, int64, float64, bool).
Vectorized Column Operations: Writing df["weight_kg"] / (df["height_cm"] / 100) ** 2 computes BMI across 120—or 12 million—rows in compiled C loops without a single Python for loop.







NoteMental Model — Indexed Laboratory Ledger vs. Loose Lists



Think of a DataFrame as a bound hospital ledger where every row has a stamped chart label (Index) and every column has a printed header and unit:

.iloc[row_pos, col_pos] counts physical lines from the top of the page starting at 0 (like Python list slicing, the stop index is exclusive).
.loc[row_label, col_label] looks up rows and columns by their printed labels (just like a dictionary, and slice endpoints are inclusive).
Wide vs. Long Format: Wide tables put repeated visits in separate columns (sbp_day1, sbp_day2)—handy for paired differences (day2 - day1). Tidy long tables stack one measurement per row (patient_id, visit, sbp)—required by Seaborn, Statsmodels, and longitudinal mixed-effects models.




17.1.1 The Modern Pandas 3.x Copy-on-Write Discipline
Older Pandas tutorials are packed with inplace=True and chained indexing like df[df["age_years"] >= 18]["bmi"] = ..., which caused notorious SettingWithCopyWarning bugs. In Pandas 3.x, Copy-on-Write (CoW) is active by default: chained assignment fails or silently does nothing to df, and inplace=True returns None. Throughout this book, we follow one ironclad rule: never mutate inputs in place—always derive new tables via out = df.copy() or .assign(...), and return the new DataFrame explicitly.

    end

    MASK -. "count groups" .-> XTAB


 Chapter 17 visual mental model: Indexing & Wide-to-Long Reshaping 



Keep two visual invariants anchored in your head as you code:

Row filters preserve old index numbers (e.g., [3, 16, 28, ...]) until you explicitly call .reset_index(drop=True).
Reshaping changes table geometry, not data truth: pd.melt stretches \(N\) patients \(\times\) \(K\) visits into \(N \cdot K\) tidy rows, whereas pd.crosstab compresses individual rows into a compact district-by-priority count matrix.







WarningPandas .std() vs. NumPy np.std() Default Trap!



By default, Pandas Series.std() computes the sample standard deviation with Bessel’s correction (ddof=1, dividing by \(n - 1\)), whereas NumPy np.std() defaults to the population standard deviation (ddof=0, dividing by \(n\)). Mixing the two in a statistical pipeline silently shifts every standard deviation and \(z\)-score!

17.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_04_data_science_math/ch17_pandas_foundations/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Google Colab and execute every cell alongside the dissections below.

17.3.1 Loading Data, Series vs. DataFrame, & Summaries
First, load the real bundled Bangladesh upazila health complex triage dataset via sharukh_tutor and inspect its shape, types, and summary statistics:
import pandas as pd
import sharukh_tutor as tutor

df = tutor.load_data("clinic_triage", as_pandas=True)

print("Shape:", df.shape)
print("DataFrame type:", type(df).__name__)
print("Series type:   ", type(df["temp_c"]).__name__)
print("Mean temp_c:   ", round(float(df["temp_c"].mean()), 2))
print("Median temp_c: ", round(float(df["temp_c"].median()), 2))
print("Std temp_c:    ", round(float(df["temp_c"].std()), 2))
Expected Output:
Shape: (120, 11)
DataFrame type: DataFrame
Series type:    Series
Mean temp_c:    37.39
Median temp_c:  37.4
Std temp_c:     0.78
Notice the single-bracket versus double-bracket distinction: df["temp_c"] extracts a 1D Series, whereas df[["temp_c"]] returns a 1-column 2D DataFrame. Wrapping aggregated values with float(round(..., 2)) converts Pandas/NumPy scalars into clean native Python floats ready for reports or JSON logs.



17.3.2 Label vs. Position Indexing (.loc vs. .iloc)
Watch the exact difference between integer-position slicing (.iloc) and label-based slicing (.loc):
print("iloc[0:3, 0:3] (exclusive stop):")
print(df.iloc[0:3, 0:3])

by_id = df.set_index("patient_id")
print("\nloc['UHC-0001':'UHC-0003', ['district', 'temp_c']] (inclusive):")
print(by_id.loc["UHC-0001":"UHC-0003", ["district", "temp_c"]])
Expected Output:
iloc[0:3, 0:3] (exclusive stop):
  patient_id    district  age_years
0   UHC-0001  Chattogram         15
1   UHC-0002      Sylhet         55
2   UHC-0003    Rajshahi         70

loc['UHC-0001':'UHC-0003', ['district', 'temp_c']] (inclusive):
              district  temp_c
patient_id                    
UHC-0001    Chattogram    37.7
UHC-0002        Sylhet    37.5
UHC-0003      Rajshahi    37.4
Compare those two slices side by side:

.iloc[0:3, 0:3] stops before position 3—returning 3 rows (0, 1, 2) and 3 columns (0, 1, 2), identical to standard Python list slicing.
.loc["UHC-0001":"UHC-0003", ...] includes both "UHC-0001" and "UHC-0003", because label slices in Pandas are closed (inclusive) intervals.




17.3.3 Boolean Masking with &, |, ~, and .isin()
To isolate clinical sub-cohorts without writing loops, build elementwise boolean Series masks and combine them with bitwise operators (& for AND, | for OR, ~ for NOT):
adult_fever = (df["age_years"] >= 18) & (df["temp_c"] >= 38.0)
target_dist = df["district"].isin(["Dhaka", "Sylhet"])

sub = df.loc[adult_fever & target_dist].reset_index(drop=True)
other_count = int((~target_dist).sum())

print("Adult fever rows (all districts):", int(adult_fever.sum()))
print("Adult fever in Dhaka/Sylhet:     ", len(sub))
print("Outside Dhaka/Sylhet rows:       ", other_count)
print(sub[["patient_id", "district", "age_years", "temp_c"]].head(3))
Expected Output:
Adult fever rows (all districts): 21
Adult fever in Dhaka/Sylhet:      4
Outside Dhaka/Sylhet rows:        90
  patient_id district  age_years  temp_c
0   UHC-0017   Sylhet         31    38.8
1   UHC-0029    Dhaka         41    38.4
2   UHC-0042   Sylhet         32    38.6
Trace three critical syntax habits here:

Parentheses around every comparison: Operator precedence binds & tighter than >=, so omitting parentheses around (df["age_years"] >= 18) raises TypeError.
.isin([...]) replaces chained | checks: Checking membership across 2 or 20 districts stays concise and fast.
.reset_index(drop=True): Without drop=True, Pandas turns the old scattered row labels (16, 28, 41, ...) into an extra column named "index".




17.3.4 Vectorized Columns, .assign(), & Pandas 3.x Copy-on-Write
Derive clinical features cleanly with .assign(...) (or out = df.copy(); out["col"] = ...) so your raw dataset remains 100% immutable:
enriched = df.assign(
    bmi=(df["weight_kg"] / (df["height_cm"] / 100) ** 2).round(2),
    is_anemic=df["hemoglobin_g_dl"] < 11.0,
)

print("'bmi' in original df?", "bmi" in df.columns)
print("'bmi' in enriched?   ", "bmi" in enriched.columns)
print("Anemic patients:     ", int(enriched["is_anemic"].sum()))
cols = ["patient_id", "bmi", "hemoglobin_g_dl", "is_anemic"]
print(enriched[cols].head(3))
Expected Output:
'bmi' in original df? False
'bmi' in enriched?    True
Anemic patients:      7
  patient_id    bmi  hemoglobin_g_dl  is_anemic
0   UHC-0001  19.56             12.1      False
1   UHC-0002  25.02             12.2      False
2   UHC-0003  27.39             14.7      False
Notice that 'bmi' in original df? is False: .assign() always returns a new DataFrame with the added columns while leaving df pristine for downstream sensitivity checks.



17.3.5 Deterministic Multi-Key Sorting with .sort_values()
Whenever two patients share the exact same fever temperature, sorting by a single column leaves tie order arbitrary. Always pass a secondary tie-breaker column (patient_id) with an explicit ascending list:
cols = ["patient_id", "district", "temp_c", "triage_priority"]
top_fever = (
    df.sort_values(
        by=["temp_c", "patient_id"],
        ascending=[False, True],
    )[cols]
    .head(5)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
print(top_fever)
Expected Output:
  patient_id    district  temp_c triage_priority
0   UHC-0004    Rajshahi    39.0        Moderate
1   UHC-0107     Rangpur    38.9        Moderate
2   UHC-0017      Sylhet    38.8        Moderate
3   UHC-0057     Rangpur    38.7        Moderate
4   UHC-0108  Chattogram    38.7        Moderate
Look at rows 3 and 4: both patients recorded 38.7 °C, and ascending=[False, True] deterministically places UHC-0057 ahead of UHC-0108.



17.3.6 Reshaping Data: pd.melt, pd.crosstab, & pivot_table
Research pipelines constantly switch between wide visit tables (one column per timepoint), tidy long tables (one observation per row), and 2D contingency/summary matrices:
wide_bp = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "patient_id": ["UHC-0001", "UHC-0002", "UHC-0003"],
        "sbp_day1": [123, 132, 140],
        "sbp_day2": [119, 128, 134],
    }
)
long_bp = pd.melt(
    wide_bp,
    id_vars=["patient_id"],
    value_vars=["sbp_day1", "sbp_day2"],
    var_name="visit",
    value_name="sbp",
)
print("Long BP shape:", long_bp.shape)
print(long_bp)

ct = pd.crosstab(df["district"], df["triage_priority"])

17.3.7 Break It On Purpose! (Pandas Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — KeyError (Nonexistent Column Name)



print(df["hemoglobin"].mean())
Python’s Traceback:
KeyError: 'hemoglobin'
Diagnosis: Column names in Pandas are exact dictionary keys—our dataset stores "hemoglobin_g_dl", not "hemoglobin".
Fix: Inspect list(df.columns) whenever you encounter a KeyError, and verify exact spelling and units (df["hemoglobin_g_dl"].mean()).








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — ValueError (Ambiguous Truth Value of a Series)



bad_mask = (df["age_years"] >= 18) and (df["temp_c"] >= 38.0)
print(bad_mask.sum())
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. Use a.empty,
a.item(), a.any() or a.all().
Diagnosis: Python’s logical and tries to collapse a 120-element boolean Series into a single scalar True/False, which is meaningless.
Fix: Replace and / or / not with elementwise bitwise & / | / ~, keeping parentheses around each comparison: (df["age_years"] >= 18) & (df["temp_c"] >= 38.0).








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — IndexError (.iloc Out-of-Bounds Row)



print(df.iloc[120])
Python’s Traceback:
IndexError: single positional indexer is out-of-bounds
Diagnosis: A 120-row DataFrame has valid 0-based positions 0 through 119. Requesting .iloc[120] steps one slot past the last row!
Fix: Use df.iloc[-1] for the final row, or check len(df) before indexing by integer position.

17.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: A district health director wants a reproducible Adult Fever-Rate Audit from clinic_triage: restrict to adult patients (age_years >= 18), compute each adult’s 2-decimal BMI and has_fever flag (temp_c >= 38.0) without mutating df, tabulate afebrile vs. febrile counts per district, calculate fever_pct rounded to 1 decimal place, and rank districts from highest to lowest fever burden.

17.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Purity & Cohort Selection Contract:

Filter adults with df.loc[df["age_years"] >= 18].copy() so the original 120-row table remains untouched (len(df.columns) == 11).
Add bmi and has_fever via .assign(bmi=lambda d: ..., has_fever=lambda d: ...) and reset the index (drop=True).

Contingency & Rate Formula:

Build a 2-column count table via pd.crosstab(cohort["district"], cohort["has_fever"]) (False \(\rightarrow\) afebrile, True \(\rightarrow\) febrile).
Compute \(\text{fever\_pct} = \text{round}\!\left(\frac{\text{febrile}}{\text{afebrile} + \text{febrile}} \times 100,\ 1\right)\).

Ranking & Hand Check:

Sort descending by fever_pct using .sort_values("fever_pct", ascending=False).
Verify row sums match the 97-adult cohort (27 + 16 + 9 + 20 + 12 + 13 = 97) and original df still has 11 columns.




17.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
cohort = (
    df.loc[df["age_years"] >= 18]
    .copy()
    .assign(
        bmi=lambda d: (
            d["weight_kg"] / (d["height_cm"] / 100) ** 2
        ).round(2),
        has_fever=lambda d: d["temp_c"] >= 38.0,
    )
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

fever_table = pd.crosstab(cohort["district"], cohort["has_fever"])
fever_table.columns = ["afebrile", "febrile"]
total_adults = fever_table["afebrile"] + fever_table["febrile"]
fever_table["fever_pct"] = (
    fever_table["febrile"] / total_adults * 100
).round(1)
ranked = fever_table.sort_values("fever_pct", ascending=False)

print(
    "Adult cohort size:", len(cohort),
    "| Original df cols:", len(df.columns),
)
print(ranked)

17.6 Stage 6 — Concept & Execution Trace Test (No Computer Allowed!)
Trace every Pandas expression carefully on paper before checking Stage 8:

Single vs. Double Brackets: Given a 120-row DataFrame df, what are the Python types and .shape attributes of df["temp_c"] versus df[["temp_c"]]?
.loc vs. .iloc Endpoint Rule: For a DataFrame with default integer index 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, how many rows are returned by df.iloc[1:3] versus df.loc[1:3]?
Series Boolean Operators: Why does (df["age_years"] >= 18) and (df["temp_c"] >= 38.0) raise ValueError, and what two edits fix it?
Operator Precedence Bug: Why does df["age_years"] >= 18 & df["temp_c"] >= 38.0 (without parentheses) fail even though & is used?
The inplace=True Return Trap: What value is stored in sorted_df after running sorted_df = df.sort_values("temp_c", inplace=True)?
Leftover 'index' Column: You filter a DataFrame to 4 matching rows (original indices 16, 28, 41, 77) and call .reset_index() without drop=True. What unexpected column gets added?
Pandas vs. NumPy Standard Deviation: For the Series s = pd.Series([10.0, 12.0, 14.0]), mean \(\bar{x} = 12.0\) and sum of squared deviations is \(8.0\). What does s.std() return (ddof=1) versus s.std(ddof=0)?

section: 17.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem
text:
17.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

17.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

df["temp_c"] is a 1D Series with shape (120,); df[["temp_c"]] is a 2D DataFrame with shape (120, 1).
df.iloc[1:3] returns 2 rows (positions 1, 2 — exclusive stop); df.loc[1:3] returns 3 rows (labels 1, 2, 3 — inclusive endpoints).
Python’s and cannot evaluate a multi-element boolean Series as a single truth value. Replace and with & and keep parentheses around each condition.
Bitwise & binds tighter than >=, so Python tries to evaluate 18 & df["temp_c"] first, raising TypeError. Always parenthesize both sides.
None — Pandas methods invoked with inplace=True return None instead of the sorted DataFrame.
An extra column named "index" containing [16, 28, 41, 77] is inserted as the first column. Always pass drop=True unless you want to preserve old labels as data.
s.std() (ddof=1) returns \(\sqrt{8.0 / 2} = \mathbf{2.0}\); s.std(ddof=0) returns \(\sqrt{8.0 / 3} \approx \mathbf{1.633}\).
(135, 3) — \(45 \times 3 = 135\) rows and 3 columns (patient_id, variable, value).
Khulna is silently dropped from the output instead of appearing with 0 Urgent patients (0.0%). pd.crosstab keeps every district and fills missing cells with integer 0.
Assigning df["bmi"] = ... directly mutates the caller’s DataFrame as a hidden side effect, breaking reproducibility if the caller expects the original schema later in the notebook.



17.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import pandas as pd

# To-Do 17.1
def add_bmi_column(df):
    """Return a fresh copy of df with 2-decimal BMI column added."""
    out = df.copy()
    height_m = out["height_cm"] / 100
    out["bmi"] = (out["weight_kg"] / (height_m ** 2)).round(2)
    return out

# To-Do 17.2
def filter_urgent_adults(df):
    """Filter adult Urgent rows, reset index, and return a copy."""
    mask = (df["age_years"] >= 18) & (df["triage_priority"] == "Urgent")
    return df.loc[mask].reset_index(drop=True).copy()

# To-Do 17.3
def select_top_fever_patients(df, n=5):
    """Return top-n fever patients sorted by temp_c desc, id asc."""
    cols = ["patient_id", "district", "temp_c"]
    ranked = df.sort_values(
        by=["temp_c", "patient_id"],
        ascending=[False, True],
    )
    return ranked[cols].head(n).reset_index(drop=True)

# To-Do 17.4
def summarize_numeric_vitals(df, cols):
    """Return {col: {'mean', 'median', 'std'}} rounded to 2 decimals."""
    summary = {}
    for col in cols:
        s = df[col]
        summary[col] = {
            "mean": float(round(s.mean(), 2)),
            "median": float(round(s.median(), 2)),
            "std": float(round(s.std(), 2)),
        }
    return summary

# To-Do 17.5
def melt_vital_measurements(wide_df):
    """Unpivot sbp_day1/sbp_day2 to long [patient_id, visit, sbp]."""
    return pd.melt(
        wide_df,
        id_vars=["patient_id"],
        value_vars=["sbp_day1", "sbp_day2"],
        var_name="visit",
        value_name="sbp",
    )

# To-Do 17.6
def pivot_district_priority_counts(df):
    """Return integer district x triage_priority counts filled with 0."""
    return pd.crosstab(df["district"], df["triage_priority"])


17.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 17 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
# Exam Task 17.1 (30 pts)
def prepare_triage_cohort(df):
    """Return non-mutating adult triage cohort with bmi and is_anemic."""
    adults = df.loc[df["age_years"] >= 18].copy()
    height_m = adults["height_cm"] / 100
    adults["bmi"] = (adults["weight_kg"] / (height_m ** 2)).round(2)
    adults["is_anemic"] = adults["hemoglobin_g_dl"] < 11.0
    return adults.reset_index(drop=True)

# Exam Task 17.2 (35 pts)
def rank_districts_by_urgent_share(df):
    """Rank districts by % Urgent patients desc, then district asc."""
    is_urgent = df["triage_priority"] == "Urgent"
    counts = pd.crosstab(df["district"], is_urgent)
    total = counts.sum(axis=1)
    urgent = (
        counts[True]
        if True in counts.columns
        else pd.Series(0, index=total.index)
    )
    out = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "district": total.index,
            "total_patients": total.astype(int).values,
            "urgent_patients": urgent.astype(int).values,
        }
    )
    out["urgent_pct"] = (
        out["urgent_patients"] / out["total_patients"] * 100
    ).round(1)
    return out.sort_values(
        by=["urgent_pct", "district"],
        ascending=[False, True],
    ).reset_index(drop=True)

# Exam Task 17.3 (35 pts)
def reshape_and_compare_visits(wide_df):
    """Melt baseline/followup Hb and return (long_df, mean_change)."""
    long_df = pd.melt(
        wide_df,
        id_vars=["patient_id"],
        value_vars=["hb_baseline", "hb_followup"],
        var_name="visit",
        value_name="hb_g_dl",
    )
    deltas = wide_df["hb_followup"] - wide_df["hb_baseline"]
    mean_change = float(round(deltas.mean(), 2))
    return long_df, mean_change


17.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 17 Failure Modes

Mutating Input DataFrames or Using inplace=True: Writing df["bmi"] = ... directly on an argument leaks columns back into the caller’s table, and df = df.sort_values(..., inplace=True) sets df to None. Always copy (out = df.copy() or .assign(...)) and return the fresh DataFrame.
Mixing Python and/or/not with Pandas Series Masks: Every Pandas boolean mask is a vector of booleans, not a single truth value. Always write (cond_a) & (cond_b), (cond_a) | (cond_b), or ~(cond_a) with parentheses around each condition.
Dropping Zero-Count Categories During Filtering: Filtering to "Urgent" rows before counting districts erases zero-urgent districts from denominator tables and prevalence rankings. Use pd.crosstab or full-table boolean sums so every district stays accounted for.








NoteUp Next — Data Cleaning, Missingness, GroupBy & Merging



You can now index, filter, sort, and reshape clean clinical tables with Pandas 3.x Copy-on-Write discipline. Real-world field datasets, however, arrive with missing NaN values, duplicate IDs, messy text labels, and multiple tables that must be joined together. In Chapter 18, you will master missing-data diagnostics and imputation, split-apply-combine .groupby() pipelines, and relational .merge() joins across multi-table clinical cohorts.

title: 18  Real-World Data Wrangling — Missing Data, Dirty Surveys, Joins, GroupBy, and Time Series
section: 18.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Real Research Data Breaks Clean Code
text:
18.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Real Research Data Breaks Clean Code
In Chapter 17, you learned Pandas fundamentals on tidy DataFrames. Real public health surveys (like the Demographic and Health Surveys, DHS) and weekly epidemiological surveillance feeds rarely arrive tidy:

Hidden Sentinel Codes: Survey interviewers record "Don't know" as 999, 99, or -99. If you compute mch["anc_visits"].mean() without neutralizing 999 first, just 8 sentinel rows out of 500 inflate average antenatal care visits from \(3.77\) to an absurd \(19.7\)!
Dirty Categorical Strings: Field enumerators type "Rural", "rural", " rural ", and "URBAN". Left unnormalized, .groupby("residence") splits one stratum into four fragmented rows and corrupts every downstream summary.
Silent Row Explosions in Joins: Joining a 500-patient registry to a lab table that accidentally contains two hemoglobin tests for one patient quietly turns 500 rows into 501+—double-counting that patient in every prevalence estimate.
Cross-District Time-Series Leakage: Computing .shift(1) or .rolling(4).mean() on a stacked multi-district table lets Chattogram’s December dengue surge bleed directly into Dhaka’s Week 1 feature!


18.1.1 Missing-Data Mechanisms: MCAR, MAR, and MNAR
Before dropping or imputing a single NaN, ask why the value is missing:









Mechanism
Meaning
Public Health Example
Safe Wrangling Action




MCAR
Missing Completely At Random
Lab vial dropped on floor
Complete-case or simple imputation is unbiased


MAR
Missing At Random (given observed strata)
Rural clinics have more missing Hb tests than urban clinics
Impute within observed strata (e.g., per-residence median)


MNAR
Missing Not At Random (depends on unobserved value itself)
Severely ill patients skip follow-up weigh-ins
Do not blindly impute; flag missingness and run sensitivity analysis









NotePandas 3.x Copy-on-Write Rule — Pure Functions Only!



Starting in Pandas 3.x, Copy-on-Write is enforced globally: chained assignments like df["anc_visits"][mask] = np.nan fail or behave unpredictably, and inplace=True is discouraged because it returns None and obscures state mutations. Adopt one clean habit for every wrangling function you write:

Start with out = df.copy().
Transform columns with direct assignment: out["col"] = ....
End with return out, leaving the caller’s raw DataFrame untouched.

18.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: Safe Merge & Split-Apply-Combine Pipeline
Trace the exact order of operations that protects research tables from sentinel distortion, join row explosions, and cross-group leakage:






flowchart TD
    subgraph Intake["1. Clean & Audit"]
        R1["Raw Survey Copy<br/>strip/title, 999->NaN<br/>to_numeric coerce"]
        R2["Group Impute<br/>groupby.transform<br/>per-stratum median"]
    end
    subgraph Guard["2. Safe Merge"]
        M1["pd.merge Left Join<br/>validate=one_to_one"]
        M2["Duplicate Key?<br/>Raise MergeError"]
    end
    subgraph SAC["3. Group & Agg"]
        S1["Split by Stratum<br/>or District Panel"]
        S2["Apply Named .agg()<br/>or Per-Group shift/roll"]
        S3["Combine Tidy Table<br/>Zero Boundary Leakage"]
    end
    R1 --> R2 --> M1
    M1 -. "fail fast" .-> M2
    M1 --> S1 --> S2 --> S3


 Chapter 18 visual mental model: Safe Merge & Split-Apply-Combine Pipeline 



Notice why stage order is non-negotiable:

You must normalize "rural" \(\rightarrow\) "Rural" before grouping to compute per-residence medians, otherwise lowercase rows form their own tiny broken group.
You must replace 999 \(\rightarrow\) NaN before evaluating thresholds like anc_visits >= 4, otherwise 999 >= 4 falsely evaluates to True!
You must sort by ["district", "year", "epi_week"] and scope .shift() / .rolling() inside .groupby("district") so every district starts cleanly on Week 1.

18.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_04_data_science_math/ch18_data_wrangling_surveys/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Google Colab and run every cell alongside the dissections below using our real bundled mch_survey_sample and epi_surveillance datasets.

18.3.1 Step 0 — Loading Bundled Research Datasets
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sharukh_tutor as tutor

mch_raw = tutor.load_data("mch_survey_sample", as_pandas=True)
epi_raw = tutor.load_data("epi_surveillance", as_pandas=True)

print("MCH survey shape:", mch_raw.shape)
print("Epi panel shape: ", epi_raw.shape)
Expected Output:
MCH survey shape: (500, 12)
Epi panel shape:  (416, 8)



18.3.2 Missingness Audit & Cleaning Dirty Surveys
# 1. Audit explicit NaNs BEFORE sentinel cleaning
raw_counts = mch_raw.isna().sum().astype(int)
raw_pct = (raw_counts / len(mch_raw) * 100).round(2)
raw_audit = pd.DataFrame(
    {"missing_count": raw_counts, "missing_pct": raw_pct}
).sort_values("missing_pct", ascending=False)
print("Explicit NaNs before cleaning:")
print(raw_audit.head(3))

# 2. Inspect dirty casing and hidden DHS sentinel 999
raw_res = mch_raw["residence"].value_counts().to_dict()
raw_anc_mean = round(mch_raw["anc_visits"].mean(), 2)
print("\nRaw residence counts:", raw_res)
print("Raw anc_visits mean (with 999!):", raw_anc_mean)

# 3. Non-mutating Pandas 3.x cleaning copy
mch = mch_raw.copy()
mch["residence"] = mch["residence"].str.strip().str.title()
mch["anc_visits"] = mch["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
mch["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = pd.to_numeric(
    mch["maternal_hb_g_dl"], errors="coerce"
)

print("Clean residence counts:", mch["residence"].value_counts().to_dict())
print("Clean anc_visits NaNs: ", int(mch["anc_visits"].isna().sum()))
print("Clean anc_visits mean: ", round(mch["anc_visits"].mean(), 2))
Expected Output:
Explicit NaNs before cleaning:
                  missing_count  missing_pct
maternal_hb_g_dl             22          4.4
household_id                  0          0.0
division                      0          0.0

Raw residence counts: {'Rural': 345, 'Urban': 140, 'rural': 11, 'urban': 4}
Raw anc_visits mean (with 999!): 19.7
Clean residence counts: {'Rural': 356, 'Urban': 144}
Clean anc_visits NaNs:  8
Clean anc_visits mean:  3.77
Look at that dramatic difference: anc_visits initially showed 0 explicit NaN values, yet hiding inside those 500 rows were 8 sentinel 999 codes that inflated the mean from \(3.77\) to \(19.7\)! Meanwhile, .str.strip().str.title() merged the 11 "rural" and 4 "urban" typos cleanly into Rural (356) and Urban (144).



18.3.3 Group-Median Imputation with .groupby(...).transform("median")
Because hemoglobin missingness differs across strata (16 Rural vs. 6 Urban missing readings, with medians \(11.4\) vs. \(11.6\text{ g/dL}\)), imputing by per-residence median respects MAR structure better than plugging in one global average:
# Check missing Hb by residence (MAR diagnostic) and group medians
hb_na_by_res = mch.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].apply(
    lambda s: int(s.isna().sum())
)
hb_med_by_res = mch.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].median()
print("Missing Hb by residence:", hb_na_by_res.to_dict())
print("Median Hb by residence: ", hb_med_by_res.to_dict())

# Impute missing Hb with per-residence median (non-mutating copy)
mch_imp = mch.copy()
group_medians = (
    mch_imp.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"]
    .transform("median")
)
mch_imp["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = mch_imp["maternal_hb_g_dl"].fillna(
    group_medians
)

post_means = (
    mch_imp.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"]
    .mean().round(2).to_dict()
)
print("Remaining Hb NaNs:", int(mch_imp["maternal_hb_g_dl"].isna().sum()))
print("Post-imputation means:", post_means)
Expected Output:
Missing Hb by residence: {'Rural': 16, 'Urban': 6}
Median Hb by residence:  {'Rural': 11.4, 'Urban': 11.6}
Remaining Hb NaNs: 0
Post-imputation means: {'Rural': 11.41, 'Urban': 11.6}
Why .transform("median") instead of .median()? .groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].median() collapses the table to 2 rows (Rural, Urban), whereas .transform("median") broadcasts each group’s median back onto all 500 rows with exact index alignment so .fillna(group_medians) fills every missing entry cleanly in one vectorized pass.



18.3.4 Safe Relational Joins with pd.merge(..., validate="one_to_one")
When linking a patient intake table to a separate laboratory table, always specify both how= (usually "left" to retain your full cohort) and validate= to enforce key uniqueness:
patients = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "patient_id": ["P-101", "P-102", "P-103", "P-104"],
        "residence": ["Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Urban"],
    }
)
labs = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "patient_id": ["P-101", "P-102", "P-104", "P-999"],
        "ferritin_ng_ml": [18.5, 42.0, 31.2, 25.0],
    }
)

joined = pd.merge(
    patients, labs, on="patient_id", how="left", validate="one_to_one"
)
print(joined.to_string(index=False))
Expected Output:
patient_id residence  ferritin_ng_ml
     P-101     Rural            18.5
     P-102     Urban            42.0
     P-103     Rural             NaN
     P-104     Urban            31.2
Notice two critical guarantees here:

Unmatched patient P-103 stays in the cohort with NaN for ferritin_ng_ml (unlike how="inner", which would silently drop her).
Orphan lab record P-999 is excluded (unlike how="outer", which would inject an unenrolled person).




18.3.5 Split-Apply-Combine with Named .agg()
Named aggregation (new_col=("source_col", "func")) produces clean, flat-column summary tables in a single readable expression:
wealth_tbl = mch_imp.groupby("wealth_quintile").agg(
    n_households=("household_id", "count"),
    stunting_pct=("child_stunted", "mean"),
    anemia_pct=("maternal_anemia", "mean"),
    mean_anc=("anc_visits", "mean"),
)
wealth_tbl["stunting_pct"] = (wealth_tbl["stunting_pct"] * 100).round(1)
wealth_tbl["anemia_pct"] = (wealth_tbl["anemia_pct"] * 100).round(1)
wealth_tbl["mean_anc"] = wealth_tbl["mean_anc"].round(2)

order = ["Poorest", "Poorer", "Middle", "Richer", "Richest"]
print(wealth_tbl.reindex(order))
Expected Output:
                 n_households  stunting_pct  anemia_pct  mean_anc
wealth_quintile                                                  
Poorest                   107          28.0        48.6      2.46
Poorer                    116          19.8        37.1      3.14
Middle                     99           5.1        38.4      4.11
Richer                     91           5.5        31.9      4.37
Richest                    87           8.0        19.5      5.20
Because child_stunted and maternal_anemia are binary 0/1 indicators, taking .mean() * 100 directly yields prevalence percentages—revealing a stark socioeconomic gradient from \(28.0\%\) stunting and \(48.6\%\) anemia in the Poorest quintile down to \(8.0\%\) and \(19.5\%\) in the Richest quintile!



18.3.6 Panel Time Series: Per-District Lags & Rolling Windows
Epidemiological surveillance data (epi_surveillance) is a panel dataset: multiple districts tracked repeatedly across weeks and years. Always sort by ["district", "year", "epi_week"] first, then run .shift(1) and .rolling(...) strictly inside .groupby("district"):
epi = epi_raw.sort_values(["district", "year", "epi_week"]).copy()
epi["prev_week_cases"] = epi.groupby("district")["dengue_cases"].shift(1)
epi["rolling_4w"] = (
    epi.groupby("district")["dengue_cases"]
    .transform(lambda s: s.rolling(window=4, min_periods=1).mean())
    .round(2)
)

cols = ["district", "year", "epi_week", "dengue_cases",
        "prev_week_cases", "rolling_4w"]
dhaka_top = epi[epi["district"] == "Dhaka"][cols].head(5)
ctg_top = epi[epi["district"] == "Chattogram"][cols].head(3)
print("Dhaka first 5 weeks:")
print(dhaka_top.to_string(index=False))
print("\nChattogram first 3 weeks (zero leakage from Dhaka!):")
print(ctg_top.to_string(index=False))
Expected Output:
Dhaka first 5 weeks:
district  year  epi_week  dengue_cases  prev_week_cases  rolling_4w
   Dhaka  2024         1            21              NaN       21.00
   Dhaka  2024         2            32             21.0       26.50
   Dhaka  2024         3            42             32.0       31.67
   Dhaka  2024         4            45             42.0       35.00
   Dhaka  2024         5            23             45.0       35.50

Chattogram first 3 weeks (zero leakage from Dhaka!):
  district  year  epi_week  dengue_cases  prev_week_cases  rolling_4w
Chattogram  2024         1            34              NaN       34.00
Chattogram  2024         2            15             34.0       24.50
Chattogram  2024         3            28             15.0       25.67
Look closely at Chattogram 2024 Week 1: prev_week_cases is NaN and rolling_4w is 34.00 (its own Week 1 count, thanks to min_periods=1). Zero cases leaked across the district boundary!



18.3.7 Break It On Purpose! (Wrangling Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — pd.errors.MergeError (Duplicate Keys Caught!)



dup_labs = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "patient_id": ["P-101", "P-101", "P-102"],
        "ferritin_ng_ml": [18.5, 22.0, 42.0],
    }
)
pd.merge(
    patients, dup_labs, on="patient_id", how="left", validate="one_to_one"
)
Python’s Traceback:
pandas.errors.MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset;
not a one-to-one merge
Diagnosis: dup_labs has two rows for "P-101". Without validate="one_to_one", Pandas would silently duplicate "P-101" in the merged table!
Fix: Deduplicate or aggregate dup_labs per patient_id (e.g., taking the latest or mean lab value) before merging.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — KeyError (Missing Join Key)



misnamed_labs = pd.DataFrame(
    {"household_id": ["P-101", "P-102"], "hb_g_dl": [11.4, 10.2]}
)
pd.merge(patients, misnamed_labs, on="patient_id", how="left")
Python’s Traceback:
KeyError: 'patient_id'
Diagnosis: patients uses "patient_id" while misnamed_labs uses "household_id", so on="patient_id" cannot find the join column on the right table.
Fix: Either rename the column first (misnamed_labs.rename(columns={"household_id": "patient_id"})) or pass explicit left_on="patient_id", right_on="household_id".








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ValueError (.astype(float) on Dirty Text)



dirty_hb = pd.Series(["11.2", "N/A", "9.8"])
dirty_hb.astype(float)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'N/A'
Diagnosis: Strict .astype(float) crashes on the very first non-numeric token ("N/A", ".", "", or "missing"), which are ubiquitous in CSV exports from clinic spreadsheets.
Fix: Always cast messy numeric columns with pd.to_numeric(series, errors="coerce") so valid numbers become floats and unparseable tokens cleanly become NaN.

18.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: A Ministry of Health policy brief needs an automated, reproducible function build_equity_brief(raw_mch) that takes a raw DHS maternal-child survey, cleans all dirty casing and sentinel codes, imputes missing maternal hemoglobin by residence median, derives WHO’s 4+ antenatal care visits (anc_4plus) indicator, and outputs a flat, sorted residence \(\times\) wealth_quintile equity table without mutating raw_mch.

18.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Non-Mutating Cleaning Sequence (Strict Order):

Copy raw_mch (df = raw_mch.copy()).
Normalize residence with .str.strip().str.title() first.
Neutralize sentinel anc_visits == 999 \(\rightarrow\) np.nan before thresholding.
Coerce maternal_hb_g_dl via pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") and impute missing values with per-residence median via .groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].transform("median").
Derive anc_4plus = (df["anc_visits"] >= 4).fillna(False).astype(bool).

Stratified Aggregation Contract:

Group with groupby(["residence", "wealth_quintile"], as_index=False) so stratification keys stay flat columns.
Compute n_households, stunting_pct, anemia_pct, and anc4_pct (each percentage scaled by \(100\) and rounded to 1 decimal place).
Sort deterministically by ["residence", "wealth_quintile"] and reset the index.

Verification Plan:

Check Rural + Poorest vs. Urban + Richest: anc4_pct should rise sharply with both wealth and urbanicity, and raw_mch["anc_visits"] must still contain its original 8 sentinel 999 entries untouched.




18.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
def build_equity_brief(raw_mch):
    """Clean DHS survey and summarize residence x wealth equity gaps."""
    df = raw_mch.copy()
    df["residence"] = df["residence"].str.strip().str.title()
    df["anc_visits"] = df["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    df["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = pd.to_numeric(
        df["maternal_hb_g_dl"], errors="coerce"
    )
    med = df.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].transform("median")
    df["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = df["maternal_hb_g_dl"].fillna(med)
    df["anc_4plus"] = (df["anc_visits"] >= 4).fillna(False).astype(bool)

    brief = df.groupby(
        ["residence", "wealth_quintile"], as_index=False
    ).agg(
        n_households=("household_id", "count"),
        stunting_pct=("child_stunted", "mean"),
        anemia_pct=("maternal_anemia", "mean"),
        anc4_pct=("anc_4plus", "mean"),
    )
    for col in ("stunting_pct", "anemia_pct", "anc4_pct"):
        brief[col] = (brief[col] * 100).round(1)
    return brief.sort_values(["residence", "wealth_quintile"]).reset_index(
        drop=True
    )

equity_brief = build_equity_brief(mch_raw)
print(equity_brief.to_string(index=False))
Output:
residence wealth_quintile  n_households  stunting_pct  anemia_pct  anc4_pct
    Rural          Middle            71           4.2        43.7      60.6
    Rural          Poorer            86          22.1        33.7      37.2
    Rural         Poorest            91          31.9        48.4      20.9
    Rural          Richer            56           5.4        33.9      58.9
    Rural         Richest            52           5.8        19.2      76.9
    Urban          Middle            28           7.1        25.0      89.3
    Urban          Poorer            30          13.3        46.7      63.3
    Urban         Poorest            16           6.2        50.0      50.0
    Urban          Richer            35           5.7        28.6      77.1
    Urban         Richest            35          11.4        20.0      88.6
Look at that single table—ready for a Lancet Global Health policy brief: only \(20.9\%\) of mothers in Rural + Poorest households achieve 4+ ANC visits (with \(31.9\%\) child stunting), compared to \(88.6\%\) ANC4+ coverage in Urban + Richest households!

18.6 Stage 6 — Concept & Execution Trace Test (No Computer Allowed!)
Trace every wrangling question carefully on paper before checking Stage 8:

MCAR vs. MAR vs. MNAR: In a maternal nutrition survey, rural clinics have \(12\%\) missing hemoglobin tests because of rural reagent stockouts while urban clinics have \(2\%\) missing. Assuming missingness depends only on observed residence (not on a mother’s true anemia severity), which missing-data mechanism is this?
Sentinel Order-of-Operations Bug: Suppose a row has anc_visits = 999 (DHS "Don't know"). If you run df["anc_4plus"] = df["anc_visits"] >= 4 before replacing 999 with np.nan, what boolean value does anc_4plus wrongly receive?
Pandas 3.x Copy-on-Write Purity: Why should a wrangling function write out = df.copy(); out["x"] = out["x"].fillna(0); return out instead of df["x"].fillna(0, inplace=True)?
Strict Cast vs. Safe Coercion: What happens if you run pd.Series(["10.5", "N/A", "12.0"]).astype(float) versus pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(["10.5", "N/A", "12.0"]), errors="coerce")?
.transform("median") vs. .median(): On a 500-row DataFrame with 2 residence categories (Rural, Urban), what is the length of df.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].median() versus df.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].transform("median")?
Row-Explosion Arithmetic: patients has 4 unique IDs (P1..P4). labs has 5 rows where P1 appears twice and P2..P4 appear once each. How many rows does pd.merge(patients, labs, on="patient_id", how="left") return without validate, and what happens with validate="one_to_one"?
Left Join vs. Inner Join Cohort Bias: In patients (4 patients) left-joined to labs (3 matching patients plus 1 orphan lab P99), why does how="inner" distort cohort denominators while how="left" preserves them?
as_index=False in Multi-Key GroupBy: What structural difference appears in the returned DataFrame when you pass as_index=False to df.groupby(["residence", "wealth_quintile"], as_index=False).agg(...)?
Cross-District Lag Leakage: A sorted DataFrame has Chattogram Weeks 1–52 followed immediately by Dhaka Weeks 1–52. If Chattogram Week 52 had 85 dengue cases and you accidentally run df["dengue_cases"].shift(1) without .groupby("district"), what value lands in Dhaka Week 1’s prev_week_cases?
Rolling Window min_periods=1: For a single district whose first three weekly dengue counts are [20, 40, 60], what are the first three values of .rolling(window=4, min_periods=1).mean() versus .rolling(window=4).mean() (default min_periods=4)?

text:
18.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

18.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

MAR (Missing At Random): Missingness depends on an observed variable (residence), not on the unobserved hemoglobin value itself—making per-residence median imputation principled.
True! Because \(999 \ge 4\), computing anc_4plus before replacing 999 with np.nan falsely classifies unknown antenatal history as meeting the WHO 4+ visit target.
Creating out = df.copy() and using direct assignment (out["x"] = ...) respects Pandas 3.x Copy-on-Write, preserves the caller’s raw data for auditability, and avoids inplace=True returning None.
.astype(float) raises ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'N/A', whereas pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") returns Series([10.5, NaN, 12.0], dtype=float64).
.median() returns length 2 (one scalar per group); .transform("median") returns length 500 (one group median aligned to every original row index).
Without validate, Pandas silently returns 5 rows (duplicating P1!); with validate="one_to_one", Pandas immediately raises pd.errors.MergeError.
how="inner" silently drops patients who lack a lab test, shrinking the cohort denominator and biasing prevalence estimates toward tested patients; how="left" keeps every enrolled patient (marking missing labs as NaN) while excluding orphan lab P99.
With as_index=False, residence and wealth_quintile remain regular flat columns instead of becoming a two-level MultiIndex.
85.0 (Chattogram’s final week leaks into Dhaka’s Week 1!). Grouping by "district" first ensures Dhaka’s Week 1 receives NaN.
With min_periods=1: [20.0, 30.0, 40.0]; with default min_periods=4: [NaN, NaN, NaN] because fewer than 4 observations are available in Weeks 1–3.



18.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# To-Do 18.1
def clean_mch_survey(df):
    """Return a cleaned copy of a dirty DHS/MCH household survey."""
    out = df.copy()
    out["residence"] = out["residence"].str.strip().str.title()
    out["anc_visits"] = out["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    out["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = pd.to_numeric(
        out["maternal_hb_g_dl"], errors="coerce"
    )
    return out

# To-Do 18.2
def audit_missingness_table(df):
    """Return column-level missing counts and percentages sorted neatly."""
    counts = df.isna().sum().astype(int)
    pcts = (counts / len(df) * 100).round(2)
    audit = pd.DataFrame(
        {"missing_count": counts, "missing_pct": pcts}
    )
    return audit.sort_index().sort_values(
        "missing_pct", ascending=False, kind="mergesort"
    )

# To-Do 18.3
def impute_group_median(df, value_col, group_col):
    """Fill NaNs in value_col using per-group medians without mutation."""
    out = df.copy()
    medians = out.groupby(group_col)[value_col].transform("median")
    out[value_col] = out[value_col].fillna(medians)
    return out

# To-Do 18.4
def safe_merge_patient_labs(patients_df, labs_df):
    """Left-join patients to labs with strict 1-to-1 key validation."""
    return pd.merge(
        patients_df,
        labs_df,
        on="patient_id",
        how="left",
        validate="one_to_one",
    )

# To-Do 18.5
def groupby_wealth_outcomes(mch_df):
    """Aggregate stunting, anemia, and ANC outcomes by wealth quintile."""
    out = mch_df.groupby("wealth_quintile").agg(
        n_households=("child_stunted", "size"),
        stunting_pct=("child_stunted", "mean"),
        anemia_pct=("maternal_anemia", "mean"),
        mean_anc=("anc_visits", "mean"),
    )
    out["stunting_pct"] = (out["stunting_pct"] * 100).round(1)
    out["anemia_pct"] = (out["anemia_pct"] * 100).round(1)
    out["mean_anc"] = out["mean_anc"].round(2)
    return out

# To-Do 18.6
def add_rolling_dengue_avg(epi_df, window=4):
    """Add per-district rolling dengue mean without boundary leakage."""
    out = epi_df.sort_values(["district", "year", "epi_week"]).copy()
    out["rolling_dengue"] = (
        out.groupby("district")["dengue_cases"]
        .transform(lambda s: s.rolling(window=window, min_periods=1).mean())
        .round(2)
    )
    return out


18.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 18 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
# Exam Task 18.1 (30 pts)
def build_clean_dhs_analytic_table(mch_df):
    """Clean DHS survey, impute Hb by residence, and flag anc_4plus."""
    out = mch_df.copy()
    out["residence"] = out["residence"].str.strip().str.title()
    out["anc_visits"] = out["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    out["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = pd.to_numeric(
        out["maternal_hb_g_dl"], errors="coerce"
    )
    medians = out.groupby("residence")["maternal_hb_g_dl"].transform(
        "median"
    )
    out["maternal_hb_g_dl"] = out["maternal_hb_g_dl"].fillna(medians)
    out["anc_4plus"] = (
        (out["anc_visits"] >= 4).fillna(False).astype(bool)
    )
    return out

# Exam Task 18.2 (35 pts)
def equity_gap_by_residence_wealth(clean_mch_df):
    """Stratify stunting, anemia, and ANC4+ by residence and wealth."""
    out = clean_mch_df.groupby(
        ["residence", "wealth_quintile"], as_index=False
    ).agg(
        n_households=("child_stunted", "size"),
        stunting_pct=("child_stunted", "mean"),
        anemia_pct=("maternal_anemia", "mean"),
        anc4_pct=("anc_4plus", "mean"),
    )
    for col in ("stunting_pct", "anemia_pct", "anc4_pct"):
        out[col] = (out[col] * 100).round(1)
    return out.sort_values(
        ["residence", "wealth_quintile"]
    ).reset_index(drop=True)

# Exam Task 18.3 (35 pts)
def prepare_epi_time_features(epi_df):
    """Engineer incidence, 1-week lag, and 4-week rolling dengue mean."""
    out = epi_df.sort_values(["district", "year", "epi_week"]).copy()
    out["incidence_per_100k"] = (
        out["dengue_cases"] / out["population"] * 100_000
    ).round(2)
    out["prev_week_cases"] = (
        out.groupby("district")["dengue_cases"].shift(1)
    )
    out["rolling_4w_cases"] = (
        out.groupby("district")["dengue_cases"]
        .transform(lambda s: s.rolling(window=4, min_periods=1).mean())
        .round(2)
    )
    return out


18.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 18 Failure Modes

Wrong Cleaning Order (999 >= 4 & Unnormalized Group Imputation): Thresholding anc_visits >= 4 before neutralizing 999 inflates ANC4+ coverage, and imputing hemoglobin before normalizing "rural" to "Rural" splits rural respondents across separate medians. Always follow: Normalize categories \(\rightarrow\) Neutralize sentinels \(\rightarrow\) Coerce & Impute \(\rightarrow\) Derive indicators.
Unvalidated Merges (Silent Row Explosion): Calling pd.merge(patients, labs, on="patient_id", how="left") without validate="one_to_one" lets duplicate lab keys silently inflate sample sizes and double-count sick patients.
Global Lags/Rolling Windows on Panel Data: Calling .shift(1) or .rolling(4).mean() directly on a multi-district DataFrame leaks one district’s final weeks into the next district’s Week 1. Always sort by [entity, time] and scope window operators inside .groupby(entity).








NoteUp Next — Exploratory Data Analysis & Publication-Quality Visualization



Your DHS maternal-child tables and weekly dengue panels are now clean, validated, and leak-free. Numbers in a printed table tell half the story—peer reviewers expect clear, colorblind-safe figures that surface disparities and epidemic waves at a glance. In Chapter 19, you will turn these exact wrangled DataFrames into publication-grade Matplotlib and Seaborn visualizations.

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

title: 19  Statistical Visualization & Publication-Ready Figures (Matplotlib & Seaborn)
section: 19.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Exploratory Sketches vs. Publication Figures
text:
19.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Exploratory Sketches vs. Publication Figures
In Chapters 16–18, you learned to vectorize math with NumPy, aggregate tables with Pandas, and scrub messy clinical surveys. Yet a journal reviewer rarely inspects your raw .csv file—the very first thing a reviewer, policymaker, or thesis examiner reads is Figure 1.
There is a massive gap between an exploratory sketch (calling plt.hist(x) with default blue bars, missing units, and overlapping labels) and a publication-ready figure:

Every axis carries units: Writing "Hemoglobin (g/dL)" and "Systolic BP (mmHg)" eliminates ambiguity across international clinical readers.
Perceptual honesty comes first: Human eyes judge aligned position and length far more accurately than pie-chart angles or dual y-axis slopes. Sorting bar charts by magnitude and stacking related time series with sharex=True makes patterns effortless to verify.
Colorblind accessibility is mandatory: Roughly \(8\%\) of men and \(0.5\%\) of women experience red-green color-vision deficiency. Replacing default red/green contrasts with the Okabe-Ito palette (#0072B2 blue, #E69F00 orange, #D55E00 vermilion, #009E73 bluish green, #56B4E9 sky blue) keeps figures legible in both color and grayscale print.
Reproducible figure functions beat throwaway cells: Wrapping each chart in a function that returns (fig, ax) lets you unit-test titles, thresholds, and artist counts—and regenerate every manuscript figure automatically when new survey waves arrive.







NoteMental Model — Canvas Frame (Figure), Drawing Panels (Axes) & Ink (Artists)



Think of Matplotlib as a medical journal page layout:

Figure (fig): The entire blank journal page (e.g., 10.5 x 4.2 inches). It owns overall margins, fig.suptitle(...), and the export printer (fig.savefig(...)).
Axes (ax or axes[i]): An individual framed chart panel sitting on the page. Every axis label (ax.set_xlabel), panel title (ax.set_title), tick mark, spine, and legend lives on an Axes.
Artists (patches, lines, collections, texts): The actual ink drawn inside an Axes—histogram bars (Rectangle patches), trend lines (Line2D), scatter points (PathCollection), and heatmap annotations (Text).




19.1.1 Why the Object-Oriented API (fig, ax) Beats plt.plot(...)
Beginners often copy tutorials using plt.plot(...), plt.title(...), and plt.xlabel(...). That state-machine interface secretly mutates whichever panel Matplotlib thinks is “currently active”—a recipe for chaos the moment you build a 1x2 or 2x1 multi-panel paper figure. By explicitly creating fig, ax = plt.subplots(...) and calling methods on ax, every line of code names the exact panel it modifies.

text:
19.2 Stage 2 — Visual Mental Model: Matplotlib Object-Oriented Hierarchy
Trace how every Matplotlib and Seaborn visualization flows from a single Figure container down to Axes panels, visual Artists, and camera-ready file export:






flowchart TD
    subgraph FigCanvas["Figure Canvas"]
        F["fig = Figure<br/>figsize, suptitle, tight_layout"]
    end
    subgraph AxesPanels["Axes Panels"]
        A0["axes[0] (Axes)<br/>set_title, set_xlabel, set_ylabel"]
        A1["axes[1] (Axes)<br/>sharex=True, spines, legend"]
    end
    subgraph Artists["Visual Artists"]
        P["Patches & Bars<br/>ax.hist, ax.bar, ax.barh"]
        L["Lines & Cutoff<br/>ax.plot, ax.axvline"]
        C["Collections<br/>ax.scatter, sns.heatmap"]
    end
    subgraph Export["Export Pipeline"]
        E["fig.savefig(..., dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')<br/>PNG (raster) + PDF (vector) -> plt.close(fig)"]
    end
    F -->|"plt.subplots()"| A0
    F -->|"plt.subplots()"| A1
    A0 --> P
    A0 --> L
    A1 --> C
    F -. "camera-ready" .-> E


 Chapter 19 visual mental model: Matplotlib Object-Oriented Hierarchy 



Notice that Seaborn sits directly on top of this hierarchy: passing ax=ax into sns.heatmap(..., ax=ax) or sns.scatterplot(..., ax=ax) draws Seaborn’s statistical artists right into your chosen Matplotlib Axes, so you retain 100% control over titles, subplots, and 300-DPI exports.






WarningThe Silent Figure Memory Leak in Batch Scripts



Every call to plt.subplots() registers a live Figure inside Matplotlib’s global manager. If a loop generates 50 district reports without calling plt.close(fig) after fig.savefig(...), all 50 figures stay pinned in RAM—triggering RuntimeWarning: More than 20 figures have been opened and eventually crashing Colab. Always pair every batch figure creation or automated test with plt.close(fig)!

19.3 Stage 3 — Line-by-Line Code Walkthrough & Error Anatomy
Open part_04_data_science_math/ch19_visualization_storytelling/01_walkthrough.ipynb in Colab and execute every cell alongside the dissections below.

19.3.1 Setup & Loading the Spine Datasets
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import sharukh_tutor as tutor

clinic = tutor.load_data("clinic_triage", as_pandas=True)
clinic["bmi"] = clinic["weight_kg"] / ((clinic["height_cm"] / 100) ** 2)
mch = tutor.load_data("mch_survey_sample", as_pandas=True)
epi = tutor.load_data("epi_surveillance", as_pandas=True)

print("clinic_triage:    ", clinic.shape)
print("mch_survey_sample:", mch.shape)
print("epi_surveillance: ", epi.shape)
Expected Output:
clinic_triage:     (120, 12)
mch_survey_sample: (500, 12)
epi_surveillance:  (416, 8)



19.3.2 Matplotlib OO API, Clinical Cutoffs & Annotations
Watch how fig, ax = plt.subplots(...) layers histogram bars, a WHO \(11.0\text{ g/dL}\) dashed anemia cutoff, a callout arrow, and clean despined axes:
OKABE_ITO = {
    "blue": "#0072B2",
    "orange": "#E69F00",
    "vermilion": "#D55E00",
    "green": "#009E73",
    "sky": "#56B4E9",
}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
hb = clinic["hemoglobin_g_dl"].dropna()
ax.hist(hb, bins=16, color=OKABE_ITO["blue"], edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(
    11.0,
    color=OKABE_ITO["vermilion"],
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=2.0,
    label="WHO Cutoff (11.0 g/dL)",
)
ax.annotate(
    "Anemic tail (<11.0)",
    xy=(11.0, 12),
    xytext=(8.8, 16),
    arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": OKABE_ITO["vermilion"]},
    fontsize=9,
)
ax.set_title("Clinic Triage Hemoglobin Distribution")
ax.set_xlabel("Hemoglobin (g/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("Patient Count")
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)

print("Patches:", len(ax.patches), "| Lines:", len(ax.lines))
print("Title:  ", ax.get_title())
plt.close(fig)
Expected Output:
Patches: 16 | Lines: 1
Title:   Clinic Triage Hemoglobin Distribution
Three publication habits are working together here:

Programmatic inspectability: ax.patches holds the 16 histogram bars and ax.lines holds the dashed cutoff line—the exact artists our automated checks verify!
Despining reduces chartjunk: Hiding the top and right box borders (ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)) increases the data-ink ratio cleanly.
Explicit cleanup: Calling plt.close(fig) releases memory immediately once the figure is inspected or saved.




19.3.3 Okabe-Ito Palette: Sorted Horizontal Bars & Grouped Scatter
Always sort categorical bars by magnitude rather than alphabetically, and encode clinical triage severity with distinct Okabe-Ito hues:
district_summary = (
    clinic.assign(is_anemic=clinic["hemoglobin_g_dl"] < 11.0)
    .groupby("district", as_index=False)["is_anemic"]
    .mean()
    .rename(columns={"is_anemic": "anemia_pct"})
)
district_summary["anemia_pct"] *= 100
ordered = district_summary.sort_values("anemia_pct", ascending=True)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
ax.barh(ordered["district"], ordered["anemia_pct"], color="#009E73")
ax.set_title("Anemia Prevalence by District (Sorted)")
ax.set_xlabel("Anemia Prevalence (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("District")
top_row = ordered.iloc[-1]
print(f"Top district: {top_row['district']} ({top_row['anemia_pct']:.1f}%)")
plt.close(fig)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
priority_colors = {"Routine": "#0072B2", "Moderate": "#D55E00"}
for priority, sub in clinic.groupby("triage_priority"):
    ax.scatter(
        sub["bmi"],
        sub["systolic_bp"],
        color=priority_colors.get(priority, "#E69F00"),
        alpha=0.8,
        label=priority,
    )
ax.set_title("BMI vs. Systolic BP by Triage Priority")
ax.set_xlabel("BMI (kg/m^2)")
ax.set_ylabel("Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)")
ax.legend(title="Triage Priority")
print("Scatter groups plotted:", len(ax.collections))
plt.close(fig)
Expected Output:
Top district: Rangpur (13.8%)
Scatter groups plotted: 2
Notice why we sorted ascending=True before calling ax.barh(...): Matplotlib draws horizontal bars from \(y = 0\) (bottom) up to \(y = N - 1\) (top), so sorting ascending places Rangpur (13.8%) squarely at the top!



19.3.4 Time-Series Seasonality & 4-Week Rolling Mean
Weekly epidemiological counts fluctuate noisily. Plotting the raw weekly curve semi-transparently (alpha=0.65) behind a bold 4-week rolling mean exposes monsoon outbreak peaks honestly:
dhaka = (
    epi[epi["district"] == "Dhaka"]
    .sort_values(["year", "epi_week"])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
x_weeks = range(1, len(dhaka) + 1)
roll_4w = dhaka["dengue_cases"].rolling(4, min_periods=1).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.8))
ax.plot(
    x_weeks, dhaka["dengue_cases"], color="#56B4E9", alpha=0.65,
    label="Weekly Cases",
)
ax.plot(
    x_weeks, roll_4w, color="#D55E00", linewidth=2.2,
    label="4-Week Rolling Mean",
)
ax.set_title("Dhaka Weekly Dengue Cases & 4-Week Trend (2024-2025)")
ax.set_xlabel("Sequential Epidemiological Week")
ax.set_ylabel("Reported Dengue Cases")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
print("Peak weekly Dhaka cases:", int(dhaka["dengue_cases"].max()))
print("Peak 4-week rolling mean:", round(float(roll_4w.max()), 1))
plt.close(fig)
Expected Output:
Peak weekly Dhaka cases: 395
Peak 4-week rolling mean: 343.5



19.3.5 Multi-Panel Subplots (1x2 MCH Wealth Equity)
When comparing two public health indicators across the same socioeconomic gradient, side-by-side panels (plt.subplots(1, 2, ...)) with an explicit quintile_order reindex let readers scan disparities instantaneously:
quintile_order = ["Poorest", "Poorer", "Middle", "Richer", "Richest"]
mch_eq = (
    mch.groupby("wealth_quintile")[["child_stunted", "maternal_anemia"]]
    .mean()
    .reindex(quintile_order)
    * 100
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))
axes[0].bar(mch_eq.index, mch_eq["child_stunted"], color="#0072B2")
axes[0].set_title("Child Stunting Prevalence")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Wealth Quintile")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Prevalence (%)")

axes[1].bar(mch_eq.index, mch_eq["maternal_anemia"], color="#D55E00")
axes[1].set_title("Maternal Anemia Prevalence")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Wealth Quintile")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Prevalence (%)")

fig.suptitle("MCH Health Inequities Across Wealth Quintiles")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Poorest vs Richest stunting (%):")
print(
    round(float(mch_eq.loc["Poorest", "child_stunted"]), 1),
    "vs",
    round(float(mch_eq.loc["Richest", "child_stunted"]), 1),
)
plt.close(fig)
Expected Output:
Poorest vs Richest stunting (%):
28.0 vs 8.0
Without .reindex(quintile_order), Pandas sorts strings alphabetically (Middle, Poorer, Poorest, Richer, Richest), destroying the socioeconomic gradient!



19.3.6 Seaborn Correlation Heatmap & 300-DPI Dual Export
For correlation matrices spanning \([-1, +1]\), always pair a diverging colormap ("coolwarm" or "RdBu_r") with center=0 and annot=True, then export both raster (300-DPI PNG) and vector (PDF) formats inside a temporary directory during testing:
num_cols = ["age_years", "bmi", "systolic_bp", "hemoglobin_g_dl"]
corr_mat = clinic[num_cols].corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.6))
sns.heatmap(
    corr_mat, annot=True, fmt=".2f", center=0, cmap="coolwarm", ax=ax
)
ax.set_title("Clinic Triage Feature Correlation Matrix")

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
    png_path = Path(tmpdir) / "corr_heatmap.png"
    pdf_path = Path(tmpdir) / "corr_heatmap.pdf"
    fig.savefig(png_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    fig.savefig(pdf_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    print("300-DPI PNG bytes:", png_path.stat().st_size)
    print("Vector PDF bytes: ", pdf_path.stat().st_size)

plt.close(fig)
Expected Output:
300-DPI PNG bytes: 115944
Vector PDF bytes:  15605








Format
Best For
Key savefig Flags




PNG (dpi=300)
Slides, Word docs, web previews, dense scatter plots
dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight"


PDF (vector)
LaTeX / Quarto journal manuscripts (infinite zoom)
bbox_inches="tight"






19.3.7 Break It On Purpose! (Visualization Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — ValueError (Mismatched x and y Lengths)



fig, ax = plt.subplots()
try:
    weeks = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    cases = [18, 29, 44]
    ax.plot(weeks, cases)
finally:
    plt.close(fig)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: x and y must have same first dimension,
but have shapes (4,) and (3,)
Diagnosis: weeks has 4 entries while cases has only 3 (often caused by dropping NaNs from y without aligning x, or slicing one series differently).
Fix: Filter and align a single DataFrame first (sub = df.dropna(subset=["epi_week", "dengue_cases"])), then plot sub["epi_week"] against sub["dengue_cases"].








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — KeyError (Missing Column in DataFrame)



fig, ax = plt.subplots()
try:
    ax.hist(clinic["hb_g_dl"])
finally:
    plt.close(fig)
Python’s Traceback:
KeyError: 'hb_g_dl'
Diagnosis: The clinic_triage table names the column "hemoglobin_g_dl", not "hb_g_dl".
Fix: Print list(clinic.columns) before writing plotting code so column names match the DataFrame schema exactly.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ValueError (Invalid Colormap Name)



fig, ax = plt.subplots()
try:
    sns.heatmap(
        corr_mat, cmap=plt.get_cmap("hospital_rainbow"), ax=ax
    )
finally:
    plt.close(fig)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: 'hospital_rainbow' is not a valid value for name.
Did you mean one of: 'gist_rainbow', 'gist_rainbow_r', 'rainbow'?
Diagnosis: "hospital_rainbow" is not a registered Matplotlib colormap (and rainbow colormaps distort perception anyway!).
Fix: Use perceptually uniform sequential palettes ("viridis", "cividis", "crest") for ordered quantities, and zero-centered diverging palettes ("coolwarm", "RdBu_r", "vlag") for signed correlations.
