import pandas as pd
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Exam Task 23.1 (30 pts)
def evaluate_screening_thresholds(y_true, y_prob, thresholds):
    """Evaluate clinical screening metrics across probability thresholds."""
    yt = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=int)
    yprob = np.asarray(y_prob, dtype=float)
    rows = []
    for t in thresholds:
        yp = (yprob >= t).astype(int)
        tp = int(np.sum((yt == 1) & (yp == 1)))
        fp = int(np.sum((yt == 0) & (yp == 1)))
        tn = int(np.sum((yt == 0) & (yp == 0)))
        fn = int(np.sum((yt == 1) & (yp == 0)))
        sens = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
        spec = tn / (tn + fp) if (tn + fp) > 0 else 0.0
        prec = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) > 0 else 0.0
        f1 = 2.0 * prec * sens / (prec + sens) if (prec + sens) > 0 else 0.0
        rows.append({
            "threshold": round(float(t), 4),
            "sensitivity": round(sens, 4),
            "specificity": round(spec, 4),
            "precision": round(prec, 4),
            "f1": round(f1, 4),
            "flagged_pct": round(100.0 * float(np.mean(yp)), 4),
        })
    cols = [
        "threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity",
        "precision", "f1", "flagged_pct",
    ]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=cols)

# Exam Task 23.2 (35 pts)
def calibration_audit_bins(y_true, y_prob, n_bins=5):
    """Audit probability calibration via equal-width bins, ECE & Brier."""
    yt = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=float)
    yp = np.asarray(y_prob, dtype=float)
    edges = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_bins + 1)
    rows = []
    ece = 0.0
    n_total = len(yt)
    for idx in range(n_bins):
        lo, hi = edges[idx], edges[idx + 1]
        if idx < n_bins - 1:
            mask = (yp >= lo) & (yp < hi)
        else:
            mask = (yp >= lo) & (yp <= hi)
        cnt = int(np.sum(mask))
        if cnt == 0:
            continue
        mp = float(np.mean(yp[mask]))
        obs = float(np.mean(yt[mask]))
        ece += (cnt / n_total) * abs(obs - mp)
        rows.append({
            "mean_pred": round(mp, 4),
            "obs_rate": round(obs, 4),
            "count": cnt,
        })
    bins_df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["mean_pred", "obs_rate", "count"])
    return {
        "ece": round(ece, 4),
        "brier_score": round(float(brier_score_loss(yt, yp)), 4),
        "bins": bins_df,
    }

# Exam Task 23.3 (35 pts)
def train_calibrated_anemia_classifier(mch_df, seed=42):
    """Train leak-free scaled + sigmoid-calibrated anemia classifier."""
    work = mch_df.copy()
    work["residence"] = (
        work["residence"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
    )
    work["anc_visits"] = work["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    work["is_urban"] = (work["residence"] == "Urban").astype(int)
    wealth_map = {
        "Poorest": 1, "Poorer": 2, "Middle": 3,
        "Richer": 4, "Richest": 5,
    }
    work["wealth_num"] = work["wealth_quintile"].map(wealth_map)
    feat_cols = [
        "maternal_age_years", "anc_visits", "wealth_num", "is_urban"
    ]
    clean = work[["maternal_anemia"] + feat_cols].dropna()
    X = clean[feat_cols]
    y = clean["maternal_anemia"].astype(int)
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=seed
    )
    pipe = Pipeline([
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)),
    ])
    pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    prob_raw = pipe.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(pipe, method="sigmoid", cv=5)
    cal.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    prob_cal = cal.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_te, prob_cal)
    best_idx = int(np.argmax(tpr - fpr))
    return {
        "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_te, prob_cal)), 4),
        "pr_auc": round(float(average_precision_score(y_te, prob_cal)), 4),
        "brier_raw": round(float(brier_score_loss(y_te, prob_raw)), 4),
        "brier_calibrated": round(
            float(brier_score_loss(y_te, prob_cal)), 4
        ),
        "youden_threshold": round(float(thresholds[best_idx]), 4),
    }


23.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 23 Failure Modes

Trusting .predict() at Threshold 0.50 on Imbalanced Outcomes: On child_stunted (13.8% prevalence), default .predict() yielded 86.2% accuracy with 0.0% sensitivity. Always inspect continuous probabilities (predict_proba[:, 1]), evaluate ROC-AUC/PR-AUC/Brier/ECE, and select a domain-appropriate cutoff such as Youden’s \(J\).
Treating Reweighting (class_weight="balanced") or SMOTE as Free Calibration: Upweighting minority cases boosts recall at 0.50 but leaves PR-AUC unchanged while more than doubling Brier score (0.1066 -> 0.2289). Either keep unweighted calibrated probabilities and tune the threshold, or apply post-hoc Platt/isotonic calibration after reweighting.
Mixing Continuous Probabilities and Binary Labels (or Dropping p == 1.0): Passing continuous scores to confusion_matrix raises ValueError, passing binary labels to roc_auc_score destroys ranking resolution, and using half-open [lo, hi) on the final calibration bin silently drops exact 1.0 probabilities.








TipBridge to Chapter 24 — Trees, Random Forests & Gradient Boosting



Now that you can rigorously evaluate discrimination (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC), calibration (Brier, ECE), and clinical decision thresholds (Youden’s \(J\)) on linear classifiers, you have the exact yardstick needed for non-linear tree ensembles (Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Histogram/LightGBM/XGBoost Gradient Boosting) in Chapter 24—where flexible splits capture complex clinical interactions and post-hoc calibration becomes even more valuable!

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Implement exact 3-feature Shapley value attribution across all \(3! = 6\) permutations, verify the Efficiency Axiom (\(\phi_0 + \sum_i \phi_i = f(x)\)), and interpret local SHAP explanations for clinical risk prediction.

section: 24.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Trees & Ensembles Rule Tabular Science
text:
24.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Trees & Ensembles Rule Tabular Science
Linear and logistic regression assume that every predictor shifts the log-odds smoothly along a straight line. Real clinical and epidemiological data rarely obey neat straight lines:

Threshold Effects: Maternal hemoglobin below \(11.0\text{ g/dL}\) signals clinical anemia, and fewer than \(4\) antenatal care (ANC) visits marks WHO-defined inadequate care. A Decision Tree discovers these exact cutoffs automatically.
Automatic Feature Interactions: Low wealth paired with fewer than \(4\) ANC visits may elevate child stunting risk far beyond the sum of either factor alone. Every root-to-leaf path in a tree is a natural interaction rule (wealth_rank <= 2.5 AND anc_visits <= 3.5).
Monotonic Scale Invariance: Because trees split on order thresholds (\(x \le t\)), you do not need StandardScaler or log-transforms for tree splits to work.

Yet a single unconstrained Decision Tree has an Achilles’ heel: extreme variance. Grow a tree deep enough and it creates one tiny leaf per training household—scoring near 1.000 training AUC while collapsing on new patients.
Modern machine learning solves single-tree fragility through two complementary ensemble philosophies:

Bagging & Random Forests (Variance Reduction in Parallel): Train \(B\) deep trees independently on bootstrap resamples of the training rows, randomly restricting each split to a subset of features (max_features="sqrt"). Averaging decorrelated trees slashes variance dramatically, and the ~36.8% of rows omitted from each bootstrap sample provide near-free Out-of-Bag (OOB) validation!
Gradient Boosting (Bias Reduction in Sequence): Train shallow trees (“weak learners”) one after another, where each new tree predicts the residual error left behind by the ensemble so far, scaled by a shrinkage learning rate \(\eta\).
Histogram Boosting, XGBoost & LightGBM: Modern engines such as XGBoost, LightGBM, and Scikit-Learn’s HistGradientBoostingClassifier bin continuous features into ~255 quantile histograms (making split search \(10\times\)–\(100\times\) faster), apply \(L_2\) leaf regularization, and learn optimal split directions for missing (NaN) values natively.

Finally, predictive accuracy alone never earns clinical trust. Peer reviewers demand interpretability—both global (which predictors drive discrimination on held-out patients?) and local (why did the model assign this specific household a 25.7% stunting probability?). Held-out Permutation Importance answers the global question without MDI’s high-cardinality trap, while Shapley values (SHAP) answer the local question with game-theoretic fairness.






NoteMental Model — Two Axes of Tree Interpretability



Always separate global from local explanations in your methods section:

Global (Held-Out Permutation Importance): Shuffle one feature column at a time on the test set and measure how much ROC-AUC drops. Noise features collapse near zero.
Local (Shapley / SHAP Values): Explain one patient’s prediction \(f(x)\) as a baseline risk \(\phi_0\) plus additive feature credits \(\phi_1 + \phi_2 + \dots + \phi_p = f(x) - \phi_0\), averaged across every possible ordering of features.

 Chapter 24 visual mental model: Bagging vs. Boosting & Interpretability 



Notice the structural contrast at a glance: in Bagging, Tree 1 and Tree 2 never communicate—they train in parallel on different bootstrap draws so their errors cancel when averaged. In Boosting, Tree 2 cannot begin until Tree 1 finishes and exposes the remaining residuals \(r_1\).






WarningThree Silent Tree & Ensemble Pitfalls in Real Studies




Default .feature_importances_ (MDI) Favors Noise: Impurity-based importance is computed on the training set and systematically inflates high-cardinality continuous features—even pure random IDs! Always audit with held-out permutation_importance.
Unbounded Depth Memorizes Small Cohorts: A single tree with max_depth=None can hit train_auc = 1.000 while dropping below a simple stump on validation. Always inspect train_auc - val_auc.
Never Assume Boosting Automatically Wins on Small \(n\): On a \(500\)-row public-health survey, shallow regularized trees or logistic models can rival or beat un-tuned ensembles. Always benchmark all three families empirically on the same stratified split!

Notice two crucial data-hygiene steps before fitting any tree:

Sentinel replacement (999 -> np.nan): If 999 stayed inside anc_visits, a tree would treat missingness as “999 clinic visits”—an extreme right-tail artifact.
Ordinal mapping (wealth_rank 1..5): Mapping "Poorest" through "Richest" to integers 1..5 preserves the socioeconomic ordering so a single split (wealth_rank <= 2.5) separates the bottom two quintiles from the upper three cleanly.
Stratified split (stratify=y): Because child stunting prevalence is imbalanced (13.83%), stratifying preserves the exact same class ratio in both train (352 rows) and test (118 rows).




24.3.2 Gini Impurity, Shannon Entropy & Greedy Decision Stump
For a node with class proportions \(p_1, \dots, p_K\), CART measures node disorder using Gini impurity or base-2 Shannon entropy:
\[G(y) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^2, \qquad H(y) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log_2(p_k)\]
A decision stump tests every midpoint \(t\) between consecutive sorted unique values of feature \(x\) and picks the threshold minimizing weighted child Gini:
\[G_{\text{split}}(t) = \frac{n_L}{n} G(y_{x \le t}) + \frac{n_R}{n} G(y_{x > t})\]
def gini_demo(y_vals):
    arr = np.asarray(y_vals)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    return round(float(1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2)), 4)

def entropy_demo(y_vals):
    arr = np.asarray(y_vals)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    return round(float(-np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs))), 4)

def stump_demo(x_vals, y_vals):
    x = np.asarray(x_vals, dtype=float)
    yv = np.asarray(y_vals)
    uniq = np.unique(x)
    mids = (uniq[:-1] + uniq[1:]) / 2.0
    best_t, best_g = float(mids[0]), float("inf")
    for t in mids:
        left, right = yv[x <= t], yv[x > t]
        wg = (len(left) / len(yv)) * gini_demo(left)
        wg += (len(right) / len(yv)) * gini_demo(right)
        if wg < best_g:
            best_g, best_t = wg, float(t)
    return (round(best_t, 4), round(best_g, 4))

print("Root Gini:", gini_demo(y_train),
      "| Root Entropy:", entropy_demo(y_train))
for col in ["wealth_rank", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl"]:
    t, g = stump_demo(X_train[col], y_train)
    print(f"Best stump on {col:16s}: thresh={t:.2f}, w_gini={g:.4f}")
Expected Output:
Root Gini: 0.2397 | Root Entropy: 0.5822
Best stump on wealth_rank     : thresh=2.50, w_gini=0.2171
Best stump on anc_visits      : thresh=3.50, w_gini=0.2259
Best stump on maternal_hb_g_dl: thresh=15.10, w_gini=0.2354
Look at the epidemiology our pure-NumPy stump just discovered automatically:

wealth_rank <= 2.50 (w_gini = 0.2171): Achieves the largest impurity drop (0.2397 -> 0.2171) by separating Poorest/Poorer households from Middle/Richer/Richest.
anc_visits <= 3.50 (w_gini = 0.2259): Rediscovers the World Health Organization’s classic 4+ antenatal care visits benchmark (<= 3 vs. >= 4) directly from data!




24.3.3 Decision Tree Overfitting & Depth Sweep
depth_rows = []
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12]:
    dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=42)
    dt.fit(X_train, y_train)
    tr_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, dt.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1])
    te_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, dt.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
    depth_rows.append({
        "max_depth": d,
        "train_auc": round(float(tr_auc), 4),
        "val_auc": round(float(te_auc), 4),
        "gap": round(float(tr_auc - te_auc), 4),
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(depth_rows).to_string(index=False))
Expected Output:
 max_depth  train_auc  val_auc    gap
         1     0.7200   0.6213 0.0987
         2     0.7544   0.6152 0.1392
         3     0.7964   0.6400 0.1564
         5     0.8854   0.6550 0.2304
         8     0.9465   0.6354 0.3111
        12     0.9993   0.5809 0.4184
This table is the textbook signature of tree overfitting:

From max_depth = 1 to 5, validation ROC-AUC climbs from 0.6213 to 0.6550.
Beyond depth 5, training AUC shoots to 0.9993 (nearly memorizing every single household!), while validation AUC plunges to 0.5809—a massive generalization gap of 0.4184!




24.3.4 Bagging, Random Forests & Out-of-Bag (OOB) Validation
When a Random Forest draws a bootstrap sample of size \(n\) with replacement, the probability that any given household is never selected in a single tree is \((1 - 1/n)^n \approx e^{-1} \approx \mathbf{0.368}\). Evaluating every household using only the ~36.8% of trees that never saw it produces the Out-of-Bag (OOB) score—free internal validation without touching the test set!
oob_rows = []
for d in [2, 4, 6, 8, 12]:
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=120, max_depth=d, oob_score=True, random_state=42
    ).fit(X_train, y_train)
    oob_rows.append({
        "max_depth": d,
        "oob_score": round(float(rf.oob_score_), 4),
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(oob_rows).to_string(index=False))
Expected Output:
 max_depth  oob_score
         2     0.8608
         4     0.8636
         6     0.8580
         8     0.8466
        12     0.8494
OOB validation cleanly peaks at max_depth = 4 (0.8636) and declines as deeper trees memorize noise in the bootstrap draws. Remember: oob_score_ reports accuracy by default, so always confirm discrimination on imbalanced outcomes with ROC-AUC and PR-AUC.



24.3.5 Gradient Boosting Residuals, Native NaNs & Ensemble Scaling
In Gradient Boosting, each tree \(h_m(x)\) fits the pseudo-residuals left over by the previous ensemble \(F_{m-1}(x)\) and updates predictions cautiously via learning rate \(\eta\):
\[r_i^{(m)} = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i), \qquad F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \eta \cdot h_m(x)\]
# 1. Sequential residual fitting intuition (3 boosting rounds)
y_hb = np.array([9.4, 10.1, 11.2, 12.6, 13.0])
x_anc = np.array([[0], [1], [3], [6], [8]])
pred = np.full_like(y_hb, y_hb.mean())
lr = 0.5
print(f"Step 0 (mean)   MSE: {np.mean((y_hb - pred) ** 2):.4f}")
for step in range(1, 4):
    resid = y_hb - pred
    stump = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1, random_state=42)
    stump.fit(x_anc, resid)
    pred = pred + lr * stump.predict(x_anc)
    print(f"Step {step} (boost) MSE: {np.mean((y_hb - pred) ** 2):.4f}")

# 2. Native NaN handling of HistGradientBoosting on all 500 MCH rows
X_full = mch[features]
y_full = mch["child_stunted"]
Xf_tr, Xf_te, yf_tr, yf_te = train_test_split(
    X_full, y_full, test_size=0.25, stratify=y_full, random_state=42
)
hgb_nan = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=42)
hgb_nan.fit(Xf_tr, yf_tr)
nan_auc = roc_auc_score(yf_te, hgb_nan.predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1])
n_nans = int(X_full.isna().sum().sum())
print(f"HGB native NaN (n={len(X_full)}, NaNs={n_nans}) "
      f"test ROC-AUC: {nan_auc:.4f}")

# 3. Ensemble scaling on a 600-row nonlinear cohort
X_syn, y_syn = make_classification(
    n_samples=600, n_features=6, n_informative=4, n_redundant=1,
    weights=[0.80, 0.20], random_state=42,
)
Xs_tr, Xs_te, ys_tr, ys_te = train_test_split(
    X_syn, y_syn, test_size=0.25, stratify=y_syn, random_state=42
)
specs = [
    ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=42)),
    ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=42)),
    ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        max_depth=4, random_state=42)),
]
for name, clf in specs:
    clf.fit(Xs_tr, ys_tr)
    p = clf.predict_proba(Xs_te)[:, 1]
    print(f"Synth {name:20s} ROC={roc_auc_score(ys_te, p):.4f} "
          f"PR={average_precision_score(ys_te, p):.4f}")
Expected Output:
Step 0 (mean)   MSE: 1.9264
Step 1 (boost) MSE: 0.7406
Step 2 (boost) MSE: 0.2439
Step 3 (boost) MSE: 0.1090
HGB native NaN (n=500, NaNs=30) test ROC-AUC: 0.7004
Synth DecisionTree         ROC=0.8162 PR=0.6082
Synth RandomForest         ROC=0.8932 PR=0.7627
Synth HistGradientBoosting ROC=0.9246 PR=0.8237
Three powerful lessons jump out of this output:

Residual Shrinkage in Action: Just three depth-1 stumps shrink MSE from 1.9264 down to 0.1090 by focusing every new stump strictly on the unexplained error of earlier rounds.
Native Missing-Value Splitting Wins: Instead of dropping 30 households with missing hemoglobin or ANC values, HistGradientBoostingClassifier trains directly on all 500 rows with 30 NaNs intact and leaps to ROC-AUC = 0.7004!
Ensemble Dominance on Nonlinear Tabular Signal: On the 600-row nonlinear cohort, HistGradientBoosting (ROC = 0.9246, PR = 0.8237) decisively beats RandomForest (0.8932 / 0.7627), which in turn crushes a single DecisionTree (0.8162 / 0.6082).




24.3.6 Interpretability: Permutation Importance vs. Default MDI Bias
Let’s test Scikit-Learn’s default .feature_importances_ (Mean Decrease in Impurity, MDI) by injecting a pure random noise column (random_noise_id) into mch_survey_sample:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
noisy = clean.copy()
noisy["random_noise_id"] = rng.uniform(0, 1000, size=len(noisy))
f_noise = features + ["random_noise_id"]
Xn_tr, Xn_te, yn_tr, yn_te = train_test_split(
    noisy[f_noise], noisy["child_stunted"],
    test_size=0.25, stratify=noisy["child_stunted"], random_state=42,
)
rf_noise = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=42
).fit(Xn_tr, yn_tr)
pi_noise = permutation_importance(
    rf_noise, Xn_te, yn_te, scoring="roc_auc",
    n_repeats=10, random_state=42,
)
imp_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "feature": f_noise,
    "mdi_impurity": np.round(rf_noise.feature_importances_, 4),
    "perm_auc_mean": np.round(pi_noise.importances_mean, 4),
    "perm_auc_std": np.round(pi_noise.importances_std, 4),
}).sort_values("mdi_impurity", ascending=False)
print(imp_df.to_string(index=False))
Expected Output:
           feature  mdi_impurity  perm_auc_mean  perm_auc_std
   random_noise_id        0.2316         0.0140        0.0185
  maternal_hb_g_dl        0.2307         0.0081        0.0229
        anc_visits        0.1795         0.0275        0.0489
       wealth_rank        0.1719         0.1135        0.0626
maternal_age_years        0.1500        -0.0129        0.0159
          is_urban        0.0362         0.0069        0.0113
Pause and absorb how staggering that table is:

Default MDI (mdi_impurity) ranked pure random noise #1 (0.2316)—above genuine socioeconomic driver wealth_rank (0.1719)! Why? Because a continuous uniform column has 352 unique split candidates to slice training noise, whereas wealth_rank only has 4 possible split points (1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5).
Held-Out Permutation Importance (perm_auc_mean) immediately unmasks the fraud: Shuffling wealth_rank on the test set slashes ROC-AUC by +0.1135, ranking it #1 by a landslide, while random_noise_id collapses to 0.0140 ± 0.0185 (indistinguishable from zero!).




24.3.7 Exact 3-Feature Shapley Values (SHAP Intuition) From Scratch
How do we explain one individual household’s predicted stunting probability \(f(x)\)? Cooperative game theory’s Shapley value treats each feature as a player joining a coalition from a reference baseline_row to x_row. Because tree models contain feature interactions, the marginal credit of revealing feature \(i\) depends on which features were already revealed. Averaging across all \(p!\) permutations yields the unique attribution satisfying Efficiency, Symmetry, Dummy, and Additivity:
\[\phi_i(x) = \frac{1}{p!} \sum_{\pi \in S_p} \Big[ f\big(S_\pi(i) \cup \{i\}\big) - f\big(S_\pi(i)\big) \Big], \qquad \phi_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i(x) = f(x)\]
top3 = ["wealth_rank", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl"]
rf3 = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100, max_depth=4, random_state=42
).fit(X_train[top3].to_numpy(), y_train.to_numpy())

def rf3_proba(v):
    arr = np.asarray(v, dtype=float).reshape(1, -1)
    return float(rf3.predict_proba(arr)[0, 1])

def shapley_3_demo(predict_fn, x_row, base_row):
    x = np.asarray(x_row, dtype=float)
    base = np.asarray(base_row, dtype=float)
    base_val = float(predict_fn(base))
    pred_val = float(predict_fn(x))
    contribs = np.zeros(3, dtype=float)
    perms = list(itertools.permutations([0, 1, 2]))
    for perm in perms:
        state = base.copy()
        prev = base_val
        for idx in perm:
            state[idx] = x[idx]
            curr = float(predict_fn(state))
            contribs[idx] += curr - prev
            prev = curr
    shap_vals = contribs / len(perms)
    return {
        "base_value": round(base_val, 4),
        "shap_values": [round(float(v), 4) for v in shap_vals],
        "prediction": round(pred_val, 4),
    }

baseline = X_train[top3].median().to_numpy()
high_risk = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 9.5])
sh = shapley_3_demo(rf3_proba, high_risk, baseline)
print("Baseline (median):", np.round(baseline, 2).tolist())
print("High-risk patient:", high_risk.tolist())
print("Base:", sh["base_value"], "| Pred:", sh["prediction"])
print("Shapley values:", sh["shap_values"])
eff = round(sh["base_value"] + sum(sh["shap_values"]), 4)
print(f"Efficiency check: {eff} ~= {sh['prediction']}")
Expected Output:
Baseline (median): [3.0, 4.0, 11.5]
High-risk patient: [1.0, 1.0, 9.5]
Base: 0.0365 | Pred: 0.257
Shapley values: [0.1839, 0.0408, -0.0043]
Efficiency check: 0.2569 ~= 0.257
Read this patient-level waterfall attribution like a clinician:

Starting from the median household baseline (wealth_rank = 3, anc_visits = 4, Hb = 11.5 g/dL), predicted stunting risk is 3.65% (base_value = 0.0365).
For a household in the poorest quintile (wealth_rank = 1) with only 1 ANC visit and Hb = 9.5 g/dL, risk jumps to 25.70% (prediction = 0.2570).
Exact Shapley values decompose that +22.05 percentage-point surge cleanly: +18.39 pp from wealth_rank, +4.08 pp from low anc_visits, and -0.43 pp from maternal_hb_g_dl.
Production Bridge (shap Library): For \(p = 3\) features, \(3! = 6\) permutations is instant; for \(p = 30\) features, \(30! \approx 2.65 \times 10^{32}\) is impossible by brute force! In full research pipelines, the shap library’s TreeSHAP (shap.TreeExplainer(model)) exploits tree path structure to compute these exact same Shapley values in polynomial time \(O(T L D^2)\).




24.3.8 Break It On Purpose! (Tree & Ensemble Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — ValueError / InvalidParameterError (max_depth=0)



bad_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=0, random_state=42)
bad_tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
Python’s Traceback:
InvalidParameterError: The 'max_depth' parameter of DecisionTreeClassifier
must be an int in the range [1, inf) or None. Got 0 instead.
Diagnosis: InvalidParameterError (a subclass of ValueError) fires because a decision tree must have at least depth 1 (a decision stump) or None (grow until leaves are pure). Setting max_depth=0 leaves zero splits possible.
Fix: Use max_depth >= 1 (e.g., 1 for a stump, 3..6 for regularized trees) or max_depth=None when intentionally testing an unpruned tree.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — ValueError (oob_score=True With bootstrap=False)



bad_rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=50, oob_score=True, bootstrap=False, random_state=42
)
bad_rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: Out of bag estimation only available if bootstrap=True
Diagnosis: Out-of-Bag scoring depends mathematically on bootstrap resampling with replacement leaving ~36.8% of training rows unused in each tree. When bootstrap=False, every tree sees 100% of rows, so no out-of-bag rows exist!
Fix: Keep the default bootstrap=True whenever oob_score=True, or use \(k\)-fold cross-validation if you deliberately disable bootstrapping.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ValueError (Passing NaNs Into Classic GradientBoostingClassifier)



bad_gbc = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)
bad_gbc.fit(Xf_tr, yf_tr)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: Input X contains NaN.
GradientBoostingClassifier does not accept missing values encoded as NaN
natively. For supervised learning, you might want to consider
sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier and Regressor which
accept missing values encoded as NaNs natively.
Diagnosis: Classic GradientBoostingClassifier (like LogisticRegression and pre-1.4 versions of RandomForestClassifier) refuses NaN inputs and crashes during .fit().
Fix: Either wrap the estimator in a leakage-free Pipeline([("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("clf", ...)]), drop incomplete rows intentionally, or switch directly to HistGradientBoostingClassifier, which learns optimal left/right branches for missing values natively.

section: 24.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
text:
24.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: Your maternal-and-child health research team needs a single reproducible benchmark function run_stunting_tree_audit(raw_df, seed=42) that takes raw mch_survey_sample (without mutating it), cleans all survey artifacts, compares Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Histogram Gradient Boosting on a stratified 75/25 split using both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, and identifies the top held-out risk driver via permutation importance on the winning model.

24.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Hygiene & Feature Engineering (Zero Mutation):

Copy raw_df first (work = raw_df.copy()).
Standardize residence casing, replace anc_visits == 999 with np.nan, derive binary is_urban, map ordinal wealth_quintile (Poorest: 1 .. Richest: 5) to wealth_rank, and drop incomplete rows across the 5 features + child_stunted.

Stratified Multi-Family Benchmark:

Split 75/25 stratified on child_stunted with random_state=seed.
Fit DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5), RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=6), and HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_depth=4), scoring test probabilities ([:, 1]) with roc_auc_score and average_precision_score.
Sort the leaderboard descending by roc_auc.

Held-Out Interpretability Audit & Verification:

Run permutation_importance (scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=10) on the winning fitted model using (X_test, y_test) to extract top_feature.
Verify complete-case size (n = 470), confirm the winning model empirically rather than assuming boosting always wins on small \(n\), and check that wealth_rank emerges as the top held-out driver.




24.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
def run_stunting_tree_audit(raw_df, seed=42):
    """Clean MCH data, benchmark 3 tree models, and audit top driver."""
    work = raw_df.copy()
    work["residence"] = (
        work["residence"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
    )
    work["anc_visits"] = work["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    work["is_urban"] = (work["residence"] == "Urban").astype(int)
    w_map = {
        "Poorest": 1, "Poorer": 2, "Middle": 3,
        "Richer": 4, "Richest": 5,
    }
    work["wealth_rank"] = (
        work["wealth_quintile"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
        .map(w_map)
    )
    feats = [
        "maternal_age_years", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl",
        "is_urban", "wealth_rank",
    ]
    df = work[feats + ["child_stunted"]].dropna()
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        df[feats], df["child_stunted"].astype(int),
        test_size=0.25, stratify=df["child_stunted"], random_state=seed,
    )
    models = [
        ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=5, random_state=seed)),
        ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=seed)),
        ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
            max_depth=4, random_state=seed)),
    ]
    rows, fitted = [], {}
    for name, clf in models:
        clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        proba = clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_te, proba)), 4),
            "pr_auc": round(
                float(average_precision_score(y_te, proba)), 4
            ),
        })
        fitted[name] = clf
    board = (
        pd.DataFrame(rows)
        .sort_values("roc_auc", ascending=False)
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    winner = str(board.iloc[0]["model"])
    pi = permutation_importance(
        fitted[winner], X_te, y_te, scoring="roc_auc",
        n_repeats=10, random_state=seed,
    )
    top_feat = feats[int(np.argmax(pi.importances_mean))]
    return board, winner, top_feat

board, winner, top_feat = run_stunting_tree_audit(mch_raw, seed=42)
print(board.to_string(index=False))
print(f"Winning model: {winner} | Top held-out driver: {top_feat}")
Output:
               model  roc_auc  pr_auc
        DecisionTree   0.6550  0.2242
HistGradientBoosting   0.6029  0.1897
        RandomForest   0.5827  0.1776
Winning model: DecisionTree | Top held-out driver: wealth_rank
Notice the authentic scientific takeaway: on a small complete-case survey (\(n = 470\), \(118\) test households), a regularized shallow DecisionTree(max_depth=5) actually outperforms default ensembles on this split—reminding us why No Free Lunch holds and why every manuscript must benchmark simple baselines fairly!

section: 24.6 Stage 6 — Concept & Execution Trace Test (No Computer Allowed!)
text:
24.6 Stage 6 — Concept & Execution Trace Test (No Computer Allowed!)
Work through all 10 tree, ensemble, and interpretability questions on paper before checking Stage 8:

Gini vs. Entropy Hand Calculation: A leaf node contains 3 stunted children and 1 non-stunted child (\(p = [0.75, 0.25]\)). Compute its exact Gini impurity by hand, and state whether its base-2 Shannon entropy is less than, equal to, or greater than 1.0 bit.
Midpoint Split Candidate: A sorted feature vector has unique values [2.0, 4.0, 10.0] with labels [1, 0, 0]. What exact midpoint threshold \(t\) produces a weighted Gini impurity of 0.0?
Reading an Overfitting Table: At max_depth=12, a Decision Tree hits train_auc = 0.9993 and val_auc = 0.5809, whereas max_depth=5 hits train_auc = 0.8854 and val_auc = 0.6550. Is the depth-12 tree suffering from high bias or high variance, and why?
Bootstrap OOB Mathematics: When a Random Forest draws a bootstrap sample of size \(n\) with replacement from a large cohort, approximately what percentage of training rows are Out-of-Bag (OOB) for any single tree—and why does setting bootstrap=False break oob_score=True?
Why max_features="sqrt" Matters: Suppose one dominant predictor (wealth_rank) always yields the best root split. If you build 100 bagged trees using all features (max_features=None) vs. max_features="sqrt", which forest produces more decorrelated trees and better variance reduction?
Bagging vs. Boosting Parallelism: Can the 100 trees inside RandomForestClassifier be trained completely in parallel across CPU cores? What about the 100 boosting iterations inside HistGradientBoostingClassifier? Explain why.
Gradient Boosting Learning Rate Trade-Off: If you shrink the boosting learning rate \(\eta\) from 0.1 to 0.01, what must you generally do to max_iter (the number of boosting trees) to avoid underfitting?
Unmasking MDI Feature-Importance Bias: A student adds a random 10-digit hospital registration ID column to a Random Forest and sees it rank #1 in rf.feature_importances_. Explain why default MDI made this error and which Scikit-Learn tool catches it.
Exact 2-Feature Shapley Hand Calculation: Suppose \(f(x_1, x_2) = 1.0 + 2 x_1 + 4 x_1 x_2\), with baseline = [0, 0] and x = [1, 1]. Trace both permutations (0, 1) and (1, 0) by hand to compute exact \(\phi_0\), \(\phi_1\), \(\phi_2\), and verify the Efficiency Axiom \(\phi_0 + \phi_1 + \phi_2 = f(x)\).
Native NaN Error Anatomy: Your dataset contains missing hemoglobin values (np.nan). You call GradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X, y) and Python raises ValueError: Input X contains NaN. Name two valid engineering fixes (one using a different tree estimator and one using preprocessing).

24.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

24.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

Gini: \(1 - (0.75^2 + 0.25^2) = 1 - (0.5625 + 0.0625) = \mathbf{0.375}\). Entropy: Less than 1.0 bit (specifically 0.8113 bits), because binary Shannon entropy achieves its maximum of 1.0 bit only at a 50/50 split.
Midpoints are (2.0 + 4.0) / 2 = 3.0 and (4.0 + 10.0) / 2 = 7.0. Threshold t = 3.0 places [1] on the left (pure, Gini = 0.0) and [0, 0] on the right (pure, Gini = 0.0), giving weighted Gini 0.0.
High variance (overfitting): The depth-12 tree has near-zero training error (0.9993) because it memorized idiosyncratic training noise, causing test AUC to collapse (0.5809).
Approximately 36.8% (\(1/e\)) of training rows are Out-of-Bag for any single bootstrap tree. Setting bootstrap=False trains every tree on 100% of training rows, leaving zero OOB rows to evaluate and triggering ValueError.
max_features="sqrt" produces much better decorrelation! With max_features=None, nearly every tree splits on wealth_rank at the root, yielding highly correlated trees whose average barely reduces variance.
RandomForestClassifier: Yes, all 100 bootstrap trees are completely independent and train in parallel (n_jobs=-1). HistGradientBoostingClassifier: No across trees, because tree \(m\) depends sequentially on the residuals of tree \(m - 1\) (parallelism happens within each tree’s histogram bin search instead).
You must increase max_iter (train more boosting rounds), because each smaller step \(\eta = 0.01\) corrects only 1% of the residual per tree.
Default MDI sums training-set impurity reductions across splits; a unique 10-digit ID offers \(n - 1\) split thresholds to memorize training labels. Held-out sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance on (X_test, y_test) exposes the ID immediately by showing near-zero (or negative) test-AUC drop.
\(\phi_0 = f(0, 0) = \mathbf{1.0}\) and \(f(1, 1) = 1 + 2 + 4 = \mathbf{7.0}\).

Order (0, 1): reveal \(x_1\): \(f(1, 0) - f(0, 0) = 3 - 1 = +2\); reveal \(x_2\): \(f(1, 1) - f(1, 0) = 7 - 3 = +4\).
Order (1, 0): reveal \(x_2\): \(f(0, 1) - f(0, 0) = 1 - 1 = 0\); reveal \(x_1\): \(f(1, 1) - f(0, 1) = 7 - 1 = +6\).
Averaging both orders: \(\phi_1 = (2 + 6)/2 = \mathbf{4.0}\), \(\phi_2 = (4 + 0)/2 = \mathbf{2.0}\). Efficiency check: \(1.0 + 4.0 + 2.0 = \mathbf{7.0} = f(1, 1)\)!


Switch to HistGradientBoostingClassifier, which learns optimal missing-value branch routing natively; or (b) wrap GradientBoostingClassifier inside a Pipeline preceded by SimpleImputer(strategy="median") fit strictly on X_train.




24.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# To-Do 24.1
def gini_impurity(y):
    """Compute Gini impurity 1 - sum(p_k^2) rounded to 4 decimals."""
    arr = np.asarray(y)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    return round(float(1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2)), 4)

# To-Do 24.2
def shannon_entropy(y):
    """Compute base-2 Shannon entropy rounded to 4 decimals."""
    arr = np.asarray(y)
    if arr.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
    probs = counts / arr.size
    probs = probs[probs > 0]
    ent = float(-np.sum(probs * np.log2(probs)))
    return round(0.0 if ent == 0.0 else ent, 4)

# To-Do 24.3
def best_stump_split(x_feature, y):
    """Find midpoint threshold minimizing weighted Gini impurity."""
    def _gini(arr):
        if arr.size == 0:
            return 0.0
        _, counts = np.unique(arr, return_counts=True)
        probs = counts / arr.size
        return float(1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2))

    x = np.asarray(x_feature, dtype=float)
    y_arr = np.asarray(y)
    uniq = np.unique(x)
    mids = (uniq[:-1] + uniq[1:]) / 2.0
    best_t, best_g = float(mids[0]), float("inf")
    n = y_arr.size
    for t in mids:
        left = y_arr[x <= t]
        right = y_arr[x > t]
        wg = (left.size / n) * _gini(left) + (right.size / n) * _gini(right)
        if wg < best_g:
            best_g = wg
            best_t = float(t)
    return (round(best_t, 4), round(best_g, 4))

# To-Do 24.4
def compare_tree_depths(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, depths, seed=42):
    """Compare DecisionTree train/val ROC-AUC and gap across depths."""
    rows = []
    for d in depths:
        clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=seed)
        clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
        tr = float(roc_auc_score(y_train, clf.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]))
        va = float(roc_auc_score(y_val, clf.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]))
        rows.append({
            "max_depth": d,
            "train_auc": round(tr, 4),
            "val_auc": round(va, 4),
            "gap": round(tr - va, 4),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# To-Do 24.5
def fit_ensemble_comparison(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, seed=42):
    """Fit DecisionTree, RandomForest, and HistGradientBoosting."""
    models = [
        ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=5, random_state=seed)),
        ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=seed)),
        ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
            max_depth=4, random_state=seed)),
    ]
    rows = []
    for name, clf in models:
        clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
        proba = clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)), 4),
            "pr_auc": round(
                float(average_precision_score(y_test, proba)), 4
            ),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# To-Do 24.6
def compute_permutation_ranking(
    model, X_test, y_test, feature_names, seed=42
):
    """Rank features by held-out ROC-AUC permutation importance."""
    res = permutation_importance(
        model, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc",
        n_repeats=10, random_state=seed,
    )
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "feature": list(feature_names),
        "importance_mean": np.round(res.importances_mean, 4),
        "importance_std": np.round(res.importances_std, 4),
    })
    return df.sort_values(
        "importance_mean", ascending=False
    ).reset_index(drop=True)


24.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 24 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import itertools
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Exam Task 24.1 (30 pts)
def exact_shapley_3features(predict_fn, x_row, baseline_row):
    """Compute exact 3-feature Shapley values over all 6 permutations."""
    x = np.asarray(x_row, dtype=float)
    base = np.asarray(baseline_row, dtype=float)
    base_val = float(predict_fn(base))
    pred_val = float(predict_fn(x))
    contribs = np.zeros(3, dtype=float)
    perms = list(itertools.permutations([0, 1, 2]))
    for perm in perms:
        state = base.copy()
        prev = base_val
        for idx in perm:
            state[idx] = x[idx]
            curr = float(predict_fn(state))
            contribs[idx] += curr - prev
            prev = curr
    shap_vals = contribs / len(perms)
    return {
        "base_value": round(base_val, 4),
        "shap_values": [round(float(v), 4) for v in shap_vals],
        "prediction": round(pred_val, 4),
    }

# Exam Task 24.2 (35 pts)
def tune_random_forest_oob(X_train, y_train, max_depths, seed=42):
    """Select best RandomForest max_depth using Out-of-Bag accuracy."""
    rows = []
    best_depth = int(max_depths[0])
    best_oob = -1.0
    for d in max_depths:
        rf = RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=120, max_depth=d,
            oob_score=True, random_state=seed,
        ).fit(X_train, y_train)
        score = float(rf.oob_score_)
        rows.append({"max_depth": int(d), "oob_score": round(score, 4)})
        if score > best_oob:
            best_oob = score
            best_depth = int(d)
    return {
        "best_depth": best_depth,
        "best_oob_score": round(best_oob, 4),
        "oob_table": pd.DataFrame(rows),
    }

# Exam Task 24.3 (35 pts)
def public_health_tree_benchmark(mch_df, seed=42):
    """Benchmark 3 tree families on MCH stunting and rank top driver."""
    work = mch_df.copy()
    work["residence"] = (
        work["residence"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
    )
    work["anc_visits"] = work["anc_visits"].replace(999, np.nan)
    work["is_urban"] = (work["residence"] == "Urban").astype(int)
    w_map = {
        "Poorest": 1, "Poorer": 2, "Middle": 3,
        "Richer": 4, "Richest": 5,
    }
    work["wealth_rank"] = (
        work["wealth_quintile"].astype(str).str.strip().str.title()
        .map(w_map)
    )
    feats = [
        "maternal_age_years", "anc_visits", "maternal_hb_g_dl",
        "is_urban", "wealth_rank",
    ]
    clean = work[feats + ["child_stunted"]].dropna()
    X = clean[feats]
    y = clean["child_stunted"].astype(int)
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=seed
    )
    specs = [
        ("DecisionTree", DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=5, random_state=seed)),
        ("RandomForest", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, random_state=seed)),
        ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
            max_depth=4, random_state=seed)),
    ]
    rows, fitted = [], {}
    for name, clf in specs:
        clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        proba = clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
        rows.append({
            "model": name,
            "roc_auc": round(float(roc_auc_score(y_te, proba)), 4),
            "pr_auc": round(
                float(average_precision_score(y_te, proba)), 4
            ),
        })
        fitted[name] = clf
    leaderboard = (
        pd.DataFrame(rows)
        .sort_values("roc_auc", ascending=False)
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    best_model = str(leaderboard.iloc[0]["model"])
    pi = permutation_importance(
        fitted[best_model], X_te, y_te, scoring="roc_auc",
        n_repeats=10, random_state=seed,
    )
    top_feature = feats[int(np.argmax(pi.importances_mean))]
    return {
        "leaderboard": leaderboard,
        "best_model": best_model,
        "top_feature": top_feature,
    }


24.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 24 Failure Modes

Passing Hard Class Predictions (.predict) Instead of Probabilities (.predict_proba[:, 1]) Into ROC-AUC / PR-AUC: Hard binary labels collapse all probability thresholds to a single operating point, distorting both roc_auc_score and average_precision_score. Always slice column 1 of .predict_proba(X).
Trusting Default MDI .feature_importances_ on Mixed-Cardinality Clinical Data: Training-set impurity gain rewards continuous or ID-like columns with many split thresholds—even pure noise! Always validate global driver rankings with held-out permutation_importance on (X_test, y_test).
Evaluating Only One Feature Order When Explaining Nonlinear Models: In models with feature interactions, changing which feature is turned on first shifts marginal credit dramatically. Averaging across permutations (exact Shapley / TreeSHAP) is the only way to preserve fair attribution and guarantee the Efficiency Axiom \(\phi_0 + \sum_i \phi_i = f(x)\).

title: 25  Unsupervised Learning — Clustering (K-Means, Hierarchical, DBSCAN) and Dimensionality Reduction (PCA)
section: 25.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Learning Structure Without Labels
text:
25.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Learning Structure Without Labels
In Chapters 21–24, every model learned a mapping \(\hat{y} = f(X)\) guided by ground-truth labels—whether a patient was anemic, needed urgent referral, or had elevated blood pressure. Yet in real clinical, genomic, and public health research, labels are often missing, incomplete, or not yet defined:

Patient Phenotyping: Do 120 patients arriving at Upazila Health Complexes naturally fall into distinct clinical profiles (e.g., pediatric febrile cases vs. older hypertensive adults) before anyone assigns a diagnosis code?
Health-System Targeting: Which Bangladesh districts share similar burdens of fever, blood pressure, anemia, and non-routine triage load so health ministries can group interventions?
Biomarker Compression: When seven physiological measurements (age_years, weight_kg, height_cm, temp_c, systolic_bp, hemoglobin_g_dl, fever_days) are strongly correlated, how many independent biological axes actually drive 85%–90% of the variation?

That is the domain of unsupervised learning: discovering latent geometry directly from \(X\) alone. Four first principles govern every method in this chapter:

Distance Depends Completely on Feature Scale: Euclidean distance sums squared differences across all features, \(\|x - z\|_2^2 = \sum_j (x_j - z_j)^2\). In clinic_triage, age_years has variance 451.44 while temp_c has variance 0.60—a 752x variance gap! Without StandardScaler, clustering and PCA effectively ignore body temperature and hemoglobin.
No Universal “Accuracy” Metric: Without ground-truth \(y\), we evaluate cluster structure using geometric cohesion and separation—inertia (within-cluster sum of squared errors) and Silhouette score \(s \in [-1, +1]\)—always backed by clinical interpretability.
Different Algorithms Assume Different Shapes: K-Means and Ward assume compact, roughly spherical clusters of comparable spread and force every point into a cluster. DBSCAN traces arbitrary dense regions and explicitly isolates sparse anomalies as label -1.
PCA Maximizes Variance & Minimizes Reconstruction Error: Projecting standardized data onto the top \(k\) orthogonal principal components preserves the maximum possible linear variance and yields the lowest possible mean squared reconstruction error—and remarkably, on standardized data, \(\text{MSE} = 1 - \text{cumulative explained variance}\)!







NoteMental Model — Two Questions Before Picking an Unsupervised Method



Never run K-Means blindly on every unlabeled table. Ask two structural questions first:

Are you grouping rows (patients/districts) or compressing columns (correlated features)? Row grouping calls for Clustering; column compression and noise reduction call for PCA.
If clustering, do you expect compact spherical groups, a nested hierarchy, or dense blobs mixed with outliers? Spherical \(\rightarrow\) K-Means; nested tree \(\rightarrow\) Ward Hierarchical; irregular shapes + anomalies \(\rightarrow\) DBSCAN.

WarningTwo Classic Unsupervised Pitfalls That Invalidate Papers




Counting DBSCAN Noise (-1) as a Cluster: DBSCAN assigns sparse outliers to label -1. Computing len(set(labels)) falsely counts noise as an extra cluster—always subtract {-1} before reporting n_clusters!
Clustering Directly on t-SNE or UMAP Coordinates: t-SNE and UMAP warp global distances and cluster diameters to preserve local neighborhoods. Never feed t-SNE coordinates into K-Means or claim two distant t-SNE islands are quantitatively “farther apart” than two close ones.

25.3.2 Why Feature Scaling Dominates Euclidean Distance
# Inspect raw feature variances across incompatible clinical units
raw_vars = pd.Series(X_raw.var(axis=0), index=feat_cols).round(2)

25.3.3 K-Means From Scratch in Pure NumPy
K-Means minimizes within-cluster inertia (sum of squared Euclidean distances to assigned centroids \(\mu_c\)):
\[J = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\| x_i - \mu_{c(i)} \right\|_2^2\]
It alternates two steps until centroids stop moving: (1) assign each point \(x_i\) to its nearest centroid, and (2) replace each centroid \(\mu_c\) with the mean of points assigned to cluster \(c\).
def kmeans_scratch_demo(X, k, max_iter=50, seed=42):
    X_arr = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    idx = rng.choice(len(X_arr), size=k, replace=False)
    centroids = X_arr[idx].copy()
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        dists = ((X_arr[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :]) ** 2)
        labels = np.argmin(dists.sum(axis=2), axis=1).astype(int)
        new_c = centroids.copy()
        for cid in range(k):
            mask = labels == cid
            if np.any(mask):
                new_c[cid] = X_arr[mask].mean(axis=0)
        if np.allclose(new_c, centroids):
            centroids = new_c
            break
        centroids = new_c
    dists = ((X_arr[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :]) ** 2)
    labels = np.argmin(dists.sum(axis=2), axis=1).astype(int)
    inertia = float(np.sum((X_arr - centroids[labels]) ** 2))
    return labels, centroids, inertia

sc_labels, sc_centers, sc_inertia = kmeans_scratch_demo(
    X_scaled, k=3, max_iter=50, seed=42
)
print(f"Scratch K-Means inertia: {sc_inertia:.4f}")
print(f"Sklearn K-Means inertia: {km_scl.inertia_:.4f}")
print("Scratch cluster sizes:",
      {int(c): int(n) for c, n in zip(*np.unique(
          sc_labels, return_counts=True))})
Expected Output:
Scratch K-Means inertia: 549.5317
Sklearn K-Means inertia: 514.0598
Scratch cluster sizes: {0: 29, 1: 40, 2: 51}
Pause and appreciate two key lessons in this output:

Vectorized Broadcasting ((n, 1, d) - (1, k, d)): One line computes every point-to-centroid squared distance in pure NumPy without a slow Python loop over patients!
Why Single-Start Inertia (549.5317) > Sklearn Inertia (514.0598): K-Means is non-convex—a single random initialization can converge to a suboptimal local minimum. Scikit-Learn uses k-means++ smart seeding across n_init=10 independent restarts and keeps the lowest-inertia solution (514.0598).




25.3.4 Choosing \(k\): Elbow Method & Silhouette Score
For each sample \(i\), the Silhouette coefficient compares mean intra-cluster distance \(a(i)\) against mean nearest-other-cluster distance \(b(i)\):
\[s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max(a(i), b(i))} \in [-1, +1]\]
Values near +1 signal tight, well-separated clusters; values near 0 indicate overlapping borders; negative values indicate misassigned points.
sweep_rows = []
for k in range(2, 7):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42)
    lbl = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    sweep_rows.append({
        "k": k,
        "inertia": round(float(km.inertia_), 4),
        "silhouette": round(float(silhouette_score(X_scaled, lbl)), 4),
    })
k_table = pd.DataFrame(sweep_rows)
print(k_table.to_string(index=False))
best_row = k_table.loc[k_table["silhouette"].idxmax()]
print(f"Peak silhouette at k={int(best_row['k'])} "
      f"({best_row['silhouette']:.4f})")

Peak silhouette at k=2 (0.3672)
Notice the classic pattern: inertia drops monotonically (663.08 \(\rightarrow\) 331.97) because adding more centroids always shrinks within-cluster distance, eventually reaching 0 when \(k = n\). Pairing inertia with Silhouette reveals that \(k = 2\) achieves the cleanest geometric separation (0.3672), with \(k = 3\) (0.2811) offering a plausible finer split if clinically justified.



25.3.5 Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (Ward Linkage)
Agglomerative clustering starts with every patient as a singleton cluster and iteratively merges the two clusters that minimize Ward’s criterion—the exact increase in total within-cluster squared variance:
ward = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage="ward")
ward_labels = ward.fit_predict(X_scaled)
ward_sil = silhouette_score(X_scaled, ward_labels)
ward_sizes = {
    int(c): int(n)
    for c, n in zip(*np.unique(ward_labels, return_counts=True))
}
print(f"Ward (k=3) silhouette: {ward_sil:.4f}")
print("Ward (k=3) cluster sizes:", ward_sizes)
Expected Output:
Ward (k=3) silhouette: 0.2847
Ward (k=3) cluster sizes: {0: 89, 1: 24, 2: 7}
Ward clustering is 100% deterministic (zero random seed sensitivity) and achieves a slightly higher silhouette (0.2847) than K-Means (0.2811) at \(k = 3\), isolating a tight 7-patient subgroup (cluster 2) alongside two broader clinical groups (89 and 24).



25.3.6 DBSCAN: Density Clustering & Anomaly Flagging
DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) defines dense neighborhoods using two intuitive hyperparameters: radius eps and minimum neighbor count min_samples. Points in sparse regions are never forced into a cluster—they receive label -1 (noise / anomaly):
db = DBSCAN(eps=1.8, min_samples=5)
db_labels = db.fit_predict(X_scaled)
n_clusters = int(len(set(db_labels.tolist()) - {-1}))
n_noise = int(np.sum(db_labels == -1))
print(f"DBSCAN (eps=1.8, min_samples=5): "
      f"{n_clusters} clusters, {n_noise} noise outliers")
outlier_preview = clinic.loc[
    db_labels == -1, ["patient_id", "age_years", "temp_c", "systolic_bp"]
].head(3)
print("Sample flagged clinical outliers:\n",
      outlier_preview.to_string(index=False))
Expected Output:
DBSCAN (eps=1.8, min_samples=5): 2 clusters, 14 noise outliers
Sample flagged clinical outliers:
 patient_id  age_years  temp_c  systolic_bp
  UHC-0008         10    38.5          106
  UHC-0021          8    36.8          129
  UHC-0023         55    36.1          102
Look at who DBSCAN flags automatically without any hand-coded thresholds: UHC-0008 (10-year-old with high fever 38.5 C), UHC-0021 (8-year-old with unusually elevated 129 mmHg systolic BP), and UHC-0023 (55-year-old with unusually low 102 mmHg BP and 36.1 C temperature). In clinical data quality audits, DBSCAN -1 labels serve as an automatic shortlist for chart review!



25.3.7 PCA From Scratch via NumPy SVD vs. Scikit-Learn
Given a mean-centered matrix \(X_c = X - \bar{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\), its thin Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) factorizes \(X_c = U \Sigma V^\top\). The rows of \(V^\top\) are the orthogonal principal component axes (loadings), the projected coordinates are \(Z_k = X_c V_k\), and the explained variance ratio of component \(j\) is simply:
\[\text{EVR}_j = \frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sum_{m=1}^{r} \sigma_m^2}\]
# 1. PCA from scratch via centered SVD
X_c = X_scaled - X_scaled.mean(axis=0)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_c, full_matrices=False)
Z_svd = X_c @ Vt[:2].T
evr_svd = ((S ** 2) / np.sum(S ** 2))[:2]

# 2. Compare directly against sklearn.decomposition.PCA
pca_full = PCA().fit(X_scaled)
cum_var = np.cumsum(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_)
print("SVD EVR (top 2):    ", np.round(evr_svd, 4))
print("Sklearn EVR (top 2):",
      np.round(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_[:2], 4))
print("Cumulative variance:", np.round(cum_var, 4))
k_85 = int(np.argmax(cum_var >= 0.85) + 1)
print(f"PCs required for >=85% variance: {k_85} "
      f"(retains {cum_var[k_85 - 1]:.4f})")

# 3. Interpret clinical loadings on PC1 & PC2
loadings = pd.DataFrame(
    pca_full.components_[:2].T,
    index=feat_cols,
    columns=["PC1", "PC2"],
).round(4)
print("Top-2 PC Clinical Loadings:\n", loadings)

Read those loadings like a clinician-scientist—they tell a crystal-clear biological story:

Exact SVD Match: Our 4-line NumPy SVD implementation reproduces Scikit-Learn’s explained_variance_ratio_ ([0.3051, 0.2519]) to machine precision!
PC1 (30.5% variance — Anthropometric / Age-Maturity Axis): Driven by age_years (+0.4951), height_cm (+0.4902), weight_kg (+0.4826), and systolic_bp (+0.3863).
PC2 (25.2% variance — Acute Febrile Illness Axis): Driven almost exclusively by fever_days (+0.6260) and temp_c (+0.6084). Together, just 2 orthogonal axes explain 55.7% of all 7 vitals, and 4 PCs capture 86.21%!




25.3.8 Nonlinear Projections (t-SNE / UMAP) Caveats
When visualizing high-dimensional datasets (e.g., single-cell RNA-seq or multi-biomarker panels), researchers frequently reach for t-SNE or UMAP. Unlike PCA, these methods optimize a nonlinear objective preserving local neighbor probabilities—which comes with strict scientific caveats:
# t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, NOT global distances or variance
for perp in [10, 30]:
    emb = TSNE(
        n_components=2, perplexity=perp, init="pca",
        learning_rate="auto", random_state=42,
    ).fit_transform(X_scaled)
    spread = [round(float(v), 2) for v in emb.std(axis=0)]
    print(f"t-SNE (perplexity={perp:2d}) embedding shape={emb.shape}, "
          f"axis SDs={spread}")
Expected Output:
t-SNE (perplexity=10) embedding shape=(120, 2), axis SDs=[14.46, 16.49]
t-SNE (perplexity=30) embedding shape=(120, 2), axis SDs=[3.22, 4.36]
Changing a single hyperparameter (perplexity=10 vs. 30) shrinks the embedding coordinate spread by nearly 4x ([14.46, 16.49] vs. [3.22, 4.36])! Always remember three rules for publication figures: (1) t-SNE/UMAP axes have no feature loadings or explained variance, (2) cluster sizes and inter-cluster gaps in a 2D t-SNE plot are not faithful Euclidean distances, and (3) always perform clustering and statistical tests in the standardized original (or PCA) space, using t-SNE/UMAP strictly for visual intuition.



25.3.9 Break It On Purpose! (Unsupervised Error Anatomy)






ImportantBreak It On Purpose #1 — ValueError (Silhouette Score With Only 1 Cluster)



all_one_cluster = np.zeros(len(X_scaled), dtype=int)
silhouette_score(X_scaled, all_one_cluster)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: Number of labels is 1.
Valid values are 2 to n_samples - 1 (inclusive)
Diagnosis: The silhouette formula requires a nearest other cluster distance \(b(i)\). When every sample has the same label (common with \(k = 1\), or when DBSCAN labels every point as -1 noise or collapses everything into 1 giant blob), \(b(i)\) is undefined.
Fix: Always sweep \(k \ge 2\) and guard DBSCAN silhouette calls by checking len(set(labels) - {-1}) >= 2 before scoring.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #2 — ValueError (PCA n_components Exceeds Matrix Rank)



PCA(n_components=12).fit(X_scaled)
Python’s Traceback:
ValueError: n_components=12 must be between 0 and
min(n_samples, n_features)=7 with svd_solver='covariance_eigh'
Diagnosis: A matrix with \(n = 120\) samples and \(p = 7\) features has at most \(\min(n, p) = 7\) orthogonal principal components. Requesting n_components=12 exceeds the mathematical rank limit.
Fix: Cap n_components <= min(X.shape)—or pass a float in (0, 1) (like PCA(n_components=0.85)) or compute k from PCA().fit(X_scaled) dynamically.








ImportantBreak It On Purpose #3 — ValueError / InvalidParameterError (Negative DBSCAN eps)



DBSCAN(eps=-0.5, min_samples=5).fit(X_scaled)
Python’s Traceback:
InvalidParameterError: The 'eps' parameter of DBSCAN must be a float
in the range (0.0, inf). Got -0.5 instead.
Diagnosis: eps defines a Euclidean neighborhood radius, which must be strictly positive (eps > 0). In Scikit-Learn, InvalidParameterError is a subclass of ValueError raised during estimator parameter validation.
Fix: Ensure eps > 0 (typically chosen via a \(k\)-nearest-neighbor distance “knee” plot in standardized space, such as eps=1.8 on 7 standardized features).

25.4 Stage 4 — The Researcher’s Problem-Structuring Blueprint
Scenario: Your health-informatics team wants a single reusable function run_clinical_phenotyping_pipeline(raw_df, feat_cols, k=3, var_target=0.85, eps=1.8, seed=42) that takes clinic_triage (without mutating it) and outputs a complete unsupervised audit dictionary: (1) minimum PCs required to retain var_target variance plus inverse_transform reconstruction MSE, (2) side-by-side silhouette comparison of K-Means vs. Ward Hierarchical at \(k\) clusters, and (3) total DBSCAN anomaly count (labels == -1).

25.4.1 Blueprint (Completed on Paper Before Coding)

Preprocessing Layer (Scale First, Never Mutate):

Slice raw_df[feat_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float) and standardize via X_sc = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X).

Three Unsupervised Audit Modules:

PCA Compression: Fit full PCA().fit(X_sc), find n_pcs = int(np.argmax(cum >= var_target) + 1), refit PCA(n_components=n_pcs), compute X_hat = pca_k.inverse_transform(pca_k.fit_transform(X_sc)), and evaluate recon_mse = np.mean((X_sc - X_hat) ** 2).
Partition Comparison: Fit KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=seed) and AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=k, linkage="ward") on X_sc and score both with silhouette_score.
Anomaly Screen: Fit DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=5) on X_sc and count int(np.sum(db_lbl == -1)).

Verification Plan:

On clinic_triage (var_target=0.85), n_pcs must be 4, cum_variance = 0.8621, and recon_mse = 0.13789 (verifying 0.86211 + 0.13789 = 1.00000!).
ward_sil (0.2847) should slightly beat kmeans_sil (0.2811), and dbscan_noise must flag 14 clinical outliers.




25.4.2 Clean Python Implementation (Verbatim in 01_walkthrough.ipynb)
def run_clinical_phenotyping_pipeline(
    raw_df, feat_cols, k=3, var_target=0.85, eps=1.8, seed=42
):
    """Scale vitals, audit PCA compression, and compare clusterers."""
    X = raw_df[feat_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    X_sc = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

    # 1. PCA compression & reconstruction MSE audit
    full_pca = PCA().fit(X_sc)
    cum = np.cumsum(full_pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
    n_pcs = int(np.argmax(cum >= var_target) + 1)
    pca_k = PCA(n_components=n_pcs)
    X_hat = pca_k.inverse_transform(pca_k.fit_transform(X_sc))
    recon_mse = round(float(np.mean((X_sc - X_hat) ** 2)), 5)

    # 2. Compare K-Means vs. Ward Agglomerative at k clusters
    km_lbl = KMeans(
        n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=seed
    ).fit_predict(X_sc)
    ward_lbl = AgglomerativeClustering(
        n_clusters=k, linkage="ward"
    ).fit_predict(X_sc)

    # 3. Flag density anomalies via DBSCAN
    db_lbl = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=5).fit_predict(X_sc)
    return {
        "n_pcs": n_pcs,
        "cum_variance": round(float(cum[n_pcs - 1]), 4),
        "recon_mse": recon_mse,
        "kmeans_sil": round(float(silhouette_score(X_sc, km_lbl)), 4),
        "ward_sil": round(float(silhouette_score(X_sc, ward_lbl)), 4),
        "dbscan_noise": int(np.sum(db_lbl == -1)),
    }

audit = run_clinical_phenotyping_pipeline(clinic, feat_cols)
for key, val in audit.items():
    print(f"{key:14s}: {val}")
Output:
n_pcs         : 4
cum_variance  : 0.8621
recon_mse     : 0.13789
kmeans_sil    : 0.2811
ward_sil      : 0.2847
dbscan_noise  : 14

25.6 Stage 6 — Concept & Execution Trace Test (No Computer Allowed!)
Work through all 10 unsupervised learning and linear-algebra reasoning questions on paper before checking Stage 8:

Variance Domination: Feature A has standard deviation 100 (variance 10,000) and Feature B has standard deviation 1 (variance 1). If you run K-Means without StandardScaler, roughly what percentage of the total squared Euclidean distance comes from Feature A?
K-Means Inertia Monotonicity: Why can’t you simply pick the \(k\) with the lowest K-Means inertia? What happens to inertia when \(k = n\) (one cluster per patient)?
Silhouette Sign Interpretation: A patient has average distance a(i) = 1.8 to points in their own cluster and average distance b(i) = 1.2 to the nearest neighboring cluster. Compute their exact Silhouette score \(s(i)\) and explain what its sign means.
Local Minima & n_init: In Section 25.3.2, our single-start pure-NumPy K-Means achieved inertia 549.53 while Scikit-Learn’s KMeans(n_init=10) achieved 514.06. Why did both converge yet reach different inertias?
K-Means vs. Ward Determinism: If you run AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage="ward") ten times without setting any random_state, will the clusters change between runs? Why or why not?
DBSCAN Label Count Trap: Suppose DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=5).fit_predict(X) returns labels = np.array([-1, 0, 0, -1, 1, 1, 1, -1]). What are the true n_clusters and n_noise, and what bug occurs if you compute len(set(labels))?
Mean-Centering Before SVD: What goes wrong geometrically if you run np.linalg.svd(X) directly on a dataset whose column means are [50, 120, 37] instead of subtracting X.mean(axis=0) first?
Singular Values to Explained Variance: A centered dataset produces singular values \(S = [6, 3, 1]\). Compute the exact explained variance ratio of PC1, PC2, and PC3 by hand (as fractions or decimals).
Standardized Reconstruction MSE Identity: After standardizing 10 clinical features, you keep \(k = 4\) principal components whose cumulative explained variance ratio is 0.8200. Without running Python, what is the exact mean squared reconstruction error np.mean((X_scaled - X_hat) ** 2)?
t-SNE Scientific Caveat: A colleague runs 2D TSNE on gene expression data, runs K-Means on the 2D t-SNE coordinates, and claims “Cluster A is 3x wider than Cluster B, so Cluster A is biologically more heterogeneous.” Identify the two methodological errors in that claim.

25.8 Stage 8 — Complete Annotated Solutions & Debugging Post-Mortem

25.8.1 A. Concept & Execution Trace Test Key

Roughly 99.99% (\(10{,}000 / 10{,}001 \approx 99.99\%\)) of squared Euclidean distance comes from Feature A, completely drowning out Feature B until both are standardized.
Inertia strictly decreases as \(k\) grows; at \(k = n\), every point sits at its own centroid so inertia equals 0.0—a useless overfitted partition!
\(s(i) = (1.2 - 1.8) / \max(1.8, 1.2) = -0.6 / 1.8 = \mathbf{-0.3333}\). A negative silhouette means point \(i\) is closer on average to a neighboring cluster than to its own cluster (likely misassigned).
K-Means optimizes a non-convex objective with multiple local minima. One random draw can trap centroids in a higher-inertia local basin (549.53), whereas n_init=10 with k-means++ explores 10 smart starts and selects the lowest-inertia basin (514.06).
No—Ward agglomerative clustering is 100% deterministic because it merges pairs strictly by minimum variance increase from the full pairwise distance matrix (no random centroid seeding).
True n_clusters = 2 (labels 0 and 1) and n_noise = 3 (the three -1 entries). Calling len(set(labels)) returns 3, erroneously counting -1 noise as a third cluster.
Without mean-centering, the first singular vector points from the origin (0, 0, 0) straight toward the data cloud’s mean vector [50, 120, 37], inflating PC1’s variance ratio instead of capturing covariance around the center.
Squared singular values are \([36, 9, 1]\), summing to \(46\). Therefore: \(\text{EVR}_1 = 36/46 \approx \mathbf{0.7826}\), \(\text{EVR}_2 = 9/46 \approx \mathbf{0.1957}\), and \(\text{EVR}_3 = 1/46 \approx \mathbf{0.0217}\).
On standardized features (unit variance per column), reconstruction MSE equals \(1 - 0.8200 = \mathbf{0.18000}\)!
First, t-SNE distorts cluster sizes and global distances to equalize local densities—visual spread on a t-SNE plot does not measure biological variance. Second, running K-Means on 2D t-SNE axes clusters a distorted nonlinear visualization rather than the true standardized feature or PCA space.



25.8.2 B. Annotated Solutions — Guided To-Dos (Mirrored in 02_guided_todos_SOLUTION.ipynb)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# To-Do 25.1
def kmeans_from_scratch(X, k, max_iter=50, seed=42):
    """Run pure-NumPy K-Means and return (labels, centroids, inertia)."""
    X_arr = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    init_idx = rng.choice(len(X_arr), size=k, replace=False)
    centroids = X_arr[init_idx].copy()
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        dists = ((X_arr[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :]) ** 2)
        labels = np.argmin(dists.sum(axis=2), axis=1).astype(int)
        new_c = centroids.copy()
        for cid in range(k):
            mask = labels == cid
            if np.any(mask):
                new_c[cid] = X_arr[mask].mean(axis=0)
        if np.allclose(new_c, centroids):
            centroids = new_c
            break
        centroids = new_c
    dists = ((X_arr[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :]) ** 2)
    labels = np.argmin(dists.sum(axis=2), axis=1).astype(int)
    inertia = float(np.sum((X_arr - centroids[labels]) ** 2))
    return labels, centroids, inertia

# To-Do 25.2
def evaluate_k_range(X_scaled, k_values, seed=42):
    """Sweep k_values with KMeans and return inertia/silhouette table."""
    rows = []
    for k in k_values:
        km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=seed)
        labels = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)
        sil = silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels)
        rows.append({
            "k": int(k),
            "inertia": round(float(km.inertia_), 4),
            "silhouette": round(float(sil), 4),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# To-Do 25.3
def fit_agglomerative_ward(X_scaled, n_clusters=3):
    """Fit Ward agglomerative clustering and summarize silhouette/sizes."""
    model = AgglomerativeClustering(
        n_clusters=n_clusters, linkage="ward"
    )
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    unique, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True)
    sizes = {int(c): int(n) for c, n in zip(unique, counts)}
    sil = round(float(silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels)), 4)
    return {
        "labels": labels,
        "silhouette": sil,
        "cluster_sizes": sizes,
    }

# To-Do 25.4
def detect_dbscan_anomalies(X_scaled, eps=0.8, min_samples=5):
    """Run DBSCAN and separate dense cluster count from -1 noise count."""
    model = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=min_samples)
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    n_clusters = int(len(set(labels.tolist()) - {-1}))
    n_noise = int(np.sum(labels == -1))
    return {
        "n_clusters": n_clusters,
        "n_noise": n_noise,
        "labels": labels,
    }

# To-Do 25.5
def pca_from_scratch_svd(X, n_components=2):
    """Center X, run SVD, and return (X_projected, explained_var_ratio)."""
    X_arr = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    X_c = X_arr - X_arr.mean(axis=0)
    _, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_c, full_matrices=False)
    X_proj = X_c @ Vt[:n_components].T
    evr = (S ** 2) / np.sum(S ** 2)
    return X_proj, evr[:n_components]

# To-Do 25.6
def components_for_variance_target(X_scaled, target_var=0.90):
    """Return smallest int k reaching target_var cumulative variance."""
    pca = PCA().fit(X_scaled)
    cum_var = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
    return int(np.argmax(cum_var >= target_var) + 1)


25.8.3 C. Annotated Solutions — Chapter 25 Coding Exam (Mirrored in 03_coding_exam_SOLUTION.ipynb)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Exam Task 25.1 (30 pts)
def select_optimal_k_silhouette(X, k_range, seed=42):
    """Standardize X, sweep k_range, and pick k maximizing silhouette."""
    X_sc = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
    rows = []
    for k in k_range:
        km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=seed)
        labels = km.fit_predict(X_sc)
        sil = silhouette_score(X_sc, labels)
        rows.append({
            "k": int(k),
            "inertia": round(float(km.inertia_), 4),
            "silhouette": round(float(sil), 4),
        })
    table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    best = table.loc[table["silhouette"].idxmax()]
    return {
        "best_k": int(best["k"]),
        "best_silhouette": round(float(best["silhouette"]), 4),
        "table": table,
    }

# Exam Task 25.2 (35 pts)
def district_risk_phenotyping(clinic_df, n_clusters=3, seed=42):
    """Aggregate district triage profiles, scale, and cluster."""
    agg = clinic_df.groupby("district", as_index=False).agg(
        mean_temp=("temp_c", "mean"),
        mean_sbp=("systolic_bp", "mean"),
        mean_hb=("hemoglobin_g_dl", "mean"),
        urgent_rate=(
            "triage_priority", lambda s: (s != "Routine").mean()
        ),
    )
    cols = ["mean_temp", "mean_sbp", "mean_hb", "urgent_rate"]
    X_sc = StandardScaler().fit_transform(agg[cols].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=n_clusters, n_init=10, random_state=seed)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X_sc).astype(int)
    agg["cluster"] = labels
    sil = round(float(silhouette_score(X_sc, labels)), 4)
    return {
        "district_clusters": agg,
        "silhouette": sil,
    }

# Exam Task 25.3 (35 pts)
def pca_clinical_compression_audit(X, variance_threshold=0.85):
    """Scale X, pick PCs for variance_threshold, and audit recon MSE."""
    X_sc = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
    full_pca = PCA().fit(X_sc)
    cum = np.cumsum(full_pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
    k = int(np.argmax(cum >= variance_threshold) + 1)
    pca_k = PCA(n_components=k)
    Z = pca_k.fit_transform(X_sc)
    X_hat = pca_k.inverse_transform(Z)
    cum_var = round(float(np.sum(pca_k.explained_variance_ratio_)), 4)
    top_idx = int(np.argmax(np.abs(pca_k.components_[0])))
    mse = round(float(np.mean((X_sc - X_hat) ** 2)), 5)
    return {
        "n_components": k,
        "cumulative_variance": cum_var,
        "top_pc1_feature_idx": top_idx,
        "reconstruction_mse": mse,
    }


25.8.4 D. Debugging Post-Mortem: Top 3 Chapter 25 Failure Modes

Running Euclidean Clustering or PCA on Unscaled Units: Leaving raw features unstandardized lets large-unit variables (age_years variance 451.44 vs. temp_c variance 0.60) monopolize both cluster boundaries and PC1 loadings. Always apply StandardScaler() before K-Means, Ward, DBSCAN, or PCA unless all features share identical physical units.
Miscounting DBSCAN -1 Noise or Crashing silhouette_score: Forgetting - {-1} turns DBSCAN outliers into a phantom cluster, and calling silhouette_score when only one cluster exists immediately raises ValueError. Always separate noise counts first and verify at least two clusters exist before scoring.
Forgetting Mean-Centering or np.abs(...) in PCA Analysis: Running np.linalg.svd without subtracting column means points PC1 toward the global mean rather than maximum variance, while taking np.argmax(pca.components_[0]) without np.abs(...) misses strong negative loadings because PCA eigenvector signs are arbitrary.

section: 26.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Notebooks Break in Peer Review and Production
text:
26.1 Stage 1 — First-Principles Intuition: Why Notebooks Break in Peer Review and Production
Across Chapters 21–25, you trained linear models, regularized regressions, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting ensembles, clustering algorithms, and explainability audits. Yet more than half of published clinical ML papers suffer from subtle methodological leakage that silently inflates reported ROC-AUC before the model ever touches a new clinic.
Four production engineering failures account for nearly every collapse between a promising Jupyter experiment and real-world deployment:

Preprocessing Leakage Across Folds: Imputing missing hemoglobin with the entire dataset’s median or fitting StandardScaler before train_test_split leaks test-set distribution statistics into training. Wrapping every preprocessing step inside a Scikit-Learn Pipeline guarantees that medians, means, and category vocabularies are learned exclusively on each training fold.
Wrong Cross-Validation Splitter for the Study Design: Randomly splitting households from the same Bangladesh DHS primary sampling unit (cluster_id) lets a model memorize village-level wealth patterns instead of generalizing to unseen communities (GroupKFold). Likewise, randomly shuffling weekly dengue surveillance rows lets a model peek at next week’s monsoon outbreak to predict last week (TimeSeriesSplit).
Tuning Optimism Bias (Reporting GridSearchCV.best_score_): When you evaluate 20 hyperparameter combinations via 5-fold CV and publish the highest CV score as your model’s generalization performance, you have overfitted the validation folds! Nested Cross-Validation separates hyperparameter selection (inner loop) from unbiased performance estimation (outer loop).
Training–Serving Skew (Saving Bare Models Without Preprocessing): Saving only a trained LogisticRegression object while keeping sentinel-999 cleanup, median imputation, and one-hot encoding scattered across notebook cells guarantees silent bugs in production. Serializing the entire fitted Pipeline with joblib locks preprocessing and model weights into one atomic artifact.







NoteMental Model — One Pipeline, Two Nested Loops, One Artifact



Think of a production ML workflow as three nested protective shells:

Inner Shell (ColumnTransformer + Pipeline): Turns messy raw clinical rows (containing 999, NaN, and unseen districts) into clean numeric tensors with zero leakage.
Middle Shell (Study-Matched CV & Nested CV): Evaluates the entire tuning procedure on held-out clusters, future epi-weeks, or untouched outer folds so reported ROC-AUC / RMSE is reviewer-proof.
Outer Shell (joblib Serialization): Packages the refitted winning Pipeline into a single reproducible file verified for bit-exact prediction parity.

WarningTwo Silent Scikit-Learn Traps to Watch For




Unseen Test Categories: OneHotEncoder defaults to handle_unknown="error", which crashes inference the instant a new district or clinic tier appears at test time. Always set handle_unknown="ignore" and sparse_output=False (required by dense-input models like HistGradientBoostingClassifier).

    GroupKFold,
    RandomizedSearchCV,

    TimeSeriesSplit,
    cross_val_score,

import sharukh_tutor as tutor

mch_raw = tutor.load_data("mch_survey_sample", as_pandas=True)
